sources.title: Sam Altman: How to succeed with a startup (YC talk)
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman - How to Succeed with a Startup
sources.summary: Sam Altman's YC talk argues success tracks how good your product is, measured by word-of-mouth. He covers choosing fast-growing markets, spotting real vs fake trends, building evangelical founders and bias-to-action teams, keeping momentum, and where startups beat big companies.

principles.text: Success approximates how good your product is: build something so good people spontaneously tell friends.
principles.quote: the degree to which you're successful approximates the degree to which you build a product that is so good people spontaneously tell their friends about it

principles.text: If you can't explain what you do simply and get at least some people interested, that signals unclear thinking or too small a need.
principles.quote: if you can't explain in a few words what you do and if people don't if at least some people don't say oh that's pretty interesting that's usually a mistake

principles.text: Pick a small market growing very fast rather than judging only by today's TAM; ride the elevator up.
principles.quote: the most important startups they are the ones that I start in small markets that are growing very very quickly

principles.text: Tell real trends from fake ones by usage: early adopters use real trends obsessively and tell friends; fake trends get bought but not used.
principles.quote: a fake trend is one where people may buy the product but don't use it or at least not enough

principles.text: Never lose momentum; keep a short, predictable winning cadence, because lost momentum is hard to recover.
principles.quote: startups survive on their own momentum if you have momentum people keep delivering results beyond what they think they're capable of

principles.text: Hire people with a bias to action who say 'I've got it' and adapt fast, since you never have enough data.
principles.quote: you want people to have a bias towards action startups especially in their early days often win by moving very quickly

sources.title: How to start a startup: the four areas to excel at (Lecture 1, part 1)
sources.originalTitle: Lecture 1 - How to Start a Startup (Sam Altman, Dustin Moskovitz)
sources.summary: Sam Altman opens YC's startup class by framing success as idea, product, team and execution, with luck as a huge multiplier. He argues that ideas matter more than the pivot-everything culture suggests, and that great ideas should be evaluated on market, growth and defensibility, not just the product.

principles.text: Startup success needs four things done well: great idea, product, team and execution; luck still swings the outcome enormously.
principles.quote: إذن المجالات الأربعة: تحتاج فكرة عظيمة، منتج عظيم، فريق عظيم وتنفيذ عظيم.

principles.text: Only start a company because a specific problem compels you and a company is the best way to solve it; passion for the problem comes first.
principles.quote: يجب أن تبدأ شركة نائشة فقط إذا شعرت أنك مجبر بواسطة مشكلة معينة وأنك تعتقد أن انشاء شركة سيكون أفضل طريقة لحلها.

principles.text: Great execution matters far more than a good idea, but the pendulum has swung too far: a bad idea stays bad however well executed.
principles.quote: والتنفيذ العظيم هو على الأقل عشر مرات أكثر أهمية و مائة مرة أصعب من الفكرة جيدة. ولكن البندول قد تأرجح أكثر من اللازم هنا. الفكرة سيئة تظل سيئة.

principles.text: Most big companies start with a great idea, not a pivot; successful pivots are toward something the founders themselves wanted.
principles.quote: ولكن معظم الشركات الكبيرة تبدأ بفكرة عظيمة، وليس ب pivot.

principles.text: Evaluating an idea means thinking through market size and growth, growth strategy and defensibility, not just the product.
principles.quote: ويشمل حجم ونمو السوق، استراتيجية النمو للشركة، استراتيجية الدفاع وما إلى ذلك.

principles.text: You may work on the idea for ten years, so the planning exercise itself is worth real time early, even if the plan isn't.
principles.quote: على الرغم من التخطيط نفسه لا قيمة له، فإن ممارسة التخطيط هو حقا عمل ذا قيمة

sources.title: Later-stage startup advice: shifting from building a product to building a company
sources.originalTitle: Later Stage Advice with Sam Altman (How to Start a Startup 2014: Lecture 20)
sources.summary: Sam Altman's final How to Start a Startup lecture covers what founders must handle after product-market fit, around 25 employees: simple management structure, HR, equity, alignment, PR and deal-making. The core shift is that the founder's job moves from building a great product to building a great, long-lived company.

principles.text: Around 25 employees, the founder's main job shifts from building a great product to building a great company.
principles.quote: as the company grows and at about this you know 25 or so employee size um your main job shifts from building a great product to building a great company and it stays there for the rest of your time

principles.text: Keep management structure simple: one clear manager per person. Innovate on product, not on org design.
principles.quote: all you need is for every employee to know who their manager is and every and there should be exactly one and and every manager should know who their direct reports are

principles.text: Delegate decisions, not research: give context and your view, then let the person decide.
principles.quote: here are the things to think about here's what I think but you make this decision I totally trust you um and let me know what you decide that's the delegation that actually works

principles.text: Write down how you do things and why; as founder you effectively write the company's law.
principles.quote: if you write this down it will become law in the company

principles.text: Keep granting equity to employees year after year, with refresher grants, despite investor pushback.
principles.quote: you should think about you know for the next 10 years you're going to be giving out 3 to 5% of the company every year because you just get bigger and bigger

principles.text: Alignment is the single most important word for keeping a growing company productive.
principles.quote: the single word that matters most I think to keep the company productive as it grows is alignment

sources.title: YC Lecture 2: Why cofounder choice is your most important team decision
sources.originalTitle: Lecture 2 - Team and Execution (Sam Altman)
sources.summary: Opening of Sam Altman's YC startup lecture on team and execution. He answers Q&A on spotting fast-growing markets and surviving the workload, then argues the cofounder relationship is the most important one in a company. Picking cofounders casually is a top cause of failure, and solo founding is rarely successful.

principles.text: The cofounder relationship is among the most important in the company, and cofounder conflict is the most common cause of startup failure.
principles.quote: 创业公司失败的最常见的问题 就是合伙人反目成仇

principles.text: Choose cofounders with at least as much care as you hire employees; casual matching is a classic mistake.
principles.quote: 你招员工的时候也不会这么随便， 选合伙人怎么能这么 漫不经心呢？

principles.text: Cofounders you barely know fall apart under pressure, because you have no shared history to carry you through hard times.
principles.quote: 有一届的YC孵化的75个团队里 有九个在YC面试之后又招来新的合伙人 这所有九个团队 都在接下来的一年内分崩离西

principles.text: Solo founders rarely build the biggest outcomes. Find a trusted cofounder, but a bad one is worse than none.
principles.quote: 在YC毕业的最有价值的20个团队里 所有的团队都至少有两个合伙人 所以我们大概在10个单人创业的 项目里，只会投资一个

principles.text: Meet cofounders where you already work or study with people: college, or an interesting company like Facebook or Google.
principles.quote: 如果你在脸谱和谷歌工作一段时间 或者类似的公司 在那里找合伙人几乎像在斯坦福一样容易

principles.text: To spot fast-growing markets, trust your own instincts about what you and your peers increasingly use.
principles.quote: 你们只需要相信直觉 想想你们用的越来越多的是什么

sources.title: Sam Altman on choosing projects: explore cheaply, cut what fails, skip the deferred life plan
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman on Choosing Projects, Creating Value, and Finding Purpose
sources.summary: Altman explains how he picks and prunes projects: try many things cheaply, be brutally honest about what works, then focus. He argues against the deferred life plan, for protecting cognitive load, and for surrounding yourself with ambitious people.

principles.text: Try many projects cheaply and quickly, expect most to fail, and double down only on what really works.
principles.quote: pursue a lot of things as cheaply and quickly as possible and then be very honest with yourself about what's working well and what's not

principles.text: The hard part is cutting what isn't working and focusing down until you reach the one or two things that are.
principles.quote: the hard part is cut all the stuff that's not working and focus down and down until you're eventually focused on the one thing that's really working

principles.text: Be brutally honest about whether a project is truly working versus what you want to believe; it is a trainable muscle.
principles.quote: it takes brutal honesty with yourself about which projects are actually working and which you would like to convince yourself are working

principles.text: Real risk is wasting your career, not short-term failure; most people are too risk-averse and think too small.
principles.quote: what risk actually looks like is that you look back at the end of your career and you're like [ __ ] I wasted it

principles.text: Don't defer what you want to do. Pick one: commit now to the ambitious thing, because people sense half-commitment.
principles.quote: the deferred life plan empirically usually does not work

principles.text: Protect a fixed daily budget of cognitive output from urgent-but-unimportant stuff, and periodically step back to check direction and time horizon.
principles.quote: I have like a like fixed budget of cognitive output per day and I can spend that on whatever but if I let it go on unimportant stuff then I never have time to get to the the really important stuff

sources.title: How OpenAI bet on one idea: Sam Altman on conviction, scale, and building in an AI platform shift
sources.originalTitle: How To Build The Future: Sam Altman
sources.summary: Sam Altman recounts how OpenAI won against better-resourced labs by concentrating on one bet (deep learning that improves with scale) and holding conviction until data said otherwise. He also covers peer groups, speed as a startup's edge in platform shifts, and why AI demos are not businesses.

principles.text: Concentrate on one bet when under-resourced; competitors spread across many things, so pick one and push hard.
principles.quote: we were far less resourced than Deep Mind and others and so we said okay they're going to try a lot of things and we've just got to pick one and really concentrate and that's how we can we can win here

principles.text: Extreme conviction on a single bet is underappreciated by most of the world.
principles.quote: most of the world still does not understand the value of like a fairly extreme level of conviction on one bet

principles.text: Conviction must be paired with truth-seeking: run on conviction without data, then follow the results the moment data arrives.
principles.quote: conviction is great until the moment you have data one way or the other and there are a lot of people who hold on it past the moment of data

principles.text: If something improves with scale, scale it; more is often more.
principles.quote: if you have something that seems like it's getting better with scale I think you should scale it up

principles.text: A startup's number one edge is speed, focus and conviction; build the same day you see a new technology, not in a quarterly plan.
principles.quote: your advantage with speed and focus and conviction and the ability to react to to how fast the technology is moving that is that is the number one edge of a startup kind of ever

principles.text: A new technology doesn't suspend business rules; demos are easy, but you still have to build a durable business.
principles.quote: everyone can build an incredible demo but building a business man that's the brass ring the rules still apply

sources.title: Sam Altman at Startup School 2026: why now is the best time to start a startup, and how to pick your big bet
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman: "Never a Better Time to Do a Startup"
sources.summary: Altman argues startups win when technology moves fast, costs fall and cycle times shrink, all true now thanks to AI. He advises founders to hold contrarian conviction for years, find a small group of believers, be helpful to many people, and ignore cynicism on social media.

principles.text: Startups win when tech moves fast, costs fall, cycle times shrink and incumbents lose their advantage.
principles.quote: startups tend to win when um the sort of like technology landscape is moving very quickly. uh when costs are coming down when cycle times are short and all of those things are happening right now.

principles.text: Find things you have reasonable conviction in that conventional wisdom says are wrong, and endure years of dismissal.
principles.quote: find the things that you can develop like reasonable conviction in that people decide like the conventional wisdom is they're just wrong. And be okay with it taking a long time

principles.text: Being dismissed by experts can be a gift: it means no big competitors while you build.
principles.quote: it was like an incredible gift because it meant we didn't have this like massive competitors and we had time to do our research and build our stuff and build our company.

principles.text: Starting the same startup as everyone else brings hype and funding but rarely the big outcomes; look for a brand new possibility.
principles.quote: if you're starting the same startup as everybody else, it's like you get a lot of hype and you can raise a lot of money, but it's it's sort of like those are much less frequently the big option, the big outcomes.

principles.text: You need only a few believers, not many; if everyone believes your idea, that is a bad sign.
principles.quote: I don't think you need to find a lot of people. And in fact, if everybody believes it, that's also like a bad a bad sign.

principles.text: A clear vision with unclear first steps is fine, but you still must take imperfect steps to get new data.
principles.quote: if the the kind of like highest level vision is clear, but the first few steps are very unclear, that's not a bad thing.

sources.title: Sam Altman: How to Build the Future - picking work, persistence, risk, and long-term thinking
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman : How to Build the Future
sources.summary: Sam Altman, interviewed by his brother Jack, shares advice for young people who want impact: pick work at the intersection of skill, enjoyment and value, work hard early so effort compounds, persist longer than feels comfortable, take real risks, and commit for the very long term.

principles.text: Pick work at the intersection of what you're good at, what you enjoy, and where you can create value for the world.
principles.quote: I think you want to look for the intersection of what you're good at, what you enjoy, and and what where you can create value for the world.

principles.text: Things get done through focus, personal connection, and deep self-belief that your idea will work.
principles.quote: the way things get done in the world are through a combination of focus and personal connection. And the additional point I would make uh after having thought about it for a while is that the third factor is self-belief.

principles.text: Work hard early in your career; effort compounds, and early years set the trajectory.
principles.quote: it's far better to put that time in at the beginning of your career uh than at the end because if you do it at the beginning, you get to benefit from it

principles.text: Most people quit too early. Make give-up decisions internally: stop when you've run out of ideas, not because of external criticism.
principles.quote: it should be an internal not an external decision. um if people aren't using it or if people are saying it's bad, that alone is not a reason to give up.

principles.text: Burnout comes from failure and lack of momentum, not from hard work; momentum is energizing.
principles.quote: burnout actually comes from um failing and things not working. Momentum is really energizing. The lack of momentum is super draining.

principles.text: Time is a remaining arbitrage: commit long-term to great companies and hold forever; strong opinions with flexible details beat random pivots.
principles.quote: one of the few arbitrage opportunities left in the market is time.

sources.title: Sam Altman at YC: Building OpenAI, contrarian conviction, hiring for slope, and why now is the best time to start
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman: The Future of OpenAI, ChatGPT's Origins, and Building AI Hardware
sources.summary: Sam Altman explains how OpenAI nearly didn't start, why working on a one-of-one idea concentrates talent, and why startups should avoid the five crowded AI ideas. He also covers hiring for slope over resume, the product overhang of reasoning models, and the resilience required to keep going.

principles.text: Ambitious things seem impossible; it takes a core of people looking each other in the eye and deciding to do it. When in doubt, lean in.
principles.quote: it really takes a core of people that like sit in a room, look each other in the eye and say, "All right, let's do this." Uh, and those are like very important moments and I think when in doubt, you should lean into them.

principles.text: Doing a one-of-one thing concentrates talent and belief; doing what everyone else does makes it hard to recruit or inspire.
principles.quote: If you are doing the same thing as everyone else, it is very hard to concentrate talent and it's very hard to get people to like really believe in a mission. And if you're doing like a oneofone thing, uh you you have a really nice tailwind there.

principles.text: Big companies start tiny. Pick a market where a big future is possible, then take one dumb step after another for a long time.
principles.quote: pick a market where it seems like there's some version of the future where it could be big if it works. But other than that, it's like one dumb foot in front of the other for a long time.

principles.text: People crowd into the same few ideas. Enduring companies usually aren't doing what everyone else is, which buys time to find the product before defensibility.
principles.quote: the best the most enduring companies are usually not doing the same thing as everybody else. And that gives you time to figure out what the great product is, how to build the technology before you have to answer the defensibility question.

principles.text: Hire smart, driven, curious, self-motivated people with a track record and team fit; early on, favor scrappy builders over polished senior resumes and look at slope.
principles.quote: I would take like young scrappy but clearly like get stuff done um over the person who has like the extremely polished track record.

principles.text: When the industry's clock cycle shifts, startups win by iterating faster and cheaper than big companies, since everyone faces the same disruption.
principles.quote: when the clock cycle of the industry changes this much startups almost always win and we've probably never seen it change this much.

sources.title: Sam Altman on starting startups in the AI era: exponentials, chaos, focus and ambition
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman - How to Start a Startup
sources.summary: Altman explains why startups have the biggest edge when the ground is shifting, and why founders should plan for models that are smarter and cheaper in a few years. He covers handling chaos, killing good projects to back the one that works, holding few convictions, and hiring and promoting people for speed.

principles.text: Startups have their biggest edge when costs and cycle times are collapsing and the ground is shifting.
principles.quote: I think startups are they have the biggest edge when the ground is shifting the most um and when costs are coming down rapidly and cycle times are coming down rapidly.

principles.text: Plan for what will be possible in 2-4 years, not just today's easy wins; scaling laws keep going.
principles.quote: being willing to truly internalize the fact that scaling laws are going to continue and planning for the things that are not possible or economical this month but will be possible in 2 years, four years, whatever.

principles.text: Handling startup chaos is learned through repetition, not taught; each survived crisis makes the next easier.
principles.quote: I don't think it's teachable. I think it's only learnable.

principles.text: Hold a small number of deep convictions about the future, stay flexible on the rest, and plan forward from the present.
principles.quote: having just a small number of things that you deeply believe about the future and being very flexible on the rest. Um, and staying very true to the core is is helpful.

principles.text: When something is really working, kill other good projects to put compute and people behind the best one.
principles.quote: there have been a lot of quite important moments in OpenAI history where one thing started to really work and we killed other good things to make the best thing work better.

principles.text: Invest in your strengths rather than fixing weaknesses; you can hire great people in areas you don't understand.
principles.quote: I am a big believer in you should try to get better at your strengths and the whole like obsession with I'm going to get better at the things that I'm just not good at at all and never going to be good at huge trap.

sources.title: Sam Altman on YC, founder traits, slow hiring and the 10% weekly growth rule (Blitzscaling 02)
sources.originalTitle: Blitzscaling 02: Sam Altman on Y Combinator and What Makes The Best Founders
sources.summary: Altman explains how Y Combinator works as a network-effect business and what separates the best founders: clarity, determination and speed. He argues for hiring as late as possible, focusing on product love over liking, growing about 10% a week, and avoiding "fake work" like fundraising theater and networking events.

principles.text: The best startups hire the fewest people; delay your first non-founder hire as long as you can.
principles.quote: أفضل شركاتنا الناشئة هي التي توظف أقل عدد

principles.text: Product focus means building something a few users love, not something many users merely like.
principles.quote: التركيز على المنتج يعني التركيز على الحب لا الإعجاب، وقضاء وقتك في كتابة الكود والتحدث إلى المستخدمين.

principles.text: Early on, a company should improve a core metric about 10% every week; the compounding is huge.
principles.quote: يجب على أي شركة أن تتحسن في شيء ما بنسبة 10%أسبوعياً في مراحلها الأولى.

principles.text: The prime directive of running a startup is never to lose momentum.
principles.quote: التوجيه الأساسي لإدارة شركة ناشئة هو ألا تفقد الزخم أبدًا

principles.text: Do the boring real work (building, talking to users, sales), not what would make good TV.
principles.quote: قم بالعمل الذي سيتم حذفه في غرفة المونتاج.

principles.text: Great ideas often look bad at first; conviction against consensus is where outsized returns come from.
principles.quote: فكرة الأفكار العظيمة التي تبدو سيئة هي بالتأكيد ما أدى إلى عوائد استثنائية في الاستثمار في الشركات الناشئة وتأسيسها.

sources.title: Office Hours with Sam Altman: first B2B customers, networks, and picking what to build
sources.originalTitle: Office Hours with Sam Altman
sources.summary: Sam Altman answers HN questions on getting the first 20 B2B customers, expanding your network, youth as a startup advantage, cofounder trust, and spotting the next platform shift. His consistent theme is to build something impressive and let a strong network pull customers in.

principles.text: Instead of chasing customers outside your network, expand your network and pull companies toward you.
principles.quote: الأخرى هي توسيع شبكتك وجذب الشركات إليها. وأعتقد أن هذا هو النهج الذي رأيته يعمل بشكل أفضل.

principles.text: Build something impressive and your network comes to you; a finished product makes cold emails stand out.
principles.quote: إذا بنيت شيئاً مثيراً للإعجاب، فإن شبكة علاقاتك ستأتي إليك تلقائياً.

principles.text: Early B2B startups in YC mostly sell to other YC companies for their first ~20 customers; sell into your community first.
principles.quote: تقريباً جميعهم يبيعون حصرياً لشركات YC في بداياتهم، أو بشكل شبه حصري لأول 20 عميلاً.

principles.text: Never start a company with someone you haven't worked with on a project; six months is the minimum.
principles.quote: لن أبدأ شركة مع شخص لا أعرفه مسبقاً.

principles.text: Develop your own convictions about what matters rather than letting others dictate what to work on.
principles.quote: أعتقد أنه من المهم جداً أن تطور قناعاتك الخاصة.

principles.text: Wait for deep per-user daily usage, not total shipments, before betting on a new platform like VR/AR.
principles.quote: سأتجاهل إجمالي الشحنات للواقع الافتراضي والمعزز، وسأنتظر حتى نصل إلى نقطة يبني فيها شخص ما جهازًا أو برنامجًا يستخدمه الناس بكثافة يوميًا بمجرد الحصول عليه.

sources.title: Sam Altman on how to get funded by Y Combinator and build a startup on growth
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman | How to Get Funded by Y Combinator
sources.summary: Sam Altman, then new YC president, explains how to start a startup: let an idea be a project before a company, set weekly growth goals, execute fast, and understand users. He also covers how YC picks founders, when to raise money, and why he funds smart, determined people with clear vision.

principles.text: Let the idea be a project first; only form a company once you have conviction in what you will build.
principles.quote: take the time to figure out uh what what you're going to do and let it be a project before it's a company

principles.text: Set a weekly growth goal early; one growth metric shapes the company and answers every question.
principles.quote: it's one metric uh to optimize for and it's one way to answer every question and the startups that do this usually succeed and startups that don't do this argue about everything else

principles.text: Deeply understand your users and iterate quickly; startups that skip this fail.
principles.quote: understand your users is one of the most important pieces of startup advice in the world a startup that does not do this will fail a startup that does this often succeeds

principles.text: Speed of execution is the best signal of a great founder; slow founders always have great excuses.
principles.quote: the best Founders you see the next day and they're like I did all of those things and these others

principles.text: Raise capital only when you must or when it is easy; small capital is still a win.
principles.quote: you generally you want to raise Capital either when you have to or when it's really easy

principles.text: Bet on the smartest, most determined people with the clearest vision, even if you don't yet see why it will be big.
principles.quote: just fund the smartest most determined people you can find with the clearest Vision even if you don't understand yet why it's going to be a big deal

sources.title: Sam Altman at Waterloo: What makes great founders, hiring on values, and moving fast
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman Startup School Video | Waterloo Engineering
sources.summary: Altman's Startup School talk covers what separates great founders (determination, focus, self-belief, clear communication), why to hire on values first and skills last, and why iteration speed and a product a few users love matter most. He also critiques a live pitch: say what you do in one sentence upfront.

principles.text: Determination, not intellect or domain expertise, is the rare and limiting trait of great founders, and it can be learned.
principles.quote: I always figure it out and I never give up would have been high on the list

principles.text: Founders must communicate what they do concisely and clearly, ideally in about 25 words; weak communicators rarely succeed.
principles.quote: they were able to very concisely and clearly communicate what they were doing in like 25 words

principles.text: Hire values first, aptitude second, specific skills third; most people reverse this order.
principles.quote: go for values first aptitude second and specific skills third

principles.text: Prefer a small number of users who love you over many who mildly like you, then find more of them.
principles.quote: it is more important to have a small number of users that love you rather than a large number of users that like you a lot

principles.text: Hold the hiring bar very high; two or three great people beat ten warm bodies.
principles.quote: it's better to like hire two or three great people than ten warm bodies

principles.text: Iteration speed compounds; a fast product cycle beats competitors with slow ones, including in hard tech.
principles.quote: if your iteration cycle is a week and your competitors is three months you know you're going to leave them in the dust very quickly

sources.title: How to start a hard tech startup: act like a software startup with 10% weekly gains
sources.originalTitle: How to Start a Hard Tech Startup with Sam Altman @ MIT
sources.summary: Altman argues hard tech founders should not think the rules differ: find a small, shippable first project, get 10% better every week, and serve a real customer fast. He covers why hard companies face less competition, why cost and cycle time matter, and failure modes like raising too much money and short-term investors.

principles.text: Hard tech startups should look more like software startups, not less; the normal startup rules still apply, if anything more.
principles.quote: don't think you're different from a software startup don't think that the rules don't apply to you they still do in fact if anything they do even a little bit more

principles.text: Find a small initial project with a real test in the world and get 10% better every week; momentum compounds.
principles.quote: if you can just get whatever you're working on no matter how small the subset is to be 10 better every week this is the whole secret of software startups

principles.text: Take detours: build intermediate products for real customers instead of racing straight to the grand mission.
principles.quote: more hard tech startups fail because they have this grand plan that sounds great in the press and they never do anything then have failed because they started with an initial project it was too small

principles.text: Cost and cycle time are the key factors for whether a field suits a startup; startups win where these fall dramatically.
principles.quote: cost for low and cycle time is fast and I think those are the two most important factors for software to be able to dominate or startups to be able to nominate in an area

principles.text: Too much money can ruin culture and focus; companies raising $40M+ Series As failed more often than average.
principles.quote: a lot of money can ruin cultures and uh you know sort of make you unfocused and try to do too many things at once

principles.text: Startups survive on momentum; build a culture of winning early, even with tiny wins, to attract and motivate people.
principles.quote: startups basically survive on their own momentum a start that is winning to keep winning they started losing

sources.title: How to raise VC money as a technical founder: Sam Altman at Startup School 08
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman at Startup School 08
sources.summary: Altman, drawing on raising Loopt's Series A from NEA and Sequoia, explains when to raise, how to run a parallel process with 6-8 firms, what VCs look for, and which terms matter. His core point is that technical founders who understand product hold real leverage, and alternatives are the name of the game.

principles.text: Avoid raising money if you can; the longer you wait, the better your product and valuation.
principles.quote: the longer you can wait uh the more likely you are to figure out the product that'll work the more likely you are to have things running well and you'll get a better valuation

principles.text: Funding is not success; building a great product and reaching consumers is.
principles.quote: raising money is not how you become successful like building a great product and getting into consumers is how you do that

principles.text: Run the fundraising process in parallel; competing alternatives are your only leverage, and speed matters.
principles.quote: the only way you ever have any leverage from investors as as a company is if they feel like they're going to lose the deal to other investors

principles.text: Make investors believe you have a great alternative you will probably take; it makes them act faster.
principles.quote: the key to doing deals in general is to make everyone feel like you have a great alternative that you're probably going to take and that makes them want it more and more likely to act faster

principles.text: Don't let fundraising consume the whole team; one person should spend about half their time on it.
principles.quote: i think it's important to have one person in the company focus on it and spend like half their time on it

principles.text: Pitch a big growing market, a great team and a product that fits; tell a big story, not an incremental one.
principles.quote: these guys don't want to hear something incremental they want to hear how you are doing something that really will become just a massive deal

sources.title: Sam Altman's Startup Investor School: invest for homeruns, back founders, ignore the crowd
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman - Startup Investor School Day 1
sources.summary: Sam Altman lays out how he invests in startups: optimize for the power law, ask how big it could be before what could go wrong, and pick exceptional founders over ideas. He also covers reputation, real vs. fake trends, and why market size in ten years matters more than today.

principles.text: Angel investing is about the size of your biggest win, not your failure rate; 95% can fail if one returns a billion.
principles.quote: you can have 95% of your investments fail if one of them returns a billion dollars and you'll be totally happy

principles.text: Ask 'how big could this be if it works?' before 'what could go wrong?', or you filter out the giants.
principles.quote: the first question is how big could this be if it works can I imagine this founder this idea this market supporting a you know massive massive company

principles.text: Don't outsource decisions to other investors; asking what you understand that others don't is your edge.
principles.quote: what do I understand that other people don't

principles.text: Prefer a small market growing fast over a huge market today; judge market size ten years out.
principles.quote: you should prefer a small market growing super quickly to a very large market today

principles.text: Execution speed predicts founder success; watch how fast founders iterate between check-ins.
principles.quote: this relentless cadence of execution is incredibly predictive of success

principles.text: Reputation with founders is how you win deals now; don't squeeze dying companies for small returns.
principles.quote: it is way more important to your future success as an investor that founders like you and say that investor did the right thing by me

sources.title: Sam Altman at StrictlyVC: founder selection, YC's edge, and OpenAI's capped-profit bet
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman in conversation with StrictlyVC
sources.summary: Altman explains how YC picks founders (clear communication, relentless work, excellence at every step), why open applications and public advice drove YC's growth, and how he thinks about OpenAI's mission, staged GPT-2 release, and capped-profit structure.

principles.text: Clear communication is the hardest-to-fake founder trait and most of a CEO's job.
principles.quote: to be an effective CEO like 95% of your job is effective communication and evangelism and telling the story of the company to people you're trying to hire and retain and sell to

principles.text: Founder selection needs little data: first minutes reveal thought process and reaction to being pushed.
principles.quote: we could make decisions that are 90 percent or 95 percent as good as we make with the 10-minute interview in five minutes

principles.text: Be honest that a hyperscale startup demands extreme work; pretending otherwise hurts founders and the ecosystem.
principles.quote: it does us no good and in fact is actively hurtful us being like the ecosystem of of Silicon Valley to pretend like you can start a startup that is going for hyper scale and not have to work extremely hard

principles.text: Open applications plus publishing all advice grew the number of good companies; global growth compounds via local success stories.
principles.quote: anyone in the world could apply and they do and sometimes they're really great and we put in the effort to find them and I think that plus another one of our very few innovations which is we don't keep any of our advice secret

principles.text: Ask early how a startup will gather concentrated talent; capital is abundant, talent is the scarce input.
principles.quote: the only thing that is cheap and easy when capital is this abundant is capital concentrated talent

principles.text: Grade founders on excelling at every step given the hand they were dealt, regardless of age.
principles.quote: whatever hand life tell you to play you have done as well as anyone we can imagine and so we grade harder unlike a 40 year old and a 20 year old

sources.title: Sam Altman at Airbnb Tech Talk 2015: Product-first growth, founder signals, long-term holding, small teams
sources.originalTitle: Fireside Chat - Sam Altman President, YCombinator and Mike Curtis, VP of Engineering, Airbnb - 2015
sources.summary: In a 2015 fireside chat, Sam Altman explains what YC looks for in founders (clarity, determination, passion), why great products win long-term, why to focus on users who love you, and why to perfect the product before ramping burn. He also covers small teams for engineering culture and holding investments for the long term.

principles.text: Ignore people who call an idea small or stupid; keep pulling the thread, since exponential growth makes early ideas look small.
principles.quote: people always make the mistake of calling an idea small or stupid because they don't understand how it's going to evolve so my advice on this always is to ignore the people that don't do anything start whatever company you want

principles.text: Founder determination is the top signal: whether they will give up when things get hard.
principles.quote: some evidence that you're not going to give up when things get hard

principles.text: Clarity matters: founders who can say clearly in a few sentences what they do and why can recruit, get press and raise money.
principles.quote: Founders that can express in a few sentences very clearly what they're doing and why that's really important that's something we look for

principles.text: Make a product a small number of users love rather than one many users merely like.
principles.quote: it's more important to make a product that a small number small number of users love than something that a lot of users like you know like six out of 10

principles.text: Asking happy users how to get them to use it more is a far better strategy than chasing churned users.
principles.quote: I think it's like a 10x better strategy to go to the people that are using it and say how can I get you to use it more

principles.text: Get the product great first, then ramp up burn; scaling spend before the product works wastes sales and marketing dollars.
principles.quote: it's almost never the wrong choice to get the product great first and then ramp up the burn

sources.title: Sam Altman on YC: loved products, retaining talent, delegation, and safe fundraising
sources.originalTitle: Startups | Sam Altman
sources.summary: Altman explains what YC teaches startups (make something a few users love, then grow with momentum) and common seed-to-Series A mistakes: neglecting retention, mis-delegating, and over-optimizing fundraising headlines. He also covers how YC picks founders in 10 minutes, what predicts breakouts, and why he's bullish on AI.

principles.text: Start with a product a small number of users truly love, then grow it with real, retained users.
principles.quote: build a product that a small number of users really love and then let's work together to figure how to grow it

principles.text: Momentum is everything in a startup; once lost it is very hard to recover.
principles.quote: momentum is everything in a start-up if if you ever take your foot off the gas and lose momentum it is incredibly difficult to recover from that

principles.text: Past seed stage, treat retaining talent as much your job as recruiting it. Give top people CEO time, new tasks and proactive comp.
principles.quote: if you don't shift to viewing retaining talent as as much of your job is recruiting talent you eventually have some level of a disaster on your hands

principles.text: Don't delegate the one or two most critical areas of the business; keep them yourself and delegate the rest.
principles.quote: whatever you think the critical piece of the business is the one or maybe two most critical pieces hold on to those yourself

principles.text: Raise with a margin of safety: don't chase the top headline valuation or run out of money before the next raise.
principles.quote: our general advice is don't push it to the limit

principles.text: Reference-check a new investor as carefully as a VP hire, since investors are far harder to fire.
principles.quote: you should treat bring out a new investor with at least as much care and thought as you would treat hiring a VP

sources.title: Sam Altman at Stanford (2015): founder traits, hiring late, pivots, and avoiding fake work
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman 2015 Definitive Startup Insights | Exclusive First Interview
sources.summary: Sam Altman, then YC president, explains what he looks for in founders and how startups win or fail. Themes: clarity of vision, speed, determination, co-founder dynamics, hiring as late as possible, pursuing good ideas that look bad, getting users who love you, and avoiding fake work.

principles.text: Founders must explain clearly what they do and why; unclear vision means they can't recruit, sell, or think well.
principles.quote: if the founder can't explain it clearly to us then a they're never going to be able to recruit hire sell talk to the press anything

principles.text: Hire as late as possible; early employees add burn, inertia and politics and reduce effectiveness.
principles.quote: our best startups hire the least and our worst startups are the ones that want to say I have 10 people working for me I'm really cool

principles.text: Chase great ideas that look bad, not derivatives of the last winner; look for a shift in the world.
principles.quote: what is the next hundred billion company that has nothing to do with the last um what is the shift in the world

principles.text: Ignore everyone except users; launch quickly so users who depend on you give you conviction.
principles.quote: you can ignore everybody if you you can ignore everybody except users

principles.text: Focus on product means building love in a small group of users, not mild liking from many.
principles.quote: focus on product means focus on love not like

principles.text: Avoid fake work like fundraising, press and networking; the real work is building and talking to users.
principles.quote: no company has ever become great because they were great at fundraising

sources.title: Sam Altman on OpenAI: non-consensus bets, killing good ideas, and iterative deployment
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman on Building OpenAI & Betting on the Impossible
sources.summary: Altman explains how startup investing shaped his approach to running OpenAI: back non-consensus, high-conviction bets, focus compute and talent on the one great thing, and ship early to learn. He also covers platform strategy, why economic adoption of AI is slower than expected, and lessons from YC, Paul Graham and Peter Thiel.

principles.text: Find the high-leverage difficult problem that continues the exponential and put your effort there.
principles.quote: Philosophically I'm very inclined to say you know try to find the like the high leverage difficult problem that will continue the exponential

principles.text: Think in power laws: take high-risk bets that are hugely valuable if they work.
principles.quote: high risk bets are okay as long as you take the ones where if they work it's super valuable

principles.text: Back founders who truly think differently and will stand by unpopular convictions, not a thin veneer on the herd's idea.
principles.quote: someone who just thinks differently than most other people and has [clears throat] is is willing to stand by convictions that are very unpopular may well be wrong but if right like at least they're going to be really right

principles.text: Killing good ideas to focus on the great one is the hardest lesson; limited compute and people force the choice.
principles.quote: killing the good ideas, like sacrificing the good ideas to go after the great ideas is is kind of the hardest lesson for any entrepreneur or business to learn.

principles.text: Ship an embarrassing v1 early and improve it from real customer feedback; speed and iteration correlate with success.
principles.quote: I'm astonished looking back at all of my data points at YC Founders over the years how much the ability the the like moving fast and being iterative correlates with success.

principles.text: Learn more from your successes than failures; apply the lessons of what worked.
principles.quote: the lessons I learned from success were very good and I should have applied those more. And the lessons I learned from failure were either fairly generic and I kind of already knew them or got in the way of something else.

sources.title: Sam Altman at DevDay: Dots, builder-first platforms, and why people always want more
sources.originalTitle: How Sam Altman Actually Uses Dots to Run OpenAI and His Life
sources.summary: Altman explains how OpenAI's new proactive assistant "Dots" gave him back his deep-work mornings. He argues AI creates a renaissance of builders rather than one all-consuming lab, and that demand for new things is limitless. He also covers speed as the next frontier after cheaper intelligence, and what he looks for as an investor.

principles.text: Demand for new things is limitless, so AI expands work rather than removing it.
principles.quote: أعتقد أن الناس يريدون ببساطة المزيد من الأشياء.

principles.text: The startup basics hold: make something people want, even as team size and leverage change.
principles.quote: عليك أن تصنع شيئاً يريده الناس. كانت هذه النصيحة صالحة منذ 100 عام.

principles.text: Open the platform because most good ideas live outside your own company.
principles.quote: الإيمان العميق بأن هناك أفكاراً جيدة خارج مبنانا أكثر بكثير مما بداخله.

principles.text: Dogfood your thesis: if tools let people build more, build more yourself.
principles.quote: نحن نحاول أن نطبق ما ندعو إليه. وإذا كنا نقول إن هذه الأدوات يمكن أن تجعل الناس أكثر إنتاجية وتبني المزيد ، وأن الناس يريدون المزيد من الأشياء، فمن الأفضل أن نبني المزيد بأنفسنا.

principles.text: Fast responses tighten the iteration loop and change how you build and think.
principles.quote: لم أدرك مدى الاختلاف الذي يحدثه الحصول على استجابات سريعة جداً في حلقة تفكيري التكرارية.

principles.text: Invest in the best founders on ambitious projects and accept high risk with them.
principles.quote: كان البحث عن أفضل المؤسسين الذين يعملون على مشاريع طموحة، وأن أكون مستعداً لتحمل الكثير من المخاطر معهم.

sources.title: Sam Altman on AI adoption, infrastructure-style business models and founder traits (Stripe Sessions)
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman in conversation with Patrick Collison
sources.summary: Altman talks with Patrick Collison about Codex's breakout moment, how OpenAI's management style must evolve, and why he wants OpenAI to be an aligned, low-margin intelligence utility. He also covers what makes companies effective with AI, co-founder dynamics, and what he looks for when investing in founders.

principles.text: Build on the side of AI getting smarter; don't make a business out of patching a model's current weakness.
principles.quote: you as a business want to be on the side of hoping that AI gets smarter.

principles.text: AI adoption works best when the CEO does it first and holds the team to it; it cascades through the company.
principles.quote: if you just do it for the leader of a company, there's like a nice fractal effect throughout the company.

principles.text: Aim to be an aligned infrastructure provider that grows with customers, even at low margin, rather than climbing the stack to capture their value.
principles.quote: I would like us to be an infrastructure provider. I'd be happy for us to be like a forever low margin as long as we can be huge and grow in fast business

principles.text: Concentrate resources behind a conviction rather than spreading them equally to keep the peace, and ignore distractions.
principles.quote: we're going to bet with conviction on this. It's not going to feel totally equal, but this is the right thing.

principles.text: Co-founders who have known each other for a long time are a top predictor of startup success.
principles.quote: One of the things that I had observed at Y Combinator was that one of the biggest predictors of success was had the co-founders known each other for a long time.

principles.text: With AI lowering the cost of building, deep user understanding now matters as much as coding skill when picking founders.
principles.quote: now people who just really deeply understand their users and can't code at all, I like want to fund those people.

sources.title: Sam Altman on focus, contrarian bets, and building OpenAI's compute and product strategy
sources.originalTitle: Sam Altman on AGI, Compute, and Human Agency
sources.summary: In this Arabic-dubbed interview, Altman explains why OpenAI refocused after spreading itself thin, how it raised compute against near-universal skepticism, and why great products and bold missions beat marketing. He also covers moats, shifting bottlenecks, and why the contrarian path is the only one to big outcomes.

principles.text: Do fewer things. Even good projects dilute you when only a few great things are possible.
principles.quote: لم نكن مركزين بما يكفي، ورغم أنها كانت في الواقع أشياء جيدة، إلا أن الخدعة تكمن في أننا في لحظة لا تصدق في التاريخ حيث لا يمكنك القيام إلا بالقليل من الأشياء العظيمة.

principles.text: Big raises work like early fundraising: most say no, you only need one or two yeses.
principles.quote: ذكّرني الأمر فعلياً بجمع التبرعات لشركة ناشئة في مراحلها الأولى. معظم الناس يرفضون، لكنك تحتاج فقط إلى موافقة واحدة أو اثنتين.

principles.text: Outsized success requires doing what others aren't; following the trend early only gets decent results.
principles.quote: أفضل الشركات وأفضل فرص الاستثمار لا تكون أبداً تلك التي تبدو شائعة جداً. يمكنك تحقيق نتائج مقبولة بمجرد اتباع الاتجاه السائد مبكراً قليلاً.

principles.text: If users keep doing something with your product, follow them there. That's how ChatGPT came about.
principles.quote: إذا لاحظت أن مستخدميك يفعلون شيئاً ما، فامضِ في ذلك الطريق.

principles.text: A truly great product markets itself; ChatGPT launched with no marketing campaign.
principles.quote: أنا أؤمن نوعاً ما بأن المنتج الرائع حقاً يسوق لنفسه. لم تكن هناك حملة تسويقية لـ ChatGPT

principles.text: Pick a harder, more important problem. A bold vision also works as a powerful recruiting tool.
principles.quote: أنا أؤمن بهذا بشدة. إنها واحدة من أكثر نصائحي تكراراً لمؤسسي YC، وقد حاولت حقاً تطبيقها في OpenAI. فقط افعل شيئاً أصعب.

sources.title: How to Be Successful: Sam Altman's 13 principles for outlier success
sources.originalTitle: How to Be Successful
sources.summary: Altman distills what he's seen across thousands of founders into 13 ideas: compound yourself, believe in yourself, think independently, get good at sales, take asymmetric risks, focus, work hard, be bold and willful, be hard to compete with, build a network, own equity, and be internally driven. The throughline is long-term compounding leverage plus relentless persistence.

principles.text: Seek compounding: favor step changes and leverage over linear opportunities.
principles.quote: Most people get bogged down in linear opportunities. Be willing to let small opportunities go to focus on potential step changes.

principles.text: Long-term thinking is the biggest competitive advantage because almost nobody does it.
principles.quote: In a world where almost no one takes a truly long-term view, the market richly rewards those who do.

principles.text: Great careers become sales jobs: communicate clearly, believe in what you sell, and show up in person.
principles.quote: My other big sales tip is to show up in person whenever it’s important.

principles.text: Make risk-taking cheap: place small bets with 1x downside and 100x upside, then scale the bet.
principles.quote: Look for small bets you can make where you lose 1x if you’re wrong but make 100x if it works. Then make a bigger bet in that direction.

principles.text: Focus on the right few priorities and execute fast; the right thing matters more than hours.
principles.quote: It is much more important to work on the right thing than it is to work many hours.

principles.text: Own equity rather than sell time, and build things people want at scale.
principles.quote: You get truly rich by owning things that increase rapidly in value.

sources.title: Startup Advice: 95 rules on product, growth, hiring, and fundraising from Sam Altman
sources.originalTitle: Startup Advice
sources.summary: Sam Altman's list of 95 startup rules, mostly heard and some given, written for a new YC batch. Core themes: build something people want, focus on growth and product quality, hire slowly and carefully, move fast, stay frugal, and raise money on clean terms from engaged investors.

principles.text: Spend your time writing code, talking to users, and building the company; most other founder activity is waste.
principles.quote: Write code, talk to users, and build the company (hire the best people you can find, get the culture right, fundraise, close sales, etc.)  Most other things that founders do are a waste of time.

principles.text: Growth solves nearly all problems, but pair it with a destination worth growing toward.
principles.quote: Growth solves (nearly) all problems.

principles.text: Hiring is the most important job: spend a third of your time on it, hire slow, fire fast.
principles.quote: Hire slow; fire fast.  Hiring is the most important thing you do; spend at least a third of your time on it.

principles.text: Better for a few users to love your product than many to sort of like it.
principles.quote: It’s better to have a few users love your product than for a lot of users to sort of like it.

principles.text: Be suspicious of work that isn't building product or getting customers; avoid infrastructure rewrite death spirals.
principles.quote: Be suspicious of any work that is not building product or getting customers.  It’s easy to get sucked into an infrastructure rewrite death spiral.

principles.text: Conflicting advice is everywhere except 'build a great product'; decide quickly and get back to work.
principles.quote: Just make a decision and get back to work.  Product/market fit is what matters.

sources.title: Hard Startups: why ambitious, difficult companies are easier to build than easy ones
sources.originalTitle: Hard Startups
sources.summary: Sam Altman argues that hard startups (needing more money, time, coordination or technology) are often easier to succeed with than easy ones, because they attract talent, help and capital. He advises thinking big, taking a reasonable next step, and committing to a long time horizon.

principles.text: Hard startups are often easier to succeed with than easy ones, provided the problem is valuable if solved.
principles.quote: The most counterintuitive secret about startups is that it’s often easier to succeed with a hard startup than an easy one.

principles.text: Talented people want meaningful work, so a meaningful mission is your best recruiting tool once past the first hires.
principles.quote: But eventually, what you have to recruit with are the mission of the company, the likelihood of massive success, and the quality of the people there.

principles.text: Your startup rises only to the level where it can still attract enough talented people.
principles.quote: your startup will rise to the level where it can no longer attract enough talented people.

principles.text: A hard startup is a tailwind: people rooting for a significant mission help with hiring, advice, partnerships and fundraising.
principles.quote: An easy startup is a headwind; a hard startup is a tailwind.

principles.text: Aim for the most ambitious version of your vision, but always keep a reasonable next step.
principles.quote: You don’t want step one to be incorporating the company and step two to be going to Mars.

principles.text: A 10-year horizon beats the typical 3-year horizon in a world of compounding advantages.
principles.quote: In a world of compounding advantages where most people are operating on a 3 year timeframe and you’re operating on a 10 year timeframe, you’ll have a very large edge.

sources.title: Sam Altman's productivity system: pick the right work, protect your energy, ruthlessly prioritize
sources.originalTitle: Productivity
sources.summary: Altman argues the biggest productivity lever is choosing the right thing to work on, then compounding small gains over a career. He shares his prioritization habits (paper lists, saying no, protected mornings, 15-20 min or 2 hr meetings) and the physical factors (sleep, exercise, nutrition) he credits with a 1.5x boost.

principles.text: Choosing the right thing to work on is the most important productivity factor; speed in a worthless direction is worthless.
principles.quote: Picking the right thing to work on is the most important element of productivity and usually almost ignored.

principles.text: Small productivity edges compound over a career, so it's worth optimizing early.
principles.quote: If you get 10% more done and 1% better every day compared to someone else, the compounded difference is massive.

principles.text: Don't fall into productivity porn; ask whether you're working on the right problems, and allocate your year, not your day.
principles.quote: Many people spend too much time thinking about how to perfectly optimize their system, and not nearly enough asking if they’re working on the right problems.

principles.text: Be ruthless about saying no and do non-critical things in the quickest way possible; keep simple written lists.
principles.quote: I try to be ruthless about saying no to stuff, and doing non-critical things in the quickest way possible.

principles.text: Schedule meetings short (15-20 minutes or 2 hours), not the 1-hour default, and protect your best morning hours.
principles.quote: I find most meetings are best scheduled for 15-20 minutes, or 2 hours.  The default of 1 hour is usually wrong, and leads to a lot of wasted time.

principles.text: Delegate or avoid work you dislike, and surround yourself with smart, positive people who don't belittle your ambitions.
principles.quote: Try to be around smart, productive, happy, and positive people that don’t belittle your ambitions.

sources.title: What I Wish Someone Had Told Me: Sam Altman's 17 lessons on starting and finishing things
sources.originalTitle: What I Wish Someone Had Told Me
sources.summary: A list of 17 compact lessons from Sam Altman on how companies get started and finished. He covers audacious goals, concentrating bets, recruiting, fast iteration, incentives, and building businesses with compounding advantages at scale.

principles.text: Pick a hard, meaningful problem: teams do it more easily than an easy, unimportant one.
principles.quote: It is easier for a team to do a hard thing that really matters than to do an easy thing that doesn’t really matter; audacious ideas motivate people.

principles.text: Concentrate resources on a few high-conviction bets and cut more than you think you can.
principles.quote: Concentrate your resources on a small number of high-conviction bets; this is easy to say but evidently hard to do. You can delete more stuff than you think.

principles.text: Plan long-term but iterate fast; speed makes up for being wrong.
principles.quote: Fast iteration can make up for a lot; it’s usually ok to be wrong if you iterate quickly. Plans should be measured in decades, execution should be measured in weeks.

principles.text: Spend more time recruiting; bet on high-potential, fast-improving people with evidence of getting things done.
principles.quote: Spend more time recruiting. Take risks on high-potential people with a fast rate of improvement. Look for evidence of getting stuff done in addition to intelligence.

principles.text: Judge by outcomes, and fight bureaucracy rather than letting process excuse bad results.
principles.quote: Outcomes are what count; don’t let good process excuse bad results.

principles.text: Build a business whose advantage compounds with scale.
principles.quote: Compounding exponentials are magic. In particular, you really want to build a business that gets a compounding advantage with scale.

sources.title: Sam Altman's life advice at 30: pick the right work, keep burn low, take risks
sources.originalTitle: The days are long but the decades are short
sources.summary: A 36-point list of life and career lessons Altman wrote at age 30. The business-relevant parts: choose the right thing to work on, focus, surround yourself with exceptional people, keep personal burn low, and take more risk than feels comfortable. He also covers cutting distractions, not wasting time, and being a doer.

principles.text: Picking the right thing to work on is critical, and most people ignore it.
principles.quote: How to succeed: pick the right thing to do (this is critical and usually ignored), focus, believe in yourself (especially when others tell you it's not going to work), develop personal connections with people that will help you, learn to identify talented people, and work hard.

principles.text: Aim to be the best in the world at your work; missing still lands you somewhere good.
principles.quote: Aim to be the best in the world at whatever you do professionally. Even if you miss, you'll probably end up in a pretty good place.

principles.text: Keep your personal burn rate low; it opens up opportunities.
principles.quote: Keep your personal burn rate low. This alone will give you a lot of opportunities in life.

principles.text: Most people are too risk-averse, and conventional advice skews conservative. Take real career risks, especially early.
principles.quote: Don't worry so much. Things in life are rarely as risky as they seem. Most people are too risk-averse, and so most advice is biased too much towards conservative paths.

principles.text: Spend time with, work for, and hire smart, ambitious people. You become the average of your closest company.
principles.quote: Go out of your way to be around smart, interesting, ambitious people. Work for them and hire them (in fact, one of the most satisfying parts of work is forging deep relationships with really good people).

principles.text: Cut cognitive load from distractions and don't let unpleasant tasks pile up. Most people waste most of their time.
principles.quote: Minimize your own cognitive load from distracting things that don't really matter. It's hard to overstate how important this is, and how bad most people are at it.

sources.title: Sam Altman: Care about opinions on a long time horizon, because being misunderstood is a strength
sources.originalTitle: The strength of being misunderstood
sources.summary: Altman reframes "how do I stop caring what people think" as the wrong question. You choose whose opinions matter and on what timescale. The most impressive people care on a very long horizon, accept short-term low status, and use being misunderstood as room to solve important problems.

principles.text: Don't try to stop caring what others think; choose whose opinions matter and on what subjects.
principles.quote: Almost everyone cares what someone thinks (though caring what everyone thinks is definitely a mistake), and it's probably important. Caring too much makes you a sheep.

principles.text: You still need to be somewhat in tune with others to build something useful for them.
principles.quote: But you need to be at least a little in tune with others to do something useful for them.

principles.text: Timescale is a second lever: most people pick whose opinions count but ignore the time horizon.
principles.quote: you can choose the people whose opinions you care about (and on what subjects), and you can choose the timescale you care about them on.

principles.text: Care about opinion on a very long horizon; let the newspapers get it wrong if history gets it right.
principles.quote: they generally care about other people’s opinions on a very long time horizon—as long as the history books get it right, they take some pride in letting the newspapers get it wrong.

principles.text: Trade short-term low status for long-term high status, usually via an eventually-right non-consensus bet.
principles.quote: You should trade being short-term low-status for being long-term high-status, which most people seem unwilling to do.

principles.text: If you're right, being misunderstood gives you and a few rebels space to solve important problems.
principles.quote: as long as you are right, being misunderstood by most people is a strength not a weakness. You and a small group of rebels get the space to solve an important problem that might otherwise not get solved.

sources.title: How to hire: Sam Altman's startup hiring playbook
sources.originalTitle: How to hire
sources.summary: Altman argues hiring is the most important thing a founder does and should consume a third to half of their time after product-market fit. He covers sourcing through personal networks, auditioning candidates with real work, selling a mission, hiring for values, paying in equity, never compromising, and firing fast.

principles.text: x
principles.quote: After you figure out your vision and get product-market fit, you should probably be spending between a third and a half of your time hiring.

principles.text: x
principles.quote: Whenever possible (and it’s almost always possible), have someone do a day or two of work with you before you hire her

principles.text: x
principles.quote: By at least a 10x margin, the best candidate sources I’ve ever seen are friends and friends of friends.

principles.text: x
principles.quote: you should spend the time to learn a role before you hire for it.  If you don’t understand it, it’s very hard to get the right person.

principles.text: x
principles.quote: A single bad hire left unfixed for long can kill a company.

principles.text: x
principles.quote: Ideally, you end up paying people slightly below to roughly market salaries but with a very generous equity package.

sources.title: How to invest in startups: access, decisions, close rate, and helping founders
sources.originalTitle: How to invest in startups
sources.summary: Sam Altman explains that good investing comes down to three things: getting access to deals, choosing well, and getting founders to choose you. He covers how to spot future great founders, why to aim only at potential $10B outcomes, and how to help founders by raising their ambition and giving tactical advice.

principles.text: Access is the easiest part of investing: just work harder than other investors, who mostly don't.
principles.quote: Getting access to investment opportunities is the easiest of the three categories: you can just work hard. It’s surprising that most investors don’t work hard, but it’s true, and a bug that you can exploit.

principles.text: Build a brand through hard things few do well, like long-form writing rather than tweeting.
principles.quote: a good example is to write long-form content (hard, few people do a good job at it) instead of tweeting (easy, everyone does a pretty good job at it).

principles.text: Judge founders by their rate of improvement, not just current ability.
principles.quote: The rate of improvement is often more important than the current absolute ability

principles.text: Only back opportunities that could become $10B companies, because the power law dominates returns.
principles.quote: You should try to limit yourself to opportunities that could be $10 billion companies if they work

principles.text: Scale up what works; think about the potential energy of future scale.
principles.quote: The central learning of my career so far has been that you can and should scale up things that are working.

principles.text: Decide fast and show conviction, and treat founders as peers, to win competitive deals.
principles.quote: If you decide quickly, and especially if you decide before others do, founders tend to appreciate that.

sources.title: Idea generation: how founders find startup ideas and test them
sources.originalTitle: Idea generation
sources.summary: Sam Altman argues that good founders generate ideas constantly, so handing them an idea rarely works. He covers environment, thinking from the future backwards, spotting tectonic shifts, and tests for whether an idea could be huge and fits the founder.

principles.text: Good founders have lots of ideas; if you can't find one, get better at idea generation before starting.
principles.quote: It turns out that good founders have lots of ideas about everything, so if you want to be a founder and can’t get an idea for a company, you should probably work on getting good at idea generation first.

principles.text: Surround yourself with optimistic, creative people who never make you feel stupid for a bad idea; avoid world-weary cynics.
principles.quote: Perhaps most of all, you want to be around people who don’t make you feel stupid for mentioning a bad idea, and who certainly never feel stupid for doing so themselves.

principles.text: Project yourself 20 years ahead and think backwards, even if your view seems radical.
principles.quote: You want to be able to project yourself 20 years into the future, and then think backwards from there.

principles.text: Look for tectonic shifts; fast change lets focused startups beat incumbents. Real trends are used a lot by a few people.
principles.quote: A key differentiator is if the new platform is used a lot by a small number of people, or used a little by a lot of people.

principles.text: Pay attention to what is possible this year but wasn't last year, especially if next year is too late.
principles.quote: Any time you can think of something that is possible this year and wasn’t possible last year, you should pay attention.

principles.text: Ask early whether the idea could be huge, meaning it builds an accumulating advantage as it scales.
principles.quote: Most businesses don’t generate a valuable accumulating advantage as they scale. Think early about why an idea might have that property.

sources.title: The Software Revolution: why it destroys jobs, concentrates power, and what to do about it
sources.originalTitle: The Software Revolution
sources.summary: Altman calls software the third great technological revolution, after agriculture and industry. He argues it will do what technology usually does: create wealth, destroy jobs, and put more power in small groups. He sees AI and synthetic biology as the biggest risks and favors sensible safeguards plus making sure the good side's technological edge outpaces bad actors'.

principles.text: Software will create wealth but destroy jobs, so don't assume it helps median wages by default.
principles.quote: It appears that the software revolution will do what technology usually does—create wealth but destroy jobs.

principles.text: Technology is leverage on ability and luck, so it concentrates wealth and drives inequality.
principles.quote: Technology provides leverage on ability and luck, and in the process concentrates wealth and drives inequality.

principles.text: Don't protect obsolete jobs. Focus on finding new meaningful work, even though it is hard to plan.
principles.quote: Trying to hold on to worthless jobs is a terrible but popular idea.

principles.text: Software puts more power in small groups, unlike nuclear weapons, which needed the resources of nations.
principles.quote: The software revolution is likely to do what technology usually does, and make more power available to small groups.

principles.text: You can't ban knowledge or stop progress. Pair sensible safeguards with a stronger technological edge on the good side.
principles.quote: I think the best strategy is to try to legislate sensible safeguards but work very hard to make sure the edge we get from technology on the good side is stronger than the edge that bad actors get.

principles.text: Respond to AI and synthetic biology threats with defensive technology, such as vaccines and good AI.
principles.quote: If we can synthesize new diseases, maybe we can synthesize vaccines.  If we can make a bad AI, maybe we can make a good AI that stops the bad one.

sources.title: Reflections: Sam Altman on building OpenAI, the firing, and the road to superintelligence
sources.originalTitle: Reflections
sources.summary: Altman looks back on two years since ChatGPT's launch: building a company from scratch around a new technology, the board crisis, and growth from about 100M to 300M+ weekly users. Strategy evolved (product company, huge capital needs) while the vision stayed fixed, and iterative release stays central to safety.

principles.text: Keep the vision fixed but let tactics evolve as you learn what the mission actually requires.
principles.quote: Our vision won’t change; our tactics will continue to evolve. For example, when we started we had no idea we would have to build a product company; we thought we were just going to do great research.

principles.text: Original work has no handbook; you learn by doing and correct mistakes as you go.
principles.quote: There is no way to train people for this except by doing it, and when the technology category is completely new, there is no one at all who can tell you exactly how it should be done.

principles.text: Build demos from observed user behavior; the breakout moment is rarely the one you predicted.
principles.quote: We had been watching people use the playground feature of our API and knew that developers were really enjoying talking to the model. We thought building a demo around that experience would show people something important about the future

principles.text: Release powerful technology iteratively so society and the product can co-evolve and improve.
principles.quote: We continue to believe that the best way to make an AI system safe is by iteratively and gradually releasing it into the world, giving society time to adapt and co-evolve with the technology

principles.text: Rapid scaling brings heavy turnover and diverging interests; expect it rather than be surprised.
principles.quote: startups usually see a lot of turnover at each new major level of scale, and at OpenAI numbers go up by orders of magnitude every few months.

principles.text: Governance needs a diverse, experienced board built on trust and credibility.
principles.quote: I also learned the importance of a board with diverse viewpoints and broad experience in managing a complex set of challenges. Good governance requires a lot of trust and credibility.

sources.title: Three Observations: the economics of AI and what they mean for society
sources.originalTitle: Three Observations
sources.summary: Sam Altman lays out three observations about AI economics: intelligence scales with the log of resources, cost per level of AI falls about 10x every year, and the value of intelligence is super-exponential. He argues agents will act as virtual coworkers, that agency and adaptability will matter most, and that benefits must be broadly distributed.

principles.text: Model intelligence scales roughly with the log of resources, so spending more yields continuous, predictable gains.
principles.quote: The intelligence of an AI model roughly equals the log of the resources used to train and run it.

principles.text: The cost of a given level of AI falls about 10x per year, and cheaper AI drives much more usage.
principles.quote: The cost to use a given level of AI falls about 10x every 12 months, and lower prices lead to much more use.

principles.text: Value of rising intelligence is super-exponential, so exponentially increasing investment should continue.
principles.quote: The socioeconomic value of linearly increasing intelligence is super-exponential in nature.

principles.text: Think of AI agents as junior virtual coworkers that need supervision, then imagine them at massive scale across knowledge work.
principles.quote: Still, imagine it as a real-but-relatively-junior virtual coworker. Now imagine 1,000 of them. Or 1 million of them.

principles.text: Agency, willfulness, and adaptability become the most valuable human skills as AI becomes a lever on individuals.
principles.quote: Agency, willfulness, and determination will likely be extremely valuable.

principles.text: Ship products early and often so society and technology can co-evolve.
principles.quote: one of our reasons for launching products early and often is to give society and the technology time to co-evolve.

sources.title: The Merge: why humans and AI are already co-evolving, and why to take it seriously now
sources.originalTitle: The Merge
sources.summary: Altman argues the human-machine merge is a gradual process that has already begun, driven by algorithms that shape our attention and decisions. He expects superhuman AI sooner than most people think, because compute and the number of AI researchers are both growing exponentially, and he urges worldwide coordination early.

principles.text: Big technological shifts are gradual, so they're easy to miss. The merge has already started.
principles.quote: I believe the merge has already started, and we are a few years in. Our phones control us and tell us what to do when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think.

principles.text: Compute and AI progress are tightly linked. Growth in both hardware and talent compounds fast.
principles.quote: the most surprising thing I’ve learned working on OpenAI is just how correlated increasing computing power and AI breakthroughs are—and the number of smart people working on AI is increasing exponentially as well. Double exponential functions get away from you fast.
