- Hard things take a long time and attract critics. YC also has the "trough of sorrow," where nobody even bothers to say it sucks because nobody cares.
- Most successful founders he has spent time with stayed on their idea for a long time, when many others would have quit.
- His framework: the decision to quit should be internal, not external. Users not using it, or people saying it's bad, is not alone a reason to stop. Pay some attention, since they might be right.
- The best entrepreneurs he knows stop "when you have run out of ideas and something is not working."
- Motivation that lasts comes from enjoying the work, an intense belief that it matters, and ideally liking the people you work with.
- He says it's fine to start out wanting money or fame. Within a few years, many people find a deeper mission. His own motivation has shifted so that money and press are no longer big factors. He now works only on things he finds interesting and important.

chunks.heading: Momentum, burnout and crises
chunks.text:
- Sam used to believe burnout comes from working too hard. In his own experience it comes from failing and things not working.
- "Momentum is really energizing. The lack of momentum is super draining." He has almost unlimited energy for things that interest him and are working, and almost none for things that don't.
- Founders who fail often assume they lack energy or passion. His advice: shut the company down, go on vacation, and try again. Many then find huge energy when working on something that works.
- Each crisis gets less scary than the one before. Company-killing events usually get survived and the world doesn't end. "On the 19th major crisis you're like, well, I survived the first 18."
- He says you can't be taught this; you have to live through it.
- Ask for what you want. You'll get told no a lot, but sometimes it works.
- Entrepreneurs shoot themselves in the foot by not asking someone to quit their job and join them, or not asking a big company to do a deal. Being somewhat aggressive is an important entrepreneurial trait.

chunks.heading: Risk, conviction and the long term
chunks.text:
- Sam says people have terrible risk calculus. They are wrong about what is risky, and most don't take enough risk, especially early on.
- Being young, unknown and poor is a gift for risk-taking that people don't capitalize on.
- Real risk is doing something you'll regret for the rest of your life. People regret what they didn't do more than what they did.
- Starting a company on an idea you're passionate about, even at the cost of a couple of years of steady income or being called a failure, is a good risk. The wrong risk is not committing because you overrate failure, reputation damage or embarrassment.
- If you fail, you'll be in about the same place you are today and can try the next thing.
- Time is one of the few arbitrage opportunities left in the market. Markets are good at high-frequency trading and short-term pricing, and worse at long-term value.
- His belief is that he should hold stock in the best companies he invests in "forever." Meanwhile he has held his grandma's birthday Apple shares and never sold one.
- Founders get paid for the wealth they create for others. The best companies create massive value and capture far less than they create, over a long period.
- A founder should pick something they can commit to for a very long time. Make that commitment to yourself and your team, because you earn more over the long horizon than from short-term moves.
- Strong opinions, flexible details: he distinguishes refinement from pivoting. Facebook kept the same core idea (a social graph and online directory) while the product changed a lot. He doesn't believe in startups on their 11th unrelated pivot.
- Successful people he knows hold "strong opinions strongly held about the future." They can be convinced by new data, but the bar is fairly high.
- He rejects the idea that the future is unknowable, and says it's okay not to be fully diversified in your investments, career or life.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman explains how OpenAI nearly didn't start, why working on a one-of-one idea concentrates talent, and why startups should avoid the five crowded AI ideas. He also covers hiring for slope over resume, the product overhang of reasoning models, and the resilience required to keep going.

chunks.heading: Starting OpenAI: lean into the improbable thing when in doubt
chunks.text:
- Sam says OpenAI came close to never starting. Through 2015 the decision was "kind of coin flippy". AGI "sounded crazy" and "was kind of a pipe dream". DeepMind looked impossibly far ahead. Sam was running YC at the time and had plenty of other good startups to work on.
- His lesson: ambitious things have good reasons not to be done. It takes a core group of people who "sit in a room, look each other in the eye and say, 'All right, let's do this.'" "When in doubt, you should lean into them."
- Early OpenAI had no products, no revenue and no idea it would ever have revenue. It started as 8 people, then 20, writing research papers. They played video games and had a robotic hand that "could sort of barely do a Rubik's cube". ChatGPT was "completely in the realm of science fiction."
- Big companies don't start out looking big. He cites Vinod Khosla: there is a big difference between a "zero million dollar startup and a zero billion dollar startup, but they both have zero dollars of revenue."
- His advice: pick a market where some version of the future could be big if it works. After that, "one dumb foot in front of the other for a long time."

chunks.heading: Concentrating talent with a one-of-one mission
chunks.text:
- Recruiting the smartest people was "easier than it sounds". Sam says "99% of the world thought we were crazy. 1% of the world really resonated with" the AGI mission. That 1% had few other places to go, so OpenAI concentrated the talent.
- His general rule from watching startups: if you do the same thing as everyone else, it is very hard to concentrate talent or get people to believe in the mission. A one-of-one thing gives you "a really nice tailwind".
- Contrarian conviction is hard. He recalls a "really mean email" from Elon Musk a few years in. Elon had just seen GPT-1 and said the project had a near-zero chance of success. Sam went home wondering "what if he's right?"
- He has no magic answer. It "gets significantly easier over time", and you "get knocked down and get back up and brush yourself off and try to keep going."

chunks.heading: Hiring: smart, driven people and slope over pedigree
chunks.text:
- Sam says hiring "really smart people who are clearly really driven and really productive and can work as part of a team" gets you 90% of the way. He is surprised by how much people focus on other things.
- His checklist:
  - Really smart
  - Driven
  - Curious
  - Self-motivated
  - Hardworking
  - A good track record of accomplishment
  - Works well as part of a team
  - Aligned with the company's vision
- Early in a startup he does not believe in hiring the senior, eminent administrator as the first hire. Neither he nor YC has had much success with that. He prefers "young scrappy but clearly get stuff done" people over the "extremely polished track record". Senior people may be needed later.
- When reading YC applications he "would never look at the resume items" such as Google or a top college. He went straight to the most impressive thing the person had done. He checked the resume only as a backup if that didn't convince him.
- He looks at what people have built and coded, their velocity, and how they think about and solve problems.
- He endorses "hire for slope, not y-intercept" as "unbelievably great advice."

chunks.heading: Building on AI: product overhang, falling prices and defensibility
chunks.text:
- Sam says the "product overhang" is large. What models can do far exceeds the products people have built. Even if models stopped improving, there is "a huge amount of new stuff to build."
- API prices keep falling. He says "last week o3 cost five times as much as it did this week and that's going to keep going." He expects people to be "astonished at how much the price per performance falls." He also says an open-source model is coming that will surprise people.
- Reasoning models are like "a new square on a periodic table that no one has built with yet." The interaction model differs from chat. He had only seen startups building for it in the previous month.
- On the "will OpenAI run over my startup" question, his answer is "don't build our core chat assistant." OpenAI will make ChatGPT the best super assistant it can, which is one small part of the opportunity. Other ideas he floated:
  - An app or agent store inside ChatGPT that drives traffic to new startups.
  - A "sign in with OpenAI" that lets users bring a personalized model to a startup.
- Herd behavior is a bigger problem. "People get excited about the same thing at the same time." If Gary listed the five ideas he hears most often, half the room would be working on one of them. Sam bets the person who builds something bigger than OpenAI is not working on any of the five.
- Defensibility: "the best, most enduring companies are usually not doing the same thing as everybody else." That gives you time to find the great product and build the technology before you must answer the defensibility question.
- ChatGPT's own path: "for a long time the only defensibility was we had the only product out in the market." Then came brand, then memory, connections and other features that are truly defensible. He admits "we didn't have any defensibility strategy" at first. You have a window in which to build one.
- He names the "seven powers" book as relevant to defensibility.

chunks.heading: Why this is the best time to start a company
chunks.text:
- Sam says: "This is the best [expletive] time ever in the history of technology ever, period, to start a company."
- On the worry that SaaS gets replaced by just-in-time generated software, he says it will happen to everybody. "The way startups win is when they can iterate faster than big companies and they can do it at a much lower cost." Big companies have advantages but "iterate very slowly", and cheap software erodes those advantages.
- "When the clock cycle of the industry changes this much startups almost always win", and he thinks it has probably never changed this much.
- One person or a small group with a lot of agency can now get far more done. Coordination costs are huge, so empowering individuals will change what gets built, not just add a little more.
- His analogy for AI is the transistor. A scientific discovery lets society and the economy build enormous value over decades, and he thinks AI will be "even faster and steeper".

chunks.heading: Product direction: memory, agents, devices and a melting interface
chunks.text:
- Memory is Sam's favorite feature launched that year. He sees ChatGPT becoming an entity that knows you, connects to all your data, runs persistently in the background, and proactively helps. It would know when to message you and when to act for you.
- He lists the ingredients: always-with-you devices, new browsers, connections to all data sources, memory and a model that runs persistently. Integrations are important, and people are starting to use ChatGPT as an operating system for their lives.
- Agents: deep research and Codex are "like a very junior employee that can work on something for a short period of time." Much of the world's computer work comes in few-hour chunks that someone then approves or rejects. He says current o3 can already support many such experiences.
- Models: the long-term aim is one integrated model that reasons when needed and generates real-time video when needed. He suggests it could write a brand-new app just in time, only for you.
- Interface: he wants the interface to "melt away". You tell the computer what you want, trust it to handle changes, and it surfaces only what matters. He compares his phone to "walking down Times Square", with notifications and flashing things.
- Hardware: there have been "two big revolutions in computer interfaces" in about 50 years (keyboard/mouse/screen, then touch). AI opens the field for a third. He is betting on Jony Ive to figure it out. He declined to describe the device but says the key to "Her" is a persistent AI companion, not a piece of hardware.
- Robots: OpenAI's strategy is to nail the model first, then connect it to a robot. He expects robots doing "super useful stuff" within a few years, though a billion robots will take a while.
- Scale: ChatGPT.com did not exist two and a half years earlier and is now the fifth biggest website in the world. He thinks OpenAI will "run the largest and most expensive piece of infrastructure in the world pretty soon". He says compute is hard to get. He would be glad to push half the ChatGPT workload onto local devices.

chunks.heading: Resilience, instincts and what he'd tell his 2005 self
chunks.text:
- Sam says he wishes someone had taught him "conviction and resilience over a long period of time". It is easy for a while, but "your reserves wear down."
- His first startup (Loopt) didn't work out. He notes many people give up after one failed startup, but "startups don't work out all the time", so you have to learn to keep going.
- He advises:
  - Build trust in your own instincts and increase it as your decision-making improves.
  - Have the courage to work on things that are out of fashion but that you believe in.
- He compares entrepreneurship to having a kid: the good parts are better and the hard parts "shockingly much harder" than anyone can express.
- On being CEO of OpenAI: "I don't recommend it." No single challenge is that hard, but the volume of simultaneous work and the number of big companies gunning for OpenAI is "more context than I thought it was possible to handle at once."
- On energy and AI: he was obsessed with both for years but only saw after starting OpenAI that energy would be the fundamental limit on intelligence. He thinks AI for science is the most exciting application, because long-term economic growth comes from discovering new science plus decent governance and institutions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains why startups have the biggest edge when the ground is shifting, and why founders should plan for models that are smarter and cheaper in a few years. He covers handling chaos, killing good projects to back the one that works, holding few convictions, and hiring and promoting people for speed.

chunks.heading: Startups win when the ground is shifting, so build for where models will be
chunks.text:
- Sam says startups have their biggest edge "when the ground is shifting the most" and when costs and cycle times are falling fast. That is happening in many places at once.
- He says a 10-week-old startup today can look like what used to take a year. He met a roughly 2-week-old startup that had rebuilt an office productivity suite (documents, presentations, spreadsheets) for AI as a first-class user. A 10-week-old startup that looks like one from 10 years ago "is in bad shape."
- He is surprised that more founders do not take on the "crazy thing" with the new tools. Most pick "AI agents for enterprise vertical X." That will work and be competitive, but he thinks it probably won't be the era's defining startup.
- His central advice to founders: internalize that scaling laws will continue. Plan for what is not possible or economical this month but will be in 2 or 4 years. It is fine to start on things that need smarter or cheaper models.
- He argues the market has not adapted to this, just as it still under-bets on high-growth young founders. He calls that "free money left in the market."
- He thinks a startup today still mostly looks like one from 10 years ago because that is the received wisdom. Hiring fewer people and spending more on tokens for Codex "doesn't seem like enough." He has met a few people building startups in a completely different way.

chunks.heading: Trusting exponentials and operating in chaos
chunks.text:
- Sam says he has developed "a great trust in exponentials" in people, companies and models. Plotting where someone is when he meets them, then checking their progress later, builds that trust.
- He says handling chaos can't be taught, only learned through reps. You need emotional peace with "this is not going to be the thing that kills you and you don't quite yet know how you're going to solve it."
- He calls this a real weakness of young founders. At YC office hours he could tell first-batch founders from experienced ones by their emotional state when talking about a problem. They learn it eventually, but "at great pain and cost and unforced errors."
- The first company-killing event feels like the world is ending. By the tenth, it's much less bad.
- He reframes bad days. The opposite of a bad experience is no experience, so he tries to be grateful for them. He cites Naval: with a fast-forward button on your life, "your life would be over."

chunks.heading: Planning: a few convictions, planned forward
chunks.text:
- Sam does not plan backwards from 20 years out. He holds "a small number of strongly held convictions about the future" as directions to head in, then plans forward from the current state: what to do now and this year. Some things need a 5 to 10 year horizon.
- He thinks many people hold too many beliefs and a rigid worldview. They end up chasing, like "space companies turn into AI companies."
- His advice is to deeply believe a few things, stay flexible on the rest, and stay true to the core.
- Critical path for him has been clear for a long time: abundant intelligence, with broadly shared prosperity and no power concentration. He has not been tempted to reconsider the goal.

chunks.heading: Mission-driven scope and supply chain alignment
chunks.text:
- A clear mission plus a deep understanding of the problem point to what to work on. You still sometimes over-expand or under-reach.
- OpenAI's mission is to make AI extremely abundant, cheap and powerful, and to put it in everyone's hands. That means building the platform: chips, energy, data centers, robots. He says OpenAI has "no desire" to build every vertical on top of it. He wants a decentralized economy where OpenAI produces "units of intelligence."
- He names the biggest bottleneck as "Transistors and then electrons in that order."
- To keep suppliers on OpenAI's timeline, he talks to them a lot. He doesn't just demand delivery dates. He shows core suppliers the upcoming model, what it enables and the research behind it, so they believe in the mission. Then he aligns incentives as much as he can.
- On the supply chain, OpenAI brought chip design and model design together. He doesn't think it needs to own electron production, which is a commodity. Execution means doing whatever step the problem requires. Financing a fab build-out, assembling a chip team and running the supply chain are each a different approach.
- He thinks there is too much focus on "algorithms that create better algorithms" and not enough on data centers that can build more data centers. A data center's thinking power could drive robots to make more data centers.
- He sees the joint stock corporation as the key invention of the industrial revolution. It aligned incentives, gave liability protection and let people pool capital.

chunks.heading: Focus: kill good projects to scale the one that works
chunks.text:
- Sam says killing a failing project is easy. The hard part is killing good projects when one thing is working very well.
- Examples: when GPT-3 worked, OpenAI shut down robotics work. When coding agents worked, it shut down Sora and the browser. Sora "would have been super successful," but compute and energy were better spent on coding agents.
- The call is "a somewhat gradual realization," not a single meeting. People accept it because they understand the mission and the stakes, even if they are unhappy in the moment.
- He admits his biggest ambition miss was under-investing in compute. He was "psyched out by the financial markets," and says he won't make that mistake again.
- He expects three waves of form factors. The first was chatbots. The second is coding agents. The third, coming soon, is persistent agents (chiefs of staff, co-workers).

chunks.heading: Asking for the hard thing: the Codex example
chunks.text:
- Sam's rule is to ask for what you want. You don't always get it, but when you do, amazing things can happen.
- Codex is his example. OpenAI was way behind Claude Code, and the consensus was that you don't try to win a category when someone else has momentum. OpenAI judged coding strategically critical, partly because of its role in recursive self-improvement (RSI) and its economic value. It asked a team to take on an extremely hard mission, and they delivered something "very rare in the history of business." He says it is now the product most of the best coders he knows use.
- To learn a new area fast, he finds experts and talks to them, and reads as much as he can. He says experts are willing to help if you ask.
- He says people overestimate the risk of most actions. When someone calls a decision high or low risk, he asks them to say why out loud. That often gets past their intellectual blocks, since people are usually wrong one way or the other.
- Buying a lot of compute was a decision he held extremely high conviction on.

chunks.heading: Leadership, hiring and building ambition
chunks.text:
- Sam says organizational pace is "90% the people you put in leadership roles." He asks whether each is a fast mover or a slow mover. Operating rhythms and management techniques matter less.
- He thinks executives should mostly be promoted internally. When hiring externally, he spends a lot of time talking to the candidate, reference checking, and trying to work together casually first.
- He rejects the meme that you can only hire in areas you deeply understand. He says he isn't strong at product or design but can tell Jony Ive is great within 30 minutes.
- He believes in getting better at your strengths. Obsessing over fixing weaknesses is a "huge trap."
- Some skills can be learned but not taught. Asking someone to explain them doesn't work. Studying them closely and sitting in meetings with them does.
- To raise ambition, he says corporate-background founders have "catastrophically low" ambition because they were punished for thinking big. The fix is "small repeated wins": try something that feels too ambitious, see it work, then try again. He doesn't give inspirational speeches.
- He admits he has gotten worse at patiently talking people through decisions and wants to go back to "let's really talk it through."
- He texts or talks with 300 to 400 people a day. He calls it a bad habit but says it gives him huge short-term context, such as knowing about an impending research breakthrough that changes a customer or supplier decision.

chunks.heading: Design, real vs fake trends, and ChatGPT's launch
chunks.text:
- From Jony Ive, Sam learned that great design is "way more about understanding the problem than the flash of insight." Rushing toward or locking into a solution gives worse results. Ive studies a domain exhaustively before designing.
- He tested TikTok while building the Sora app. It pulled him in for hours, so he deleted it. He also turned off most notifications. He doesn't want to build products that absorb time without benefit.
- He says real trends differ from fake ones by persistence: people design their lives around the product instead of leaving it on a shelf (VR is his example of a fake one). He developed this by watching many startups at YC and analyzing the data.
- Reading ChatGPT's launch: usage rose to a higher peak each day, and the researchers called it a flash in the pan. Sam recognized from YC the "spectral signature" of organic growth. On day five it crossed a million users, and he knew OpenAI was about to become a big company very fast.
- Running the research lab and running the product company felt like "two almost completely unrelated jobs." The research lab didn't prepare him for the product company.
- On the 28-country, 35-day world tour, he got on planes in "marginal situations," following Brian Chesky's advice. He prefers bundling international travel into 7 to 10 day chunks instead of spreading out one-day trips.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains how Y Combinator works as a network-effect business and what separates the best founders: clarity, determination and speed. He argues for hiring as late as possible, focusing on product love over liking, growing about 10% a week, and avoiding "fake work" like fundraising theater and networking events.

chunks.heading: Why Y Combinator exists and how it works
chunks.text:
- Sam describes YC's role as enabling as much innovation as possible, with startups as the vehicle. YC funds about 250 startups a year in its core program.
- A new "fellowship" program offers a tenth of the funding and less advice, and will be expanded.
- The goal: if a company is in YC, it gets "a hundred times" the advantage it would otherwise have, through advice, connections and access to the community.
- The most valuable thing is the alumni community, with more than 2,000 funded founders at that point. Alumni help each other raise money, hire, and buy each other's products.
- Sam sees YC as somewhere between a product company and a traditional investment firm.
- In 2005, when Sam went through YC's first batch (eight companies), investors wanted businessmen, business plans and financial models rather than engineers. YC was different: "our people", engineers who cared about the product. Founders in that batch were confident this was the future of investing.

chunks.heading: YC as a network-effects business
chunks.text:
- Sam says YC is a network-effects business, which he thinks nobody knew ten years earlier.
- There were about 200 accelerators in the world. Eight companies worth over $1B had come out of any accelerator, and all eight were from YC.
- His explanation: there is a real network effect at the earliest funding stage. He doesn't think it exists as strongly at the venture stage, where five or ten great firms all do well.
- On YC's stage, the gap between first and second place is "like the difference between Facebook and my high school yearbook".
- YC is the first investor, so founder loyalty is stronger than toward later investors. Series A investors bought before success was obvious. Series C/D investors invest mostly on a financial model. Public shareholders "will sell your stock if your earnings drop a penny".
- Because of that loyalty, founders give back to the community.
- YC builds the network on purpose:
  - Takes all its founders camping once a year.
  - Runs physical spaces where founders gather.
  - Runs private online social networks for founders.
- Being a founder is "very lonely", so having peers to say "this is really hard" to matters more than it seems.
- Enterprise founders get their first customers from within the YC community, which is now standardized. Without a network like that, Sam says it is hard to do, and he no longer advises non-YC companies.

chunks.heading: Sam's path and the case against being a venture investor
chunks.text:
- Sam left Stanford (computer science) in 2005 to start Loopt. He and friends were already working on it when YC was announced, and he applied the day before the deadline.
- He became a part-time YC partner in 2011, and his company was acquired in 2012.
- After the acquisition he raised a venture fund and learned he did not want to be a venture investor. He felt like a public stock picker, allocating capital where many others were also allocating, and trying to win deals with a better sales pitch.
- By contrast, in 2009 and 2010 he wrote $15K checks as an angel when founders had no other options, and that is where he felt he made a difference.
- He wanted to enable new companies, so he took the YC presidency.
- He says a great Series A board member is the most important thing to focus on, and that YC is not good at providing that. If he were a later-stage investor, he'd be a hands-off one.
- Taking over as YC's president was less jarring than most CEO transitions because he had been involved from the start. He says every successful new CEO has to "refound" the company in some way. Internally, the mission is clear and the work is the same.

chunks.heading: What the best founders have in common
chunks.text:
Sam says YC tracks founder traits across about 20,000 applicants a year and develops interview questions that correlate with outcomes. In no particular order:

- **Clarity.** Can the founder explain exactly what they do and why? Without it they can't hire, sell or talk to press, and it signals unclear thinking. Airbnb knew exactly why they were staying on air beds in strangers' homes, even though it seemed odd to YC at first.
- **Determination and passion.** Some founders "bend the world to their will" and won't take no; others retreat at each small obstacle. Great companies are also mission-driven in some way.
- **Raw intelligence.**
- **Speed of execution and decision-making.** Not the same as determination, since some determined people are slow. Speed and quality of decision-making correlate almost perfectly with YC's successful founders. Founders who look great on paper but fail often lack it.
- **Problem-solving.** He recommends *The Martian* as "the best startup book" he has read in a long time. The skill is facing an unfamiliar problem and solving it quickly.

chunks.heading: Founding teams, cofounders and hiring
chunks.text:
- YC prefers teams of two or three cofounders but doesn't rule out solo founders. Dropbox and Instacart had no cofounder when YC said yes, but each got one before the program or shortly after.
- Reasons against going solo: there is a lot of work, and the psychological toll is underestimated even by people who think they're strong.
- A bad cofounder is worse than none. Founders who bring a cofounder just because they think YC will like it end up heartbroken "100% of the time". Start without one if you must, but "never stop looking" for one.
- Three cofounders works well (Airbnb is the example). Four is harder, since someone usually leaves in the first two years.
- On diversity within a team: diversity of background and perspective is good. The bad kind is diversity of vision, where founders disagree on what kind of company to build (culture, decision-making, whether to sell, who to hire, how to handle disagreements).
- Conflict also arises when two founders want the same thing for themselves, like both wanting to be CEO and on a magazine cover. YC wants teams with a shared vision and varied skills.
- All cofounder pairs have big fights at some point. YC has sometimes told founders a relationship was over and one needed to move on.
- Hiring: the best YC startups hire the fewest people, and the worst rush to say "I have 10 people working for me".
  - Employees add burn, organizational inertia, internal conflict and career-path worries.
  - Before the company is ready to scale, extra hires create "potential energy" that causes problems.
  - Airbnb took about nine months to hire its first person, Stripe took about as long, and Dropbox took a very long time.
  - YC likes companies that find out how long they can wait before hiring the first non-founder.
- On firing: the biggest universal mistake great founders make is waiting too long to fire people. If someone fires easily, that is a worry. Keeping someone too long hurts them more: fired after 2-3 months, it won't go on a resume, but after a year it does.
- How Sam fires someone:
  - Treat them as a person and make it a win for them.
  - He never fired anyone without finding them a new job first.
  - Be clear the decision is firm (hesitating creates a power dynamic).
  - Offer generous severance, help finding a job, and let them stay or work from home until ready to announce their next move.
  - Don't bring a final paycheck, termination letter and legal papers to the meeting. Lawyers' advice here is bad because it makes it feel hostile.
  - Ask on what terms they want it to happen, and handle paperwork later.
  - If hiring someone was a mistake, he sees it as his own.

chunks.heading: Ideas, conviction, pivots and product focus
chunks.text:
- Sam endorses Peter Thiel's line that the best ideas look bad. Good assets get competed away and bad assets are bad, so the opportunity is in great ideas that look bad.
- This is harder than it sounds because everyone is swayed by trends. Investors chased the next Facebook in 2006-2008 and again in 2009-2010, when the real opportunities were Uber and Airbnb, which looked nothing like Facebook. Investors flocked to ad tech around Google's IPO, which was the wrong bet.
- Today, he says, people are building "Uber for X" (food, dog walking). He expects the next $100B company to be something new, not a narrow vertical on Uber's model. Ask what has changed in the world that allows a new giant, then build that. It will look bad.
- Two ways to build conviction:
  - Launch fast and get users who love it. Uber was mocked but grew roughly 10x a year.
  - Be able to explain what changed in the world that others missed (e.g. everyone suddenly had an internet-connected device in their pocket).
- Whom to ignore: everyone except users. If users say the product is bad and no other users like it, listen.
- Hard tech: Sam sits on two nuclear boards. YC put hard-tech companies in the same program as web startups. Their view was that these companies failed because they weren't startup-like enough. Hard-tech companies should break their work into small, measurable internal products and find a metric to improve 10% each week. Compounded over three or four years, that makes a big company. He said they wouldn't know whether it worked for about five years.
- On pivots: Silicon Valley misunderstands pivoting and he dislikes how people brag about them. Failure is tolerable but still bad, and he thinks it is overglorified.
- The only pivots he has seen work:
  - Founders building what they wanted to build all along (Instagram: Kevin Systrom first built Bourbon, then the photo-filter idea he cared about).
  - Founders discovering it while building something that didn't work (Airbnb, which ran out of money and rented an air-mattress space to cover rent; also Slack, which came out of the Glitch game's internal tool, and Stripe, which came from Patrick Collison being unable to accept payments in an iPhone app).
- A pivot made by sitting at a whiteboard to brainstorm a new idea has never worked, in his experience. If there is no real pivot, he tells founders to shut down, return the remaining capital to investors, travel, and wait for an idea that arises naturally.
- Product focus: a startup can have many users who "like" it or a few who "love" it. Every successful company he has worked with was in the second group. The aim is to build until some users would be very sad if it disappeared. Spend nearly all time writing code and talking to users.
- Bitcoin, as an example: he said he wouldn't buy much because it had not yet found product-market fit and few people use it daily.

chunks.heading: Momentum, fake work, fundraising and running the company
chunks.text:
- After Demo Day, there is often a slump. Founders then must clean up tech, organizational and cultural debt, but should spend about 10% of energy on that, not 50% or 100%, because losing growth creates more problems. He quotes a board member's line: "sales solves all problems", later amended to "growth solves all problems". The core rule of running a startup is never lose momentum.
- Employees often sense momentum changes before founders do.
- "Fake work": do the work that would be cut in a reality-show edit, like coding for 12 hours or running user interviews and sales meetings. That is boring to watch but is how you win. Fundraising feels exciting, but no great company became great because it was good at fundraising.
- Distractions: press, "30 under 30" lists, conferences, and networking events. He once got pulled into CEO events and realized he had been out of the office more than in it.
- Valuations: he thinks headline valuations are fantasies except when buying shares (as an investor, or an employee getting options). Employees shouldn't assume their equity is a percentage of the headline valuation because liquidation preferences distort it. The real question is what the company will be worth in five years and what share you own. He often tells startups not to chase the highest valuation, and sometimes not to raise.
- Career advice: if joining a company, join the most successful fast-growing one you can find, since seeing a successful company scale is the only prior training of real value. Start a startup only if you have an idea you believe matters, not for the sake of it. Joining an early company you believe in may have a higher expected value because few startups succeed.
- Hard hours, short years: when he was 23, someone told him he'd have roughly 20 years of the intensity needed to be a great startup CEO. Since the time is limited, he says to think about opportunity cost and what you most believe in.
- Location: the Bay Area is still the best place to start a startup, and cost of living is the main downside because every extra month of runway matters. Over half of YC's funded founders were not born in the US, with about 40 countries represented in the latest batch.
- Education: he sees no strong correlation between years of schooling and founder success; extremes in either direction are worse.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman answers HN questions on getting the first 20 B2B customers, expanding your network, youth as a startup advantage, cofounder trust, and spotting the next platform shift. His consistent theme is to build something impressive and let a strong network pull customers in.

chunks.heading: Getting the first 20 B2B customers: expand your network so customers come to you
chunks.text:
- Sam says the question assumes you must reach companies outside your network. The approach he has seen work best is the other one: expand your network and pull customers into it.
- The right channel depends on the company:
  - If all your customers go to one trade show, go there and meet them.
  - If there are only about 10 possible customers in the world, find any way to reach them: cold email, referrals, or anything else.
- Founder-to-founder sales tends to work well, so he suggests asking how to meet more entrepreneurs, or how to build a bigger network that reaches your early customers.
- At YC, the community was built so that most B2B companies get their first 20 customers from other YC companies. He says this has been "extremely valuable".
  - Almost all YC B2B companies sell almost exclusively to YC companies early on.
  - This was somewhat less true when the network was smaller, and is still less true for companies in a niche that is rare in the YC community.
  - It usually starts with Bookface (the YC internal network) or emails to YC founders, selling to the YC community.
- Even if you are not in YC, he says to think the same way.

chunks.heading: Building a network from scratch, and why a great product beats outreach
chunks.text:
- Sam did this himself at 18 or 19 in Silicon Valley, when he knew nobody. He messaged founders he respected in his city and proposed meeting, for example by booking a table for ten and inviting nine of them.
  - Some of those people stayed in touch and became close friends 12 or 13 years later.
  - He says it is harder outside a startup hub, because these relationships are easier to build in person.
- Silicon Valley has a strong culture of helping others, with startups as a dominant economic engine. He says not to be afraid to email people you want to talk to.
- On conferences and meetups:
  - Some are good, but most are not.
  - Ask people you respect who have attended before you go.
  - He is shy in big groups and finds most attendees not very special.
  - Speaking at a conference is easier for an introvert because people come to you, though it may still be a waste of time.
- His key point is that if you build something impressive, your network comes to you.
  - "Hi, I'm starting a company, please reach out, I'm trying to find customers" makes you look like many other people.
  - "Hi, I built this great product, here it is, take a look" gets you taken seriously.
  - That puts you in the top 1% of people sending cold emails.

chunks.heading: Advantages and disadvantages of being young, and whether college matters
chunks.text:
- Advantages of young founders:
  - Fewer life obligations such as boards and families, so more focus and stamina.
  - Boldness, including willingness to move across the world for a good opportunity.
  - Used to living cheaply. Sam had rats in his kitchen and a mattress on the floor until he was 25. Low living costs are a big advantage over startups whose founders need a lot of money just to live.
  - The biggest advantage: they lack the scars of experience. They are willing to try again and again. Founders often say they would not have started if they had known how hard it would be, how the industry would turn out, or how long it would take.
  - Young people are often at the front of new technology shifts and have a better-than-chance sense of the next big wave.
- Disadvantages:
  - Probably not good at managing people.
  - Very lacking in business experience.
  - Probably not as good an engineer as they will be later in life.
  - So bring in experienced people for specific areas.
- On college: he did two years, loved it, learned useful things and is glad he went. He says most people at YC do not know where he or most others went, and that it never comes up as a topic.
- He still thinks Silicon Valley's network is worth the cost, and says you can still live cheaply in hidden corners of the Valley. He calls the idea that you can't succeed there "a myth".

chunks.heading: Non-technical founders: what's needed and how to pick a technical cofounder
chunks.text:
- Sam says Evan Spiegel and Brian Chesky are not fully non-technical. Both know a little. Brian is a great designer who built the first version. Both are great at product.
- A non-technical founder needs:
  - Strong product skills and great leadership.
  - A very strong idea and attention to fine detail.
  - The ability to convince really capable technical people to follow them. You need only a little technical or design ability.
- How to evaluate a technical cofounder:
  - Only start a company with someone you already know.
  - Look at things they have built. Even if you can't read their code, you can see that they built something good, built it fast, and kept improving it.
  - Work on a project together first.
  - Minimum "known for a while" is 6 months.
- To get more technical yourself, take a few computer science classes. There are also many free online options, some from YC companies. He learned Python "the hard way".
- How technical you need to be depends on what you build:
  - A nuclear reactor needs deep engineering and nuclear physics.
  - A not-especially-complex iPhone app needs little for the first version. Hire world-class technical talent later.
  - What matters early is building a product people love. Code quality in the first version matters little at first, but matters a lot later.

chunks.heading: Choosing what to work on: form your own convictions and explore broadly
chunks.text:
- Sam says it is a bad strategy to let someone else dictate what is important and then go do it. Develop your own convictions, because you understand and care about them, and the other person may be wrong. His advice to a high schooler:
  - Study the world and history.
  - Look at the latest in technology.
  - Read what smart people say.
  - Analyze it all and make your own list of the most important things. You can make your own predictions.
- He studied AI and computer security in college and thinks both remain very good areas.
- Areas he names as promising:
  - Synthetic biology or biotech, which is where he would have gone if he'd stayed in school longer.
  - Cheap, clean energy. He chairs two nuclear energy companies. He argues quality of life and energy cost are tightly linked, and that the planet is at risk without cheap, clean energy. Cheaper energy over 20 or 30 years could replace current forms.
  - Education, which he calls huge and under-tapped.
  - VR and AR, which will be an important computing platform.
- How he found his own path:
  - He took one class in everything, read one book on every topic, and made smart friends in very different fields.
  - He tried many things. He was an investment banker for a day and disliked it. He built a lot of software and became interested in AI and mobile.
  - He loved theoretical physics but wasn't smart enough for it.
  - He ended up loving investing in tech companies and helping founders.
  - His summary: breadth-first, then depth-first search works. He ended up deeply specialized in a few areas.
- Needs versus value ("value" being a polite word for money):
  - Many world needs are obvious from history, science and economics. If you identify an obvious need, it is probably a real one.
  - Some things are great but unpaid.
  - He once wanted to be a writer but realized the world doesn't need or value the "7 millionth novel", and it is hard to earn enough from it.
  - It also works in reverse. Being very good at something is satisfying.

chunks.heading: Spotting the next platform wave: use intensity of use, not shipments
chunks.text:
- Sam says transformative companies tend to be founded in clusters when a new platform rises:
  - The internet, 1996 to 2000.
  - Mobile after the iPhone in 2007, roughly 2007 to 2011. He puts Facebook mostly in the mobile category.
- Many people think VR and AR are next, and he thinks it's still a bit early.
- His test for when to focus: look at usage rate per individual user, not total shipments.
  - Smartphones existed before the iPhone, but people used them only a few times, did little beyond calls and a calendar, and didn't carry them every day.
  - The iPhone didn't sell much in its first year compared with the number of phones Nokia and others sold in 2007. But owners loved it and used it all the time.
- So he ignores VR/AR shipment totals and waits until someone builds a device or software that people use heavily every day once they have it.
- This holds regardless of price. The first iPhone was expensive, but owners loved it, and prices eventually fall.

chunks.heading: Equity crowdfunding for startups: why it fell short
chunks.text:
- Sam calls it disappointing. He wouldn't call it a failure, but it hasn't had the success he hoped for.
- What still goes wrong: it is easy for companies that don't need it, because they already have known investors.
- So far the public hasn't been willing to back companies without professional investor support. It has become a way, though not the only one, to increase the money raised from full-time professional investors.
- He still believes crowdfunding should matter, but says the right product hasn't been built yet.
- As an investor he wants to know the company and founders well and in person, and probably wouldn't invest in people he'd never met through a crowdfunding platform.

chunks.heading: Surviving an acquisition as a key non-founder employee
chunks.text:
- Sam says most acquisitions don't go smoothly, so go in knowing it will be hard.
- The most important thing he has seen is an agreement before closing about the target company's autonomy. He urges founders to secure one that lets the team operate as independently as possible.
- Build bridges. You don't want to be caught between warring factions.
  - Want the acquirer to support you and you to support them.
  - Want people to get along.
- As a key leader, make it your personal job to build strong relationships with as many people as possible at the acquiring company, and be the bridge when tensions inevitably rise.
- On how long to stay: six to nine months is enough before deciding it won't work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman, then new YC president, explains how to start a startup: let an idea be a project before a company, set weekly growth goals, execute fast, and understand users. He also covers how YC picks founders, when to raise money, and why he funds smart, determined people with clear vision.

chunks.heading: Sam's pre-company stage: project first, company second
chunks.text:
- Sam says the foundation of a startup is critical: get it right at the start and it works, get it wrong and "it's usually fatal."
- He warns against starting a startup for the sake of having a startup, then hunting for an idea. People who sit in a co-working space thinking "I need a startup" and "I need my idea" have a much harder time.
- Declaring something a company instead of a project creates pressure to settle on an idea quickly. The idea also can't sound too crazy once you have to tell people about "my startup." Early ideas are delicate and need room to develop.
- His advice: spend time figuring out what you are passionate about, let it be a project before it is a company, then make the company the vehicle to support it.
- The founder can force the process by spending a lot of time thinking about ideas and building projects. The moment to call it a company is when you have conviction: "this may not work but I really believe in this."
- Raising money before you know even generally what you will build is usually problematic. Investors make you feel you owe them progress.
- The thinking phase takes a while. Once you commit to building, you go as fast as you can.

chunks.heading: Growth as the organizing metric
chunks.text:
- Sam says the best startups set growth goals from the earliest days, and that startups and growth are "incredibly interrelated."
- Airbnb's founders drew a forward-looking projected growth graph and put it on their bathroom mirror and fridge door. They tried to grow 10% every week.
- A growth target shapes the company. It gives one metric to optimize and "one way to answer every question."
- Startups that do this usually succeed. Startups that don't "argue about everything else."
- In a later Q&A he confirms that 7% to 10% weekly growth is the benchmark YC watches.

chunks.heading: Customer understanding and the limits of Lean Startup
chunks.text:
- Sam calls "understand your users" one of the most important pieces of startup advice. A startup that doesn't do it will fail, and one that does often succeeds. He agrees with deeply understanding users and iterating very quickly.
- What he thinks lean methodology can miss: very ambitious startups often take a long time to work, or a long time to look ambitious.
- Examples he gives:
  - Reddit began as a joke of an online forum and became a "weird collective consciousness."
  - Facebook began as college profiles and became universal connectivity.
  - Something like a nuclear reactor company simply takes a long time to get going.
- He thinks it is important to allow that kind of slow start to happen.

chunks.heading: Speed of execution as the main founder signal
chunks.text:
- Sam says the best founders "execute so quickly." One way YC identifies great founders is how much progress they make between meetings.
- Mediocre founders, seen a week later, are still doing the things they said a week ago. The best founders, seen the next day, have done all of it and more.
- Slow founders always have detailed, good-sounding excuses: the product wasn't good enough, lawyers found a problem, a PR issue, a competitor moved, a VP got sick.
- He says "the hours matter" in the earliest days, not the weeks.
- Speed can be taught to a degree. YC can often take a slow, limp mover and make them a fast, fearsome one by focusing on decisiveness. Some people never get there, which he calls a disposition issue.
- His own time management: over the previous six months he got good at saying no to things that were not a high-impact use of his time. His list of priorities as YC president:
  - grow YC
  - get the best companies in the world to apply
  - pick them well
  - advise them well
  - develop the YC network

chunks.heading: What YC is, how it recruits, and how it selects
chunks.text:
- He doesn't like the word "incubator." He describes YC as a source of funding, advice and a network, with YC as "a passenger in the back seat." Companies are their own and don't live in a dorm.
- He says the differences are:
  - the strength of the alumni network
  - full-time advisers rather than a pool of mentors
  - a track record of funding many billion-plus-dollar companies, which he says no other accelerator had done
- Recruiting works through several channels at once: the alumni network, Hacker News, and putting great content online. A class he taught with guest lecturers the previous fall got millions of views, and applicants rose roughly 40% to 60%.
- Outreach moves diversity numbers more than anything else. YC funds women, minorities and international founders at about the rate they apply (for example about 3% of applicants and about 3% of funded founders were black). Outreach included visiting HBCUs and holding a conference for women considering startups.
- The batch had 114 companies and high-30s countries, up from one country in the first batch.
- YC is deliberately unfiltered. It requires no intros and no network, sees tens of thousands of applications a year, and spends 90% of its time advising founders. So the interview is about 10 minutes. He admits it is imperfect and that YC rejects companies that would have been great.
- Criteria he lists: clarity of vision, clarity of explanation, determination, passion, and evidence of past accomplishment.
- YC tracks rejected applicants with custom software. He said it had not yet missed a billion-dollar company that applied, but was sure it would.
- On what to fund: "fund the smartest most determined people you can find with the clearest vision even if you don't understand yet why it's going to be a big deal." YC does best funding things others don't think will matter yet, and likes when other investors question a pick, then beg to invest two years later.

chunks.heading: Raising capital and staying lean
chunks.text:
- When to raise: "either when you have to or when it's really easy." That means the company desperately needs money, or someone offers easy money on good terms (often at the end of YC), which can then be used for good things.
- He thinks the culture has gone wrong: founders who haven't raised a lot don't think they are a real startup. When YC started it invested about $12,000 to $20,000 per company, and people now say they need a million dollars to build a product.
- He says it is still "an incredible win" to operate on small amounts of capital and build the product yourself rather than hire developers.
- Technical founders: it is very hard, from YC's data, to build a company with no technical founder. It is "not impossible but a significant headwind." Such companies find it harder to get a product built cheaply and to hire and evaluate engineers. His advice for non-technical founders is to spend whatever time it takes, even in another job, building a working relationship with a technical cofounder, not picking someone random.

chunks.heading: Location, scale and company structure
chunks.text:
- Silicon Valley: he expects it to stay dominant. People there want to get rich but will wait 8 to 10 years, and equity in a startup is the top prestige path, unlike finance in New York or film in Los Angeles. He noted that as far as he knew New York had not produced a $5B-plus tech company since Bloomberg. Housing cost is the main risk.
- Many foreign founders still want to come to the Valley for the 3-month batch. YC doesn't push them to stay, and some return home to their users.
- Talent is spread around the world, and he found Beijing especially impressive. He singled out Waterloo for engineering skill and a focus on what users want.
- YC could in theory run a batch outside the Valley, but it is not high on the list.
- He has no desire to run a public company and hopes YC never goes public. YC invests its own money with no outside LPs. He doesn't want a public shareholder or a bank calling about missing quarterly earnings "by a penny."
- Ethics policy: if a founder violates it, YC takes back the equity (the founder keeps the cash) and removes them from the program. He said it had happened twice.
- Government as a market: he sees the government as the largest enterprise customer in the world and says that bigger customers move slower. His advice is to start with small, bite-sized projects that agencies can act on quickly. He expects the area to become big and noted YC had funded many government-related startups in the past year.
- Mission: he argues growth must return to the economy and that startups are the main remaining driver of innovation, so there is a "moral imperative" to make more startups happen.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman's Startup School talk covers what separates great founders (determination, focus, self-belief, clear communication), why to hire on values first and skills last, and why iteration speed and a product a few users love matter most. He also critiques a live pitch: say what you do in one sentence upfront.

chunks.heading: Mindset and the traits of great founders
chunks.text:
- Sam says the two phrases top founders would use to describe themselves are "I always figure it out" and "I never give up." He puts this ahead of intelligence, domain expertise, network or connections.
- He calls the trait determination, or "relentlessly resourceful" (Paul Graham's phrase). Many people have everything else, so this is the rare, limiting trait.
- He thinks it can be learned by practicing it, as with any other skill.
- Three things he has seen successful founders do to get things done: focus, self-belief, and personal connections. Momentum is a "crazily self-fulfilling prophecy."
- Focus means a relentless single goal and ignoring shiny objects. The connections matter for recruiting, selling, raising money and talking to the press.
- Silicon Valley's strengths, in his view, are a relentless belief in the future, a critical mass of people who will not mock ambition, density, and a culture of paying it forward.
- He says people elsewhere should not grade themselves on a curve. Talent is evenly distributed, and apart from access to capital, everything else (office space, hiring engineers) is harder in Silicon Valley.
- He advises finding a few people you can call late at night with a wild idea who will engage with it instead of saying "that's dumb." Most ideas are bad, but the rare good ones get killed if everyone around you cuts them down.
- Live in the future: Alan Kay tries to think 30 years out and build what is 15 years out. Sam notes that this can look crazy in the present, and you will be mocked for it.
- He recommends working very hard early in your career. Hard work "pays off like compound interest," so doing it in your late teens and 20s gives it the most working years to pay off.

chunks.heading: Communication, vision and recruiting
chunks.text:
- Sam says he did not used to think clear communication mattered this much, but now does. Almost all the best startups' founders could explain what they do in about 25 words from the first meeting. Founders who can't tend not to succeed.
- Recruiting the first employees is very hard, and "it is easier to start a hard startup than it is to start an easy startup." An inspiring, exciting vision attracts people, while a fine but forgettable business does not.
- He says to be genuine rather than charismatic. Help people even without an immediate payoff. Sam describes this paying off years later in investments, partner hires and relationships.
- He holds up Brian Chesky as a model of communicating a vision, saying he makes Airbnb feel important.
- His advice on hiring: be realistic that you will only hire a few people and will get less done than you want. Hold the bar very high, because "two or three great people" beat "ten warm bodies." YC is always behind its hiring plan.

chunks.heading: Hiring framework: values, then aptitude, then skills
chunks.text:
- Sam's hiring order is values first, aptitude second, specific skills third. He says most people reverse this, and that "I need an engineer with a background in node" is the worst way to choose a co-founder.
- Treat the first ~10 hires as nearly co-founder level. They should believe in the mission, share your values and be very talented.
- He has "almost never gone wrong" hiring inexperienced but committed, talented people, and expects them to be a bit less productive for the first month. He has bet on many leaders without domain experience. The exception is a role like general counsel, where he would not hire a non-lawyer.
- He hires slowly and spends a lot of time with direct-report candidates: four or five meals, many hours in the office, and talking through life stories and goals. He says he cannot judge someone from two one-hour meetings.
- YC makes new partners go through roughly a year: office hours, then part-time partner for 6 to 12 months, then a trial period. Even with a friendly candidate, YC says no if it does not feel right.
- Example: YC set up a growth fund to invest $50M+ at a time. Everyone advised hiring an experienced growth-equity investor "in cufflinks and suits," but every candidate he met failed the values test. He hired the Twitter CFO, who had never invested, and it "worked out fantastically well." Specialists were hired under him.
- He is skeptical of founders who lack experience themselves but say they will only hire people with 20 years of experience.

chunks.heading: Ideas, timing and waves
chunks.text:
- Sam says people overrate the idea. There are many good ideas, but few people willing to put in years of effort. Still, a bad idea is also bad.
- YC funded 21 companies whose founders were strong but who had no idea. All 21 failed in the first year, the worst experiment they had run. Wait for an idea you believe in so passionately that a startup is the best way to pursue it.
- Original thought is rare, and copying is disastrous. After Facebook there were over a thousand social networks, and after Instagram over a thousand photo apps. The first mover usually wins. The year he joined Helion's board, there were 10,000 photo startups and one nuclear fusion startup.
- Good sources of ideas: problems in your own life (a high percentage of transformational companies began this way), and spotting a "great wave" of technology early.
- Founders can't create a technology wave, but they can notice one coming while others call it a toy and serve it. Waves explain clusters in time: the late-90s internet wave (Amazon, Google, Yahoo) and the post-2007 mobile wave (Uber, Airbnb, Snapchat, Instagram, WhatsApp). He says Facebook straddled both. He asks what the current wave is.
- His one bet he feels confident enough to name: machine learning applied to every vertical is "as close to a guaranteed shot as you can have," though it is brutally competitive and there will be $100M companies in it. He tells people to trust their own convictions over his.

chunks.heading: Co-founders and company culture
chunks.text:
- YC has a significant preference for co-founders, and about 10% of funded companies are single-founder. Sam says a solo founder is better than a bad co-founder, and cites Amazon as essentially a single-founder company.
- He wants shared history, like a relationship, so that goodwill carries you through the stressful stretch where a startup's expected value dips. He says co-founder pairs formed just to get into YC fall apart when stressed.
- Co-founders pull each other up on low days. Solo founders have no one to do that, so they need strong internal conviction.
- Don't pick a co-founder on technical skill alone. Pick for determination, and pick humble over entitled. A company reflects its founders' culture for a long time, and Sam says arrogance is poisonous.
- He says he has seen introverted founders conclude they need "a really outgoing, kind of arrogant" co-founder because that's what success looks like in movies, and he says that mistake hurts.
- On boards: a board's role is "advice and consent." It should fire a bad CEO, but otherwise give the CEO wide latitude. If you don't respect your board, fix the board.
- Good co-founder teams compromise heavily and each knows what the others care most about. He says a power-drunk CEO usually drives co-founders out. A good team staying together 10 to 20 years is very valuable.
- On decision-making at YC (18 partners), he describes explicit rules: things any one partner can do, things needing three partners, domain owners, and full-partnership votes for rare big decisions like raising the growth fund. He suggests spelling out up front who owns what.

chunks.heading: Product, users and iteration speed
chunks.text:
- Sam says "nothing but a great product will save you." The common startup mistake is doing well at marketing, hiring and fundraising while ignoring the essential task of making a great product, then blaming "conspiracy theories" when it fails.
- He cites Paul Buchheit's advice: a small number of users who love you beats a large number who like you a little. Get users who love it, then find more people like them. He says this is counterintuitive, since most think they need many users on day one.
- How many is enough depends on the product: for an enterprise product paying hundreds or thousands of dollars a year, ten could be enough, while a consumer product probably needs thousands.
- On the "magic moment," Alex Schultz of Facebook talks about the one thing that makes users love a product enough to tell friends. Airbnb asks how to deliver an "11-star experience" and then works back to a 6-star one so good people tell friends. Sam says there are trade-offs: a magic feature that makes the rest suck is probably not worth it.
- Iteration speed compounds. If your product improves 10% per cycle, a one-week cycle against a competitor's three months leaves them in the dust. He says most hard-tech startups fail because their cycles are about three months, "which basically rounds to infinity."
- He says hard-tech founders arrive saying they can't get anything done in 90 days, and leave saying it was the most productive 90 days of their lives. Ginkgo Bioworks' founder said doing YC at the start could have compressed their first seven years into one.
- Be a "strong ideas, weakly held" company: have one idea you believe is best, and change your mind on new data. Don't say "we could do these seventeen things."

chunks.heading: Evaluating hard-tech momentum: the Cruise example
chunks.text:
- Sam says investors are right that momentum matters, and that it can show up as fast growth or as continual breakthroughs in the lab. In hard tech you identify it by spending time in the lab, and he can often tell from one weekly research meeting.
- He sets a goal with each hard-tech startup for the end of the YC program. Founders who engage in a genuine brainstorm about an aggressive milestone are good, while those who say there's no intermediate milestone for three years usually fail.
- Cruise: YC funded the self-driving car company in January 2014, before self-driving cars were cool. It was run by a former Justin.tv co-founder with no car expertise. Investors thought it was crazy, and Google would win.
- They compromised on a goal: a car that drives itself on the highway from San Francisco to Mountain View by demo day. It did, with computers hanging out the back, 90 days later.
- Later investors passed on the A round (self-driving "isn't going to be a thing"). Sam wrote his biggest check of the year, and about seven months later GM acquired the company. Investors who had passed then asked him for more self-driving companies.
- His lesson: you can evaluate progress by going to the office, even without a daily-active-users chart. Most hard-tech companies, he notes, are not in fact progressing quickly.

chunks.heading: Pitching and investing advice
chunks.text:
- Sam gave live feedback on a pitch from Lucid Labs (AI skin cancer diagnosis). His first point was to state what you do in one simple sentence early, e.g. "We use AI to diagnose skin cancer better than the best human doctors." He says that 95% of pitches miss this and that investors want it most.
- Lead with the strongest proof, that the product works and beats human dermatologists, before the problem and market statistics. Replace long problem slides with a quick statement of the error rate and death toll.
- What you leave out matters as much as what you say. Show the roadmap for the next two years: how to get from here to clinics, revenue and impact.
- He says the competitive-landscape 2x2 where the startup sits in the upper right is "always terrible," and that no one ever says "we're a small market." Show how you win the market, e.g. get into 90,000 clinics.
- Put the big vision (an AI doctor for everything) at the end, after the focused starting point.
- On his own investing: his edge is a very long time horizon (holding 15 to 20 years), which most investors claim but do not really have. His personal system is a nightly list of three big tasks plus about 50 small ones, with mornings for creative work. He has used it for 15 years, and he says there's no secret beyond knowing what to get done and guarding your time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues hard tech founders should not think the rules differ: find a small, shippable first project, get 10% better every week, and serve a real customer fast. He covers why hard companies face less competition, why cost and cycle time matter, and failure modes like raising too much money and short-term investors.

chunks.heading: Hard tech startups follow the same rules as software startups
chunks.text:
- Sam's main point is to do as little differently as possible. The common mistake is thinking "I'm different because I'm saving the world, the normal rules of startups don't apply to me."
- Founders in that mode take a long time, use a lot of capital, skip finding a customer, and sit in a lab for five years without talking to anyone.
- YC briefly tried running hard tech companies as a separate group. Sam calls that "really bad" and stopped.
- Hard tech companies now sit in the mix with all other YC companies, whether they build nuclear reactors, synthetic biology or photo apps.
- His reasoning: "the market does not care" about a noble purpose. If you don't build a real thing for a real customer that is better and cheaper, or ideally both, you fail.
- The problem with hard tech companies is that they don't look enough like successful software companies, not that they look too much like them.
- In his view the rules apply "even a little bit more" to hard tech.

chunks.heading: Ship something in three months and improve 10% every week
chunks.text:
- Sam asks founders with a seven-year nuclear reactor plan what can be done in three months. They first say nothing, then find something, for example getting the heat system running.
- By the end of YC, companies "are always able to do more than they thought they could."
- Momentum "becomes a product of itself." Small incremental wins build on each other.
- He calls getting 10% better every week "the whole secret of software startups." Facebook started small and not very good, then improved 10% a week for years.
- With Ginkgo Bioworks, the first meeting was spent finding what they could make 10% better every week, ignoring how fast they thought they could move.
- The key step is a small initial project with a real test in the world that you complete on a short timeframe.
- Startups "survive on their own momentum." A startup that is winning keeps winning, and one that starts losing keeps losing. A founder should make the company win from the start, even with tiny wins.
- The common mistake is to "sit around and do nothing and talk a lot." Companies that win start doing things and get laughed at for how small they are. They build a culture of winning, and the critics eventually stop mattering.
- Momentum attracts good people and makes them work harder. If nothing ships for three years it doesn't matter whether you start today or tomorrow, but if something ships this week each day counts.

chunks.heading: Cost and cycle time decide whether a field suits a startup
chunks.text:
- Sam says the two factors that let software startups dominate are low cost and fast cycle time. Unit economics also help: another copy is usually free, and scale arrives fast enough to build network effects and monopoly.
- To judge a new field, check whether cost has come down dramatically and cycle time has gotten much faster. If so, startups can overcome their natural disadvantages. Genomics is his recent example.
- If you can't see how your work drives cost down and iteration speed up, "you have to think really hard about starting a startup there."
- Both variables are changing in almost every field, so he calls this a wonderful time to start a company in any of them.
- Time will always be against a small company. If you can get weekly improvement, big competitors won't match it and "you can really win."
- He says not to make excuses. Life is not fair and big companies don't play by fair rules, but complaining won't win. It is the founder's duty to find a way to get 10% better every week.
- Software founders can change course quickly, so they are specific about what they'll do. Hard tech founders are usually vague.

chunks.heading: Why hard companies can be easier to start than easy ones
chunks.text:
- Sam says it is often easier to start a hard company than an easy one. The 11,000th photo sharing app makes people roll their eyes, so hiring, investors and press are all hard.
- A synthetic biology or similar company draws people who want to help. He thinks this is "really badly underestimated."
- Few people try. He says there were about four private nuclear fusion companies in North America, which is an automatic competitive advantage.
- Cruise Automation (from MIT, YC) is his example. Founder Kyle was pressured to build another video streaming site and chose self-driving cars instead. The company didn't exist about two and a half years earlier, and GM signed an acquisition deal for a huge amount.
- SpaceX and Tesla had little competition for the same reason, since few people were starting rocket or electric vehicle companies.
- He argues good ideas are undervalued. Maybe 70 or 80% of venture capital chases the current fad (the next Facebook, then the next Workday), with founders moving like a school of fish.
- Taking time up front to find a great idea and a new technology you can explain gives an automatic advantage.
- He argues people misprice risk. If you work hard on a startup for a couple of years and fail, you still have nothing but great experience. The real risk is never trying a great idea.
- His advice on market choice is not to worry about competitors but to ask whether you believe you can build a $10 billion company in that market.

chunks.heading: Take detours with real customers
chunks.text:
- Founders hate detours but they are "worth it." Sam says to hold yourself to building something you can give a real customer in a short timeframe, which prevents the mistake that has killed most hard tech startups.
- Tesla built the expensive, "okay" Roadster, then the expensive but great Model S, and then used that revenue to build the Model 3. The mass-market electric car was released the month before this talk.
- SpaceX wants to go to Mars but resupplies the ISS and may build an internet network in space on the way.
- It is hard to go from zero to a colony on Mars with no intermediate steps.
- More hard tech startups fail from a grand plan that sounds good in the press and never produces anything than from a first project that was too small. Finding the "Goldilocks" project is "somewhat of an art."
- For a one-goal company like nuclear fusion, list the biggest risks and the risks you can test first, then find where they intersect to set the order. A first goal might be a stable plasma for a set time.
- Rigetti (quantum computing) is his example. In their first office hours Sam and Chad filled several whiteboards with steps to a working 40-qubit system. The first milestone was a software proof for the design, planned for three months and done in two.
- He also recommends government as a customer. He says it went out of fashion because of VC groupthink, that government is slower but its people want things better and cheaper, and that more YC companies now sell to it.

chunks.heading: What kills hard tech startups: short-term money, negativity, too much cash
chunks.text:
- **Short-term investors and partners:** Many say they are long-term and then push for a sale in a year. "The more time an investor spends trying to convince you that he or she is a very long-term oriented shareholder the less you should believe it."
- Sam keeps a separate list of investors willing to hold shares past 10 years, the typical VC fund lifetime.
- If you want a 15 to 20 year company, make sure the people around you will sign up for it. He has no problem with starting an easy software company first and doing the hard thing next.
- **Negative people:** Someone who says all day that it won't work will wear you down however tough you are, so remove them.
- **Too much money:** It can ruin culture and focus. YC data (small sample) showed companies that raised $40 million or more in their Series A failed far more often than the average Series A company, and he thinks the pull toward slowness is stronger in hard tech.
- **Only science skill:** Someone already on the team must get good at business. Sam says it is "not hard" and "less fun," and it is better than bolting on a business person later. He recommends YC or hands-on practice over business school.

chunks.heading: Funding, team and company-building answers from Q&A
chunks.text:
- **Co-founders:** The best sources are school and working together. Co-founder meetups are the worst. Startups bring out the worst in people, and a prior relationship lets you keep working together after expected value dips below zero. He advises being a solo founder over starting with someone you just met at a meetup, and trying a small project together first.
- **Control:** VCs learned from Google and Facebook that they make the most money when founders keep control. In today's climate you shouldn't be asked to give up board or voting control, and at most an investor lets you vote their shares.
- **Investors and small wins:** If an investor doesn't care about small wins, you don't want them. The right ones understand this is the only path for these companies.
- **Management at OpenAI:** What worked was getting the right people and setting short-term milestones against a chosen attack vector on how to build AI. His preferred theory is to get smart, motivated people who believe in the same mission, so you don't have to manage much.
