- **Patents:** YC advises every hard tech company to file a provisional patent. It takes about an afternoon and about $1,000 and buys a year before filing the full patent, which costs $15,000 to $20,000. He says it is a rare worthwhile task outside talking to users and building product.
- **Hardware and location:** Launching hardware and delivering the first thousands of units gets easier every six months and is no longer the problem that kills companies. YC started in Boston and moved to the Bay Area. Sam's concern is that Bay Area rent is very high (about $5,000 for a one-bedroom) and that people there think in two-year stints. Boston and Silicon Valley both work, and a natural reason can justify other places.
- **Lifestyle businesses:** They are fine, but YC's model loses money most of the time and relies on hits, so it does not fit them.
- **Fear of failure:** It is normal and "failing sucks," but nobody thinks about you as much as you do. Silicon Valley judges you on your biggest success rather than your biggest failure.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman, drawing on raising Loopt's Series A from NEA and Sequoia, explains when to raise, how to run a parallel process with 6-8 firms, what VCs look for, and which terms matter. His core point is that technical founders who understand product hold real leverage, and alternatives are the name of the game.

chunks.heading: Sam's case for not raising money early
chunks.text:
- Sam says a technical founder who also understands what the product should be and how to build it "is forced to be reckoned with" in Silicon Valley. He says this is valued more here than anywhere else, and that founders have more leverage over investors than they realize.
- If you can avoid raising, or wait, he says that is "hugely to your advantage". Raising lots of money can work well, but it can also slow you down.
- Good reasons to raise:
  - The company needs a lot of money to execute.
  - Funding will help win sales or partnerships by showing partners you will be around.
  - The money will help scale the business.
- The longer you wait, the more likely you are to have figured out a product that works, and the better your valuation.
- Raising money on day one is "almost always a mistake".
- Bad reasons he says he hears more and more:
  - Legitimizing the company, or wanting a VC behind you just to feel real.
  - Getting great PR from the funding.
  - "Funding will make me successful." He says funding does not make you successful, and that raising VC is "the beginning of a very long process".
- Sam says Loopt raised its Series A (NEA and Sequoia) "probably earlier than we should have". The reason was legitimacy with the wireless carriers. After Y Combinator and as college sophomores, the company was out of money by the time it signed.

chunks.heading: Angel vs VC, and how to run the process
chunks.text:
- **VC vs angel:** VCs almost always do more work for you than angels, whatever the angels say.
  - Fundraising is a VC's full-time job.
  - They have large networks, and the whole partnership works to help you.
- **Exit options:** An angel round leaves the "sell early" option open in a way a VC round does not. Founders must decide whether they want to build something big or flip it quickly.
  - If an early exit is the strategy, he would be disinclined to do a VC round.
- **Angel terms:** Angels usually, but not always, invest faster and on slightly more favorable terms.
- **Starting materials:** a one-page executive summary and a 10-15 slide deck. Use the summary to get intros to firms.
- **Focus:** Go after the good firms. Good companies are rare, so a good team doing something interesting has an easy time raising.
- **Number of firms:** Six to eight firms is what works most often.
- **Run the process in parallel,** for two reasons:
  - Investors only give you leverage-relevant attention when they fear losing the deal. "The more alternatives you have the better", which he says is true of all deal making.
  - Going serially (first choice, a month of process, then second, then third) means three months gone if the first three pass. Competitors will have "blown past" you, since "speed is the key to a startup". You also now have a shopworn reputation, because later VCs will see that good firms passed.
- **Timeline and meetings:** The number of meetings varies. Sequoia met Loopt 10 times before funding, while other firms issued term sheets with zero meetings.
  - You meet more and more partners, then reach a Monday partners' meeting, and they decide.
  - During diligence, help them: let them talk to users and customers, and give financial projections, past finances and product and technology detail. User adoption data matters most.
- **Herd behavior:** If one primary firm wants a deal in a space, every other firm wants one too. Getting your company talked about at the Friday-afternoon drinks scene is a net win. The key to deals is making everyone feel you have a great alternative you will probably take.
- **Term sheets:** The first one typically arrives four to six weeks in. Once word leaks, many more arrive. He never figured out why a business is a good deal today but was not yesterday.
  - Multiple offers let you negotiate. Valuation and ownership percentages move little, but other terms move a lot.
- **Stay focused:** Put one person on fundraising, spending about half their time. He has seen companies die because all three or four people agonized over the process.
- **Closing takes longer than expected:** After signing the term sheet, expect four or five or more weeks for lawyers to reach definitive documents.
  - Loopt had no idea definitive documents existed and had no money in the bank. They only closed when they called both sets of lawyers and said they needed to close by the next night because they were out of money.

chunks.heading: What investors look for and the pitch
chunks.text:
- Sam says investors look for a great market, a great team, and a product that addresses the market. VCs increasingly want revolutionary rather than incremental businesses, because of how their model works.
- **Big growing market:** "You need to surf someone else's wave." He says startups cannot create markets, and probably cannot create a market opportunity.
  - Example: fast internet, lots of bandwidth and a good Flash codec let you build YouTube.
  - You need a big, fast-growing market for a 10x or 100x return. Without it, the business probably does not suit VCs.
- **Customers with their hair on fire:** such customers overpay, act fast, take a risk on a young company, and do not mind bugs in a first version.
- **Unfair advantage:** The VC must be comfortable that competitors will not fund someone exactly like you who then crushes you.
  - Examples: technology no one else has, a smarter team, a unique partnership, or built-up network effects. It is probably not patents, though a case can be made.
- **Team and product:** A great team and a great product "get deals done". He thinks a great team can correct product deficiencies more easily than a product can make up for a team.
  - Most VCs say one of team, market or product comes first, and which one they say is instructive about the VC.
- **Demand by proxy:** In a new market with no data on what works, this is the second-best thing. Loopt's example: it showed where your friends are on a map, and "where are you" is the most common text message sent in the world.
- **The story to convince them of, in four points:**
  1. This is an exploding market.
  2. Nothing currently good addresses the customer's needs.
  3. We have the best solution.
  4. We have the best team.
- Convince an investor of those and "you will be most of the way to a term sheet".
- Tell a big story. VCs do not want to hear something incremental. They want to hear how it will become a massive deal.
- He says there are about 450 VC firms in Silicon Valley and only the first 15 or 20 make a profit, so go for good investors.

chunks.heading: Terms: valuation, ownership and option pool
chunks.text:
- Sam says technical founders usually understand terms poorly, but this is not an area to spend much time on.
- **Definitions:**
  - Pre-money is the value an investor assigns before investing.
  - Post-money is the value after investment.
  - The option pool is what you earmark for employees.
- **Option pool:** Make it as small as possible. At a funding stage it comes out of only the founders' share, not the new investors'.
- **Think in ownership percentages,** not pre-money valuations, even though investors will push the valuation framing.
- **Raising more raises valuation:** Investors have a minimum ownership target. A professional VC Series A needs 20-25% and cannot go below.
  - Raising more money can mean a higher pre-money valuation too, with the same investor percentage.
- **Raise twice what you think you need.** Raising is time-consuming and things rarely go as planned.
- **Worked example:** With a $7M pre-money valuation, $3M invested and a 25% option pool, you might expect to own 70%, but you would not.
  - The investor's ownership comes out of post-money. Add the investment to pre-money, then divide investment by post-money.
- **Don't fight over fractions:** Do not focus on tenths or hundredths of a percent. It wastes a lot of time, and you are better off with the right partner and a little less equity.
  - Giving up a little more equity for a better partner is better than a second-rate partner.
- He says that if outside investors own more than 50% after a couple of rounds, "it's not such a bad thing".

chunks.heading: Terms: board, vesting, liquidation preference and watch-outs
chunks.text:
- **Board composition** is a major term. Current practice is three or five seats.
  - Three seats for smaller rounds: two founders and an investor.
  - Five seats for bigger rounds: two founders, two investors and one outside director.
  - The board decides change of control, going public, and can fire the CEO, so pay attention to it.
  - Founders should have veto rights on change of control.
- **Vesting:** Standard is four years. Founders who have been working a while often get one year accelerated up front, with the rest over three years.
  - Ask for some acceleration on a change of control.
- **Liquidation preference:** how much investors get before anyone else.
  - A 1x preference on a $5M investment means the first $5M of a sale. He thinks that is fair.
  - Some investors ask for 3x or 4x. With multiple term sheets you should be able to negotiate this down to 1x.
- **Preferred vs participating preferred:** Participating preferred is "double dipping". Investors take their preference first, then also share in the rest.
  - Push them to plain preferred.
- **Anti-dilution and pro rata:** It is fair for investors to maintain their ownership.
  - Avoid "super pro rata", where an early investor gets the right to buy all of the next round. It scares off new investors, who will not talk to you if they know one investor can take the whole round.
- **Founder-shares:** Founders sometimes set up a special stock class (such as Series FF) they can sell in the B round, set up ahead of time so it does not distort common stock strike price.
  - It is controversial. Pushing hard for it can signal that the founder wants a quick flip and not to build value.
  - He has seen investors pass on deals over it. If it matters to you, think about why you want it and how you ask.

chunks.heading: Leverage, investor selection and keeping going
chunks.text:
- Alternatives are "the name of the game". Loopt started by talking to just one VC with no alternatives. As soon as word got out that they were talking to a few, "the whole thing changes".
- **Two-firm deal:** Loopt did one, almost by accident, and calls it wonderful.
  - You get two firms' connections and two sets of advice.
  - The two investors keep each other in check and stop either from behaving badly.
- **Reference-check the investor:** Investors do heavy diligence on you, and you should do the same.
  - Talk to CEOs the investor funded, and look for ones who failed to hear what working with that investor was like.
- **Getting intros without connections:**
  - NEA gets about 10,000 business plans a year over the wire and has never funded one. Sequoia has funded a few.
  - Events like Startup School are the route. You can reach any VC through 10 different paths by talking to people there.
  - Ask people directly: "I'm looking to get to these VCs, this is my idea, if you think it's exciting could you help me out?"
  - VCs need you. You will have a successful company with or without funding, but they have no job if they do not find companies to fund.
- **Don't get discouraged:** The summer of Y Combinator, Loopt looked like it would blow up every day. Sam says it was a joke: "what can be the worst thing to happen to us this week, it'll probably happen". Stay focused on a great company, product and team, and "more often than not things work out".

chunks.heading: Carrier deals and justifying how much to raise
chunks.text:
- **Carrier deals (Sprint and others):** Sam says they are very difficult, with no way around the red tape.
  - Loopt raised early partly for legitimacy: Sequoia's backing said "this is a real company, they're not going anywhere".
  - The first use of the money was hiring an experienced carrier business development executive, someone doing it for 20 years.
  - High-level relationships and press matter, since carrier executives read The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times.
  - A compelling product where you do most of the work and the carrier just turns it on and markets it is very appealing.
- **Justifying the amount:** VCs want financial plans, but they can be rough: how many people, the average cost, marketing spend, "we need to buy a thousand servers".
- **Don't inflate the number.** Raise more by asking for a longer horizon: "we want it for the next two, two and a half years" so you do not need to raise again, and because spending ramps up.
- Loopt did not have financial projections until late in the process, and Sam says they did not know how to use Excel until then.
- He notes that if you are going to raise, the current economy (2008) is a reason to do it then.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman lays out how he invests in startups: optimize for the power law, ask how big it could be before what could go wrong, and pick exceptional founders over ideas. He also covers reputation, real vs. fake trends, and why market size in ten years matters more than today.

chunks.heading: Sam's reasons for investing in startups (and what he says about angel investing)
chunks.text:
- Sam cites energy, shaping the future, and leverage on time as the draws of startup investing. He says founders are "not burned out on the world at all" and will try things that people with more battle scars won't.
- Most investments lose money, but "occasionally you do get to make a hundred or a thousand x". He compares the appeal to a slot machine.
- Founders sometimes tell him that something he did eight or ten years earlier made or broke their career. He calls this deeply gratifying.
- He writes his confidence interval and expectations on a Post-it on the back of every stock certificate. He says this teaches you that you are usually wrong, and that the habit has helped him in everything else.
- He says you can get better at this quickly if you treat it as deliberate practice.

chunks.heading: The two biggest investor mistakes: copying other investors and misreading the power law
chunks.text:
- His number one early mistake was caring too much about what other investors thought. He estimates 80% of investors outsource 80% of their decision-making to others. "The first question that most people ask... is who else is investing in your round."
- This creates a schooling effect, where a company gets hot for no discernible reason because a few people liked it.
- His second mistake was not understanding the power law. His single best investment returns more than all the rest combined, and his second best beats investments three through infinity combined.
- Most investors ask whether they can hit a bunch of singles. He says that works for stocks or bonds, but "angel investing is a business of homeruns."
- Asking about an acceptable failure rate is "totally the wrong question." You can have 95% of investments fail if one returns a billion dollars.
- When he meets a startup, the first question is "how big could this be if it works?", not what could go wrong. Asking what could go wrong first filters out the companies that could be giant.
- The best companies sit at the intersection of "sounds like a bad idea" and "is a good idea." The best investments are the easiest to talk yourself out of.
- YC numbers at the time: about 1,600-1,700 companies funded. The top five represent about two-thirds of the value created, and the top one nearly one-third.

chunks.heading: Finding deals: open networks, referrals, and reputation
chunks.text:
- Many generation-defining companies come from out-of-network, unknown founders. Word of mouth from existing founders is the best way to find them. YC tries to make founders like it so much that they refer their friends.
- For new angels, he says the most successful approach he has seen is helping founders for free. Even without investing in those companies, the referrals come later.
- He argues for an open network. Many angels brag about being hard to reach. YC lets anyone apply, answers emails, and takes people with no brand, reputation or network seriously. He calls this one of the "two or three most important secrets of YC."
- He recommends staying open to random emails and odd introductions: "nine times out of ten you waste your time [and the] other time makes it totally worth it."
- There are now far more investors than good startups, so founders hold the leverage, and the asymmetry is unlikely to return. Founders talk to each other.
- Reputation is the key to winning deals. Founders do reference checks on investors, increasingly using what other founders say about them.
- He warns against fighting over a dying company for small sums (e.g. $10,000) because of the long-term reputational damage. Under the power law, those companies never mattered anyway.
- Other things that help: being fast to decide, being clear about reasoning, and being responsive and available.

chunks.heading: Price, terms, and what to invest in
chunks.text:
- On bargain-hunting, he says value investing is not a winning strategy for angels. With one or two exceptions, his best investments felt the most expensive at the time, including rounds that were huge step-ups from rounds three months earlier.
- The exceptions were companies where he understood something no one else did, so there was no competition.
- Example: a company had about 10 seed investors, and all 10 asked for advisor shares, each claiming to be the only one who works hard.
- His investment filter is whether he believes it could be a $10 billion company. He has no other rules on stage, sector or business model, because the top-spot companies are so rare.
- He thinks it is easier to start a hard company than an easy one. Ambitious companies attract hires, press, advisors and help. "If you are starting the 20 million photo sharing application it's really hard; if you are starting a nuclear fusion company a lot of people want to help."
- A key filter is whether the company can recruit hundreds of talented people who could otherwise start their own companies.

chunks.heading: Evaluating founders
chunks.text:
- YC mostly picks founders, because it is hard to tell at the idea stage that an idea will be huge, though you can tell when one won't. With practice you can identify founders who have a chance.
- Four traits from YC partner Paul Buchheit (the transcript renders it as "Pabu hi"): obsession, focus, formidability and love.
- Intelligence and idea generation: YC once funded 20-odd teams of strong founders who had no ideas, and all failed. Good founders have ideas all the time, so he looks for creative, independent thinking.
- Communication skills: founders are evangelists for hiring, fundraising, sales and setting direction. Founders of super successful companies tend to be great communicators.
- Execution speed: between weekly or ten-day office hours, how much did the founders try, test and learn? This relentless cadence is "incredibly predictive of success." He contrasts it with founders who look great on paper but always have reasons they didn't do things.
- Rate of improvement: don't compare a seed founder to Brian Chesky. Look at the founder's growth rate. In YC's ten weeks you can often see it. He has seen it about ten times and says he has been right every time he felt a founder would develop into a great leader.
- Motivation: starting up takes more than a decade and many days of wanting to quit. Founders who want to get rich quickly or add a resume item don't last. Every time YC thought a company would go well and it didn't, the founders lacked a deep sense of mission.
- "Scenesters" are people who like startup parties and being called founders. He treats this as a red flag, along with low integrity.
- He says he has never made a lot of money backing a founder he thought was only okay in an otherwise good business. He wants founders he'd want to work for.

chunks.heading: Markets, trends, and product quality
chunks.text:
- He says investors wrongly fixate on market size today. What matters is market size in ten years. "You should prefer a small market growing super quickly to a very large market today." Facebook, Uber and others started in markets that barely existed.
- Chasing what worked last time (more social networks, more ride-sharing apps) is much harder than finding the next fast-growing market, which requires independent thought.
- Real vs fake trends: in a real trend, few people use it yet but those who do use it hourly and spontaneously tell friends. The iPhone had only a million or two sales in year one, but owners used it for hours daily and evangelised it.
- By contrast, he says VR headsets (in 2018) mostly sit on shelves. He would invest heavily in VR once users wear headsets for hours daily and tell everyone to buy one.
- He quotes Sequoia: "you cannot create a technology wave... but you can surf one if you can find the wave." He says most of the biggest tech companies form soon after a platform shift.
- He looks for good ideas that look bad. Roughly 90% of angel capital goes to bad ideas that look good, such as chasing what worked two years ago, markets with hundreds of similar companies, or founders working hard to convince you they aren't a commodity.
- Great products matter. Growth hacking and sales machines can grow a mediocre product for a while, but they don't build a Facebook-size company. His test: did a trusted friend spontaneously tell him about it? If the startup won't get there, it won't be the number one power-law return.
- Human intuition about exponential growth is terrible (e.g. 25% monthly growth for 36 months). He models it out, applies a growth decay rate, and asks how big a word-of-mouth company could be in five years.
- He wants a company that gets stronger as it grows: more pricing power, easier user acquisition, harder to compete with (network effects, moats). Almost all the value comes from earnings in years 10 and 11 onward, so be skeptical if you can't answer this.
- He asks "what do I understand that other people don't?" If he has no answer, he has no edge. An acceptable answer can be being more bullish than everyone else because of a specific insight about the market.

chunks.heading: Q&A: adding value, pro rata, and judgment calls
chunks.text:
- Helping founders: the top request is hiring (finding people, helping interview, sourcing), followed by fundraising help. As an angel he made himself available for tactical advice, even for a two-minute call on a Friday night.
- Founder flaws: he separates traits that can change from those that can't. Don't compromise on integrity, but accept many gaps (like not knowing what a valuation is) if the founder is improving fast and mission-driven.
- Integrity: ask about past decisions, because founders will often tell you the unethical things they've done. YC makes its decisions in 10-minute interviews and has been fooled sometimes, but caught it hundreds of times.
- Pro rata: studies by several venture firms conclude you should always exercise pro rata if the up round is led by a top-quartile VC. Pro rata is the right to invest in future rounds to maintain ownership.
- ICOs and security tokens: he thinks they will change financings, but not as most people expect. Securities laws exist for a reason, and many ICOs fall between incompetence and scams. Better mechanical tracking of investments is plausible.
- Good ideas that look bad: Reddit (in his 2005 YC class) was dismissed by people he trusted. His own conviction vanished when they said it was a bad idea. Dropbox was dismissed because "Google, Microsoft... guaranteed to crush them."
- Uber's market size was repeatedly underestimated in articles. Look at shifts in consumer behavior: Uber replaced limo booking, then taxis, then public transit, then car ownership.
- Solo non-technical founders: he has done it and says it can work. YC strongly prefers at least one technical co-founder and at least two founders, but treats these as preferences, not absolutes.
- Self-awareness: willingness to take feedback and a drive to improve matter, as does believing you can succeed in spite of your flaws.
- Time allocation: "only fund founders that you want to allocate a lot of time to." If you don't want to help them, that is a red flag for the founder.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains how YC picks founders (clear communication, relentless work, excellence at every step), why open applications and public advice drove YC's growth, and how he thinks about OpenAI's mission, staged GPT-2 release, and capped-profit structure.

chunks.heading: Selecting founders: what Sam looks for at YC
chunks.text:
- Sam observes that most great founders come from stable, upper-middle-class backgrounds, not the very poor or the very rich. He calls this "a real shame" but says you need enough stability, a great education and loving parents to compound through early life long enough to start a company.
- YC interviews started at 40-45 minutes (his own batch-one interview) and were cut to about 10 minutes. He thinks 5 minutes would reach decisions "90 percent or 95 percent as good", but says that isn't socially acceptable.
- Much of what matters shows up in the first few minutes: how someone thinks and how they react when pushed on their idea.
- A good interview feels like the company's first office hours: "let's talk together about how to build this company into something really big."
- Open contempt between cofounders is a sign to "walk away slowly". He says there are no secret physical tells.
- The trait he looks for most is clear communication. About 95% of a CEO's job is communicating and evangelizing: hiring, retaining, selling and fundraising. "If you cannot clearly communicate an ambitious vision we will probably not fund you," and it is hard to fake.
- YC has a cottage industry of interview coaching, but Sam says they can usually tell who has used it, and it doesn't help.

chunks.heading: Age, work ethic and honesty about the founder life
chunks.text:
- YC's best investments have mostly been founders in their mid-20s to mid-30s. The same batch once included a 15-year-old, with parents signing documents, and a founder around 78-80.
- Age matters less than evidence of excelling at every step: "whatever hand life dealt you, you have done as well as anyone we can imagine." He grades a 40-year-old harder than a 20-year-old.
- He says age is often shorthand for willingness to work extremely hard. It is "a real disservice" to pretend you can build a hyperscale startup without making it the priority of your life for some period.
- YC tries to be upfront about this. The only time founders regret YC is when they feel they weren't told how much they would have to sacrifice.
- "One of the worst things that can happen to you is that your company succeeds when you're really young." It takes over your life more than people believe.

chunks.heading: YC's real innovations and the funding climate
chunks.text:
- Sam says YC has had maybe five total innovations. Two he names:
  - Anyone in the world can apply, and YC puts in the effort to find the good ones. Before YC, you needed a business school pedigree, a business plan, experienced managers and a warm intro from "the right economic class".
  - YC publishes all its advice and keeps nothing secret.
- Together these increased the number of good companies in the world that people decide to start.
- Most of YC's current growth is outside the US. One success in a new market, such as Rappi from Bogota, sends a flood of applicants from that country. He thinks YC has "an easy 10x" of growth ahead over 10-20 years.
- On funding, if he could control the market he would not have YC companies raise millions or tens of millions at the end of YC. He says that happens without enough diligence or discipline on price, and it hurts companies in their next round. He expects capital to normalize over time.
- A question he now asks early is how the company will concentrate enough really good people. Capital is abundant, so "capital concentrated talent" is the scarce resource.
- On the next Silicon Valley, he says there will never be another one in a single place; talent will diffuse everywhere.

chunks.heading: Sam's self-assessment and who he relies on
chunks.text:
- He says his main strengths are thinking further into the future than most people and appreciating exponential curves more than most.
- He calls himself a good leader but a bad manager. He doesn't want daily one-on-ones about feelings. He prefers "there's this interesting thing, let's go figure out how to get it done."
- He says YC's success was mostly Paul Graham and Jessica Livingston's work and that he "was basically handed a thing that all I had to do was not screw up".
- He says that as you become prominent, people filter and pre-plan what they tell you. He therefore relies on a small set of people for honest life advice: his parents, his partner, and Paul and Jessica.
- His mom pushed him to pick the computer science path he wanted over a full-ride scholarship elsewhere.

chunks.heading: OpenAI's mission, business model and capped-profit structure
chunks.text:
- OpenAI's goal is building safe AGI. Sam believes some group will build a system smarter than humans in every way within decades, and it could quickly become a million or billion times more capable. He says the timeline debate is a distraction.
- The company had about 90 employees and no revenue, and no current plans for it. The "soft promise to investors" is that once they build a generally intelligent system, they will ask it to figure out how to generate a return.
- He says capital needs are unknown: "billions for sure, tens of billions maybe, hundreds of billions I sure hope not." Funding had mostly come from individual investors, and he expects institutions as capital needs grow.
- The first-round investors' cap is 100x. Later rounds get a lower cap, and he hopes it "will come down to hopefully 1x near the end".
- His reasoning is that if AGI works, a group could "capture the light-cone of all future value in the universe", which one group of investors should not own. A 100x return from a seed-stage bet seemed fair to him.
- Hiring is hard because they are "badly outgunned financially" by big tech. The pitch is the mission, working on behalf of the world, and the thrill of discovery rather than optimizing ad clicks.
- OpenAI's differentiators, in his words, are that they "do the best research in the world" and "care the most about how it gets deployed".
- At this stage, all work is pure research: reinforcement learning, robotics, video games, and unsupervised learning such as a text model that learns to predict the next word without labels.
- He believes the best route to solving climate change is to build strong AI first. He is open to working with the military depending on conditions.

chunks.heading: Staged release of GPT-2 and AI risk
chunks.text:
- OpenAI did not release the full GPT-2 weights and instead released increasingly large models in stages. He says society hasn't built "antibodies" for fake text the way it has for photoshopped images.
- The academic ML community objected because it went against the norm of open sharing. Most of the rest of the world found it reasonable.
- He expects to release less and less as systems approach general intelligence, and says people will be upset. He argues "I'd much rather be a little bit too early than a little bit too late" with something you can't un-push.
- He says much of AI progress will come from scaling systems bigger and bigger. The criticism that GPT-2 was just 10x compute is, in his view, partly true.
- On press attention, he says OpenAI produces approachable, interactive blog posts and demos, but doesn't call journalists. He was caught off guard by GPT-2's attention.
- His near-term risks are autonomous weapons and cybersecurity, which he calls "eye-wateringly bad and not taken particularly seriously". He says systems get roughly one order of magnitude more powerful per year.
- He believes the tech industry has "failed the good faith test" on assuming it will be thoughtful, so OpenAI must show it will be.

chunks.heading: Economic growth, immigration and policy views
chunks.text:
- He says "democracy only works in a growing economy" and that most people are not enamored with the tech industry as winners win bigger.
- He believes only something on the order of general AI's impact can restore global economic growth equitably.
- To stay less insulated, he travels and stays in touch with people outside the Silicon Valley bubble.
- If he could pick one policy for the global economy, it would be to fix immigration. Immigrants are a high share of tech founders, and concentrating talent in the US has been a major advantage.
- On facial recognition, he is more concerned than not and says details matter. He thinks society needs a real conversation about how privacy and speech rights should evolve when everything is digitally captured.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2015 fireside chat, Sam Altman explains what YC looks for in founders (clarity, determination, passion), why great products win long-term, why to focus on users who love you, and why to perfect the product before ramping burn. He also covers small teams for engineering culture and holding investments for the long term.

chunks.heading: Founding YC: breadth, speed and long time horizons
chunks.text:
- Sam notes YC gets about 15,000 applications a year and funds about 200. He estimates roughly half of the applicants are fundable, high-quality companies. YC has not yet figured out how to fund 7,500 a year, but he says it needs to be able to fund 1,000+ per year.
- The YC model (speed of iteration, doing things quickly and cheaply) has worked beyond software. YC has funded four or five nuclear energy companies, plus rocket, quantum computing and synthetic biology companies.
- His stated vision is for YC to be a "Hub of innovation in the world". He wants to put more new innovation into the world than Google does, and he is flexible on how that looks.
- He says there is a big premium for being willing to hold an illiquid security for a long time. Most people try to trade around earnings and get less value than someone holding 10+ years.
- YC is not a trader. It uses its own money with no limited partners, so it can hold shares on a 20-year outlook, which a venture fund with a 10-year life cannot do.
- He has never sold a share in a company unless a founder asked him to (for example, to provide liquidity). He hopes YC still holds its Airbnb shares, bought six years earlier, another six years and well beyond.
- He calls this "infinite time Horizon" investing one of the secrets of YC's success, and the reason YC can back nuclear energy while most investors can't.

chunks.heading: Don't dismiss ideas as small or stupid
chunks.text:
- Sam's pet peeve is journalists and others who never create companies complaining that YC and founders fund "small" companies.
- His examples: Google was mocked as a 13th search engine and not even a portal. Facebook was "a social network of college students who cares". Airbnb was mocked constantly: "who's going to like stay on like a air mattress in some stranger apartment", and he admits it didn't sound that appealing to him either.
- His reasoning: "exponential growth is this very powerful force", and people wrongly call an idea small or stupid because they can't see how it will evolve.
- His advice: ignore people who don't build anything, start whatever company you want, and "continue to pull at that thread and see where it goes". Sometimes it stays small and sometimes it becomes Google, Facebook or Airbnb.
- He avoids criticizing what others work on. His experience is that if you bet on smart people, they eventually figure out their way into the big idea.

chunks.heading: Where he wants more startups: energy, AI, synthetic biology
chunks.text:
- Cheap energy: if he could snap his fingers to improve life for the poorest 3.5 billion people, it would be really cheap, clean, safe energy. He is uninterested in companies that compete with subsidies to be barely as cheap as oil or gas. Energy at "a penny a kilowatt" would be transformational, and most wars get fought over energy.
- Nuclear: he says nuclear's safety record is 1,000 to 10,000 times better than coal, yet people prefer to live next to a coal plant. His explanation is that people overweight theatrical extreme risk and underweight boring slow risk. He is convinced the 22nd century will be powered by nuclear energy of some sort, or solar and wind.
- Machine learning: it is working well and has a long way to go. YC had just agreed to fund a semi-company, semi-nonprofit doing AI safety research.
- Synthetic biology: a company he met that day is building a generic antiviral because the founders got scared of engineered viruses.
- His test for new startup areas is cost and cycle time. When both fall, a startup can exist where it couldn't before. Genomics is the example: sequencing costs fell faster than Moore's law, so a company can now diagnose infectious disease by sequencing every nucleic acid in a blood sample and matching it, which "becomes a computer science problem".

chunks.heading: What he looks for in founders
chunks.text:
- Clarity of vision: founders who can say clearly in a few sentences what they do and why. He says the correlation with success is strong, probably because unclear communicators can't recruit, get press or raise money. A clear idea helps even if it doesn't sound great.
- Determination: the trait YC looks for most. Most startups fail in the first couple of years because the founders give up, so he looks for evidence they won't, from this company or other points in their lives.
- Passion over polish: a common failure case is an MBA with a polished idea and market research who picked it to make money. Better is someone like Brian Chesky who cares about the idea and is unpolished on details. Sam recalls telling Brian his first financial model was financially illiterate, and says it didn't matter.
- Intelligence: easy to judge in a 10-minute conversation. Determination is much harder to judge.
- Red flag: co-founders fighting in the room.
- His record is imperfect: "no one gets this right all the time and that's sort of why it's fun."

chunks.heading: Choosing between starting a company and joining one
chunks.text:
- He uses two frameworks that can conflict: impact maximization and regret minimization.
- Regret minimization: if you'd regret for life not starting a particular company you're in love with, you might start it even if joining Airbnb as employee 30 would give more impact.
- Impact maximization: job satisfaction rises with impact on the company or world, and a huge success as an employee can beat a mild success as a founder.
- The hard part is weighing the two and getting the probabilities right.
- On picking what to work on, he says his famous post glossed over the question, and the "do what you're passionate about" advice is incomplete. His advice is to trust your own read of where the world is going in a domain you understand, shape your career toward it, and ignore what others say, which is the hardest part.
- Example: when he agreed to take over YC, people called it a joke and told him not to. He thought hard about how the world and the company would evolve, limited himself to four opportunities he understood well, and applied the two frameworks.

chunks.heading: Product first, then growth spend
chunks.text:
- He argues great products win in the long run. Enduring companies win on product. Examples he gives are Apple, Google (Search, Gmail, Maps), Airbnb and Facebook.
- Weak products can survive for a while through sales and marketing or a monopoly (Microsoft for years), and you can get acquired two years in on good press. That does not create enduring value.
- He doesn't let anyone off the hook on sales and marketing: "if you build the best product in the world and don't get anyone to use it uh that still kind of sucks". Without it you don't get the flywheel going.
- This is why engineers and designers start winning companies: if you are bad at everything else but make a great product, you can still win as a startup.
- On burn: founders get in trouble by investing in growth before the product works. If users don't stick around, sales and marketing dollars are wasted.
- He says VCs push burn up too early. They earn a 2% management fee only on capital deployed, and they raise the next fund on marked-up valuations, so they want you to spend and raise again.
- His rule: "it's almost never the wrong choice to get the product great first and then ramp up the burn". Ramping first and praying works only occasionally ("sometimes lightning strikes").

chunks.heading: Listening to users
chunks.text:
- Both A/B tests and one-on-one conversations have weaknesses: users are often bad at explaining what they want, and metrics can lie.
- North Star: make a product that a small number of users love rather than one that many users like (a "six out of 10"). It's much easier to go from a few users loving it to many than the reverse.
- Tactics: have lots of one-on-one conversations, still watch the metrics, identify your best users, find where more of them are, and work out how to make them like it more.
- He calls the common approach of interviewing users who churned ("why didn't you like this?") much weaker. Asking people who already use the product how to get them to use it more is "a 10x better strategy".

chunks.heading: Engineering culture and team size
chunks.text:
- The thing most companies get wrong: talented engineers together easily produce bad interpersonal dynamics. Strong cultures don't let conflict fester and don't keep brilliant but toxic engineers.
- Companies pay lip service to putting people and work environment first, then drop it when the trade-off is a missed deadline versus a happy team.
- On founders asking how to make engineers work 15 hours instead of 9, he says to make them like the work and believe in the mission. Demanding more office hours is something only bad founders say.
- A good engineering culture is one where everyone believes the work will really matter and likes their environment and colleagues. Management mechanics like project sizing matter but are secondary.
- Team size: tools and languages are so powerful that work needing thousands now needs hundreds and soon dozens. Keeping the team smaller than anyone thinks possible, for a long time, makes culture better. He keeps the YC team intentionally small for this reason.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains what YC teaches startups (make something a few users love, then grow with momentum) and common seed-to-Series A mistakes: neglecting retention, mis-delegating, and over-optimizing fundraising headlines. He also covers how YC picks founders in 10 minutes, what predicts breakouts, and why he's bullish on AI.

chunks.heading: YC's mission and what Sam added to Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- Sam wants YC to be "the organization that enables the most innovation in the world." He says that is Google today and he hopes it is YC in the not so distant future.
- His logic is that economic growth is needed, growth requires more innovation, and so YC should maximize innovation, including things that may not make money.
- Programs he added after taking over (he had been president for about two and a half years):
  - Funding hard-science companies: self-driving (Cruise, later acquired by GM), nuclear energy, biotech, space and aircraft. These need huge capital and existing investors would not fund them, so YC started doing it.
  - A growth fund, to keep supporting companies that come out of the portfolio.
  - The YC Fellowship, a light-touch early-stage program. The goal is to eventually touch 10,000 companies a year, because the core program is too small.
  - YC Research, a nonprofit group funding important technology that does not fit a for-profit startup (AI, basic income, education, possibly synthetic biology).
- He objects to analogies like "university" or "DARPA" for YC. He thinks it is a fundamentally new structure that will take about 50 years to fully figure out.
- He would invest in things that take 100 years: the biggest investor advantage is "a longer time horizon than everybody else" and a willingness to take more illiquidity and volatility.

chunks.heading: Core startup lessons: build something a few people love, and protect momentum
chunks.text:
- The old YC motto was "make something people want." Sam says it should be updated to "make something people love."
- Choice for a startup: a small number of users who really love it, or a large number who only like it. Large-audience, low-love products get taken by big companies.
- The best companies in the YC portfolio all share this trait: some initial users loved what was built, became evangelists, and told others to use it (Stripe, Airbnb). He says they all had this, "full stop."
- YC's process: build a product a small number of users love, then work out how to grow it.
- Growth matters for two reasons. It shows people actually love the product, provided it is real growth with retained users and not users who churn. It also builds momentum.
- "Momentum is everything in a startup." Losing it is extremely hard to recover from. Startups that win keep winning, and startups that lose keep losing. Startups live and survive off their own momentum.

chunks.heading: Seed to Series A mistakes: retention, new responsibilities and compensation
chunks.text:
- Founders put huge effort into recruiting and almost none into retaining talent, then pay for it later. Retention must become as much of the job as recruiting, usually learned only after losing half the team.
- Sam cites Zuckerberg's rule of hiring only people you would report to. Good people have as many options as you, so if the role is not good enough that you would stay in it, you will struggle to keep your best people.
- Retention tactics (none are hard, they just take time):
  - Give your best 5-10 people time with the CEO. Some of the best CEOs take each of their top people to a one-on-one dinner or drinks every month. Sam calls it a big commitment of dinner slots but says it works, because those people crave it and want to be asked their opinion and listened to.
  - Keep giving people new tasks and more responsibility. Slotting VPs into one function and never moving them makes them leave. New or additional tasks each year keep them happier.
  - Proactively re-up compensation for the top 5-10 people. Many founders are bad at this and many YC companies have failed at this transition.

chunks.heading: Delegation: don't burn out on one bad hire, and keep your critical function
chunks.text:
- Founders get delegation wrong in both directions.
- Under-delegating usually follows one bad experience (a bad VP hire) after which the founder swears off delegation. Sam's advice is to trust that delegation is still a good idea despite one disaster.
- Over-delegating happens when a board member says to hire five VPs for five areas and the founder hands off the area they care about most.
- His rule: whatever the one or maybe two most critical pieces of the business are, and whatever you enjoy most, do those yourself.
  - A product-loving founder should not hire a VP of Product, because both will want the same thing, you will dislike how they do it, and they will dislike your interference.
  - A finance-loving founder should skip the CFO and hire a controller.
- Keeping your critical piece also makes you better at delegating everything else.

chunks.heading: Fundraising: don't push every round to the limit
chunks.text:
- Problems come from overextending: taking the highest possible price without being able to beat it in the next round, or ramping burn to the maximum while keeping only 9-12 months of runway.
- He applies the "margin of safety" idea from investing, which everyone understands except startup CEOs raising venture rounds.
- Advice:
  - Don't take a difficult-to-work-with investor just because they beat your best offer by 3% or 10%.
  - Don't run a plan where you run out of money three months before you begin your next fundraise.
- Founders fixate on the headline pre-money valuation because it is easy to compare, while terms and investor quality are hard to compare. He ties this to competitive founders optimizing the one quantitative metric they can win on.
- "Fundraising does not have to be hard" if the company is great and does not depend on "gigantic monster outside capital to survive."

chunks.heading: Choosing investors: diligence them like a VP of Sales
chunks.text:
- Founders typically make 12 reference calls before hiring a VP of Sales and 0-2 before adding a board member.
- Sam says to treat a new investor with at least as much care as a senior hire.
- Call the CEOs for whom things went badly (the "awfulest" ones), including ones the firm did not recommend you talk to. He says founders have walked away from deals they were about to take after these calls.
- Spend many hours together in person before adding someone to the board or cap table. A VP can be fired but an investor is extremely difficult to remove.

chunks.heading: Picking winners and judging founders (YC's 10-minute interviews)
chunks.text:
- YC decides in 10-minute interviews because of the volume of companies it must see. The only question is whether the person has "some seed of what it takes to be the next Mark Zuckerberg," not whether they definitely will be.
- Traits assessed, in rough order of ease:
  - Intelligence: easy to tell, in much less than 10 minutes.
  - Determination: the hardest trait to read, and the main source of YC's misses in either direction.
  - Clarity of vision, communication skills and non-obvious brilliance of the idea: quite a lot of data is available but not always right.
- New YC partners can be trained to do this in a year or two, so he thinks it is not an incredibly difficult skill. He notes YC had not missed many future billion-dollar companies, though at its current scale it has surely rejected some.
- Predicting breakouts: winners tend to do something new, so rules of thumb are hard, but he looks for:
  - Users who love the product.
  - Founder quality (the traits above).
  - A market that is small today but growing fast. He calls "how big is your market" a terrible question: you would not decide on current revenue, you want to know how it will grow.
  - Capturing a large share of a small market already, for example Airbnb with a significant amount of existing New York apartment renters by the end of YC, and Stripe with nearly 100% of YC batch companies that needed to process payments.

chunks.heading: Judging a team as an investor: meet the direct reports and test the recruiting pull
chunks.text:
- As an investor before YC, Sam would not make a large investment without meeting all of the founder's direct reports. He calls it incredibly high signal and says it was the most effective non-obvious thing he did, and that it changed his decision both ways.
- Reasoning: the team you build is the company you build.
- To judge a founder's ability to recruit: notice how tempted you are to join the company after spending time with them. Naturally great recruiters leave everyone they meet with the feeling that they should go join.

chunks.heading: AI: the next platform and Sam's stance on risk
chunks.text:
- AI is at minimum the next computing platform, and new platforms are where great investments come from. He also calls it possibly the next life form, the "children of humanity."
- Timeframe may be 10 or 100 years, but he says that is a blink in human history. Everyone agrees it is coming and argues only about timing.
- It could be "the best or the worst thing ever to happen to humanity." He is working to make it the best but says he would be lying if he claimed to be 100% confident in the plan, since controlling or understanding something more powerful than its creator is hard to guarantee.
- His hope: AI is widely distributed, with agents serving individuals the way the neocortex serves the limbic system, so the collective of humanity can stop any individual's misuse.
- He expects an economic shift on the scale of the agricultural and industrial revolutions, with short-term turbulence. He believes human demand is limitless so new work will appear. YC is running a basic income experiment to help ease the transition.
- A possible long-run outcome is global GDP growing around 100% a year for some number of years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman, then YC president, explains what he looks for in founders and how startups win or fail. Themes: clarity of vision, speed, determination, co-founder dynamics, hiring as late as possible, pursuing good ideas that look bad, getting users who love you, and avoiding fake work.

chunks.heading: Why YC exists and how the network effect works
chunks.text:
- Sam says YC funds about 250 startups a year in its core program, plus a new Fellowship program: one tenth of the money and less advice, built to scale far beyond the core batch.
- He describes YC as "somewhere between like a product company and a traditional investing firm."
- Its goal is to give a founder "a 100x leg up" through advice, connections and an alumni community of 2,000+ funded founders.
- He calls YC a network-effect business at the earliest stage of funding. Alumni help each other fundraise, buy each other's products and give advice.
- Of the eight accelerator-born companies worth $8B+, all eight came from YC, out of roughly 2,500 accelerators worldwide.
- Founder loyalty to investors falls fast with each round. The first check-writer gets the strongest bond, so YC founders give back to the community more readily.
- YC builds the community on purpose: an annual camping trip, shared office space and private online networks. Founding is lonely, and peers matter.

chunks.heading: Why Sam preferred seed investing to venture investing
chunks.text:
- After his company was acquired in 2012, he raised a venture fund and learned he did not want to be a venture investor or "public equity picker."
- Venture felt like allocating capital in a crowded field, trying to spot the best companies slightly sooner and pitch slightly better to win a deal.
- Early seed checks of about $15,000 in 2009-2010 felt like real impact: founders had no other options, and without the money the company might not exist.
- He took the YC job because he wanted "maximal impact," and says running YC is much more like being a CEO than an investor.
- He still says a great board member in the Series A is the most important thing to optimize for. YC itself is not good at that stage.
- A leadership handoff worked because he knew the organization and was YC's first check. He says a successful new CEO must "refound" the company.

chunks.heading: Founder qualities YC tracks
chunks.text:
YC rates founders on traits and watches what correlates with success. His list, in no particular order:

- **Clarity of vision.** Can the founder explain exactly what they do and why? If not, they cannot recruit, sell or talk to the press. Airbnb's founders explained the airbed idea and the end-state vision clearly even though it later evolved.
- **Determination and passion.** Founders "bend the world to their will" and do not turn around at the first impediment. The best companies are mission-oriented.
- **Raw intelligence.**
- **Speed of getting things done.** Quick, decisive decision-making correlates almost exactly with YC's successful founders. Many on-paper strong founders fail because they lack it.
- The ability to solve novel problems fast, which he compares to the novel The Martian: a stream of problem-solving.
- YC calibrates its interview questions on data from about 20,000 applicant companies a year.

chunks.heading: Co-founders, conflict and hiring
chunks.text:
- YC prefers 2-3 person founding teams but funds solo founders. Dropbox and Instacart each had a co-founder before or soon after YC.
- Reasons for a co-founder: the workload, and the psychological toll of going solo, which even tough people underestimate.
- Few $10B+ tech companies lacked co-founders by six months in. Four founders is harder because someone usually leaves within a couple of years.
- Bad co-founder is worse than none. "Bringing on a co-founder because they think we'll like it" ends in heartache "100% of the time."
- Diversity of skills and backgrounds is good. The harmful kind is diversity of vision: different beliefs about culture, decisions, selling, hiring and handling disagreement.
- Conflict arises when founders want different things for the company, and when both want the same thing for themselves (for example both want to be CEO).
- The current best pattern is two strong technical people, one owning product and one owning technology.
- On hiring: "our best startups hire the least." Airbnb and Stripe took about nine months to hire their first person, and Dropbox took longer.
- Early hires add burn, organizational inertia and politics. Hiring before the vision is clear creates communication overhead.
- Founders should not hire for status or force diversity hires.

chunks.heading: Ideas, conviction and pivots
chunks.text:
- Sam argues the best ideas look bad. Great ideas that look bad are undervalued assets, whereas obvious ones get brutally competed.
- Investors in 2006-2008 chased the next Facebook, and in 2009-2010 the next Facebook again when the real winners were Uber and Airbnb. Today's "Uber for X" startups are thin verticals; the next $100B company will be something new.
- Ask what has shifted in the world that enables a giant new company. For Uber, it was that everyone suddenly had an internet-connected device in their pocket.
- Ways to build conviction: launch quickly, so users who love the product give you proof, and be able to explain which change in the world others missed.
- He says you can ignore everyone except users. If users say the product sucks and you cannot find others who like it, listen.
- On hard tech, YC applies the software cadence: find a core metric and improve it about 10% a week. "If you compound... 10% a week is a lot."
- On pivots, he says Silicon Valley "gets the pivot thing wrong" and that bragging about pivots is bragging about failing.
- Pivots he has seen work: (1) what the founder wanted to build all along (Instagram, from Burbn), and (2) something discovered while building the first thing (Airbnb, Slack, Stripe).
- Pivots that fail: sitting at a whiteboard to invent a new idea. If you have neither kind of pivot, shut the company down, return the capital and wait for an organic idea.
- Learn more from success than from failure. Failure should be tolerated but not celebrated.

chunks.heading: Focus on product, growth and fake work
chunks.text:
- With about 70 productive hours a week, spend almost all of them on talking to users and building product.
- Focus on love, not like: "get the product to the point where some people would be really really bummed if it went away." Every successful company he has worked with had a small group of users who loved it.
- His board member's line: "sales solve all problems," later refined to "growth solves all problems."
- After YC, founders try to stop growth to fix technical, organizational and cultural debt. His advice is to spend about 10% of bandwidth on those, not 50-100%.
- Employees sense a loss of momentum before founders do. The prime directive is "never lose momentum."
- He warns of "fake work": fundraising, press, 30-under-30 lists, conferences, networking events, lawyers and logos. "No company has ever become great because they were great at fundraising."
- The real work is boring: coding, user interviews, sales meetings. Triage by letting small fires burn.
- Career advice: join the most successful, fastest-growing company you can find, and learn from watching it scale.

chunks.heading: Firing, valuations and other advice
chunks.text:
- The biggest mistake great founders make is waiting too long to fire bad people. Firing early hurts the person less.
- His method: treat them as a human, be firm that the decision is made, and make it look like a win for them.
- He has found a job for every person he fired before they left, and they announced a resignation plus the new role.
- Be generous with severance. Say "this isn't working," let them choose when to leave, and avoid the lawyer-style termination packet, which makes it adversarial.
- On valuations, he says intermediate valuations are "complete fictions" and he ignores them. They matter only when buying equity or joining as an employee, where liquidation preferences make the headline number misleading. Ask what the company will be worth in 5 years and what your ownership will be.
- YC counsels startups not to chase the highest valuation, and sometimes not to raise.
- On Bitcoin, he said it lacked product-market fit because few people use it daily, and he does not invest past YC stage in companies without it.
- Founders should be generalists. School length does not correlate with success.
- Do not start a startup for its own sake. Join a company you believe in, or start one only if the idea matters.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains how startup investing shaped his approach to running OpenAI: back non-consensus, high-conviction bets, focus compute and talent on the one great thing, and ship early to learn. He also covers platform strategy, why economic adoption of AI is slower than expected, and lessons from YC, Paul Graham and Peter Thiel.

chunks.heading: Sam's role: research and compute over product
chunks.text:
- Most of Sam's effort goes to research and compute. He says "the most important thing that we can do is to create smart models and to be able to run them efficiently and abundantly for a lot of people. If we can get that right, I believe that everything else will follow."
- His rule: find the high-leverage, difficult problem that continues the exponential. For OpenAI that means models and compute.
- Scaling compute is a complex problem: supply chain, partnerships, financing "probably already or at least rapidly becoming the most expensive infrastructure project in history," chip design, fabs, racks, and power systems.
- He admits he wishes he had more time for product. OpenAI has great product people, but he spends his own time where the leverage is highest.
- He frames the AI product phase as "smartphones before the iPhone". The technology pieces exist but the product ideas that change how people interface with computers do not yet. He calls his own habit of using computers the old way "mostly a product failure."

chunks.heading: Startup investing and research management follow the same power law
chunks.text:
- Sam says the closest thing to startup investing in his career is managing a research program.
- Both are power-law games: "your best investment will outperform all of your other investments put together," and AI research works the same way. Brains are not naturally wired to think this way, so you have to reprogram them.
- High-risk bets are fine if the ones you take are super valuable when they work.
- In 2015, people said AGI was nearly impossible. Later, focusing on large language models drew a second round of criticism ("completely ridiculous").
- Who he backs:
  - People with non-consensus, fresh, high-energy, "non-standard" thinking who will stand by unpopular convictions.
  - Not founders with "a thin veneer on the same idea that everybody else has."
- Example: in late 2015 there were very few AGI efforts (DeepMind and one or two others), while thousands of founders were starting photo-sharing apps.
- Same rule for researchers: many chase whatever last worked, a few hold high conviction on a new idea. OpenAI aims to be the best lab for the second group.
- He thinks there is a small chance an outsider approaches AI from an angle nobody has considered.

chunks.heading: Why investor-then-founder helped
chunks.text:
- Sam says investing first is unusual (the common path is founder, then investor) and strongly recommends it.
- As an investor he watched many crux moments across companies: strategy shifts, firing executives, founder mistakes. A single operator only gets a handful of these.
- He now pattern-matches on them when running OpenAI: "this is what happened when this company had a similar thing."
- He says running a company is far harder than investing.
- He learns more from successes than failures:
  - Failure lessons tend to be generic (grit, what not to do) and causation is hard to pin down because "most things don't work."
  - Success lessons, such as understanding which parts of YC or OpenAI worked, are easier to apply going forward.
  - Lessons taken from failure "either were fairly generic ... or got in the way of something else."
- Entrepreneurship advice is unglamorous and repetitive, and founders need constant reminders: talk to users more, ship earlier, get more feedback, raise the hiring bar and hire faster.

chunks.heading: Focus: kill good ideas for great ones
chunks.text:
- Sam calls sacrificing good ideas for great ones "the hardest lesson for any entrepreneur or business to learn," and says he is bad at it himself.
- Last year OpenAI killed Sora (a good, fun product that used a lot of compute and mattered less than Codex, where the compute went) and killed its Atlas web browser (a great browser, but the talent was needed elsewhere).
- The decision: with limited compute, people, and resources, general intelligence for knowledge work and eventually science is the most important thing. Everything upstream of that (chips, data centers, infrastructure software, model training) is in. Offer the AI as a service and avoid many other things.
- Platform strategy:
  - One interface (a ChatGPT and Codex merger that started as a chatbot and moves toward a persistent agent) plus one API.
  - "Sell great AI at every point on the cost-performance curve": high-end for science, cheap for high-volume work.
  - "I don't think we should go build every product category. I don't think we should compete with all our customers." The aim is 100 million new businesses and 8 billion people building on it.

chunks.heading: Peter Thiel's advice on ChatGPT: double down on what works
chunks.text:
- About two months after ChatGPT launched, growth was fast but felt unstable and "low value." Many people inside the company wanted to pursue five or six other directions.
- Sam asked Peter Thiel. His answer: it is an obvious mistake to do anything other than double down on the thing that is growing, which is rare.
- Thiel's reasoning:
  - It has "the power of the Google text box": type anything and it does the right thing.
  - It lacked what Silicon Valley wisdom demanded (feeds, network effects, lock-in, and this was before memory), but the market had chased the Google model for 20 years and this was the first thing like it.
  - "Why don't you just double down on that."
- Sam went "super hard onto it." He says Thiel and Paul Graham are the two people he calls on non-obvious problems because he can't predict what they'll say.
- Principle: when something is working, going deeper beats spending time exploring alternatives.

chunks.heading: YC lessons: ship embarrassingly early, move fast
chunks.text:
- Sam says Paul Graham pushed the startup ecosystem toward "ship a v1, be embarrassed early," because customer feedback improves the product faster than polishing does.
- He shipped ChatGPT knowing it was early and embarrassing. He didn't ask Paul whether to launch because he knew the answer.
- Looking back across YC founder data, "how much the ability of moving fast and being iterative correlates with success" astonishes him.
- He applies the same approach to safety: put products into the world, watch where they break, learn. "That is the way you make a good product. That is also the way you make a safe product."
- He compares it to aviation: robust, clear-eyed accident reporting and public postmortems, and sharing learnings with other AI builders.
- He says he and OpenAI would not exist without the ecosystem YC created: capital flowing to young technical founders and ambitious work without a proven resume.

chunks.heading: Building a research lab with no customers (the exception to YC advice)
chunks.text:
- It took 4.5 years from founding to the first product, the opposite of YC advice. He had no pattern for how to replace customer signal.
- What they did:
  - Spoke to people with experience at past great labs (including Alan Kay).
  - Used a leaderboard during the Dota 2 RL work so people could see how ideas performed objectively.
  - Used external demos for eminent people researchers wanted to impress.
  - Tried fake deadlines, which didn't work.
- Early days: on the first day, around January 2016, 11-12 people met at Greg Brockman's apartment. They got a whiteboard and then had no idea what to do. They wrote papers and tested ideas. Over years of "mostly chaotic stumbling" they found a rhythm for making and evaluating research bets, then the big discoveries (unsupervised sentiment paper, GPT-1, scaling laws).
- He says his dominant memory of the early period is trying and failing to raise money. They had no Bell Labs-style cash machine.

chunks.heading: Adoption is slower than expected, and the opportunity for small businesses
chunks.text:
- Sam admits he expected software to be "up for grabs" much sooner after GPT-4 (2023). He now thinks the economy's inertia and force of habit make adoption slower and the transition smoother. He disagrees with Toby Lütke's view that 2026 is the year every business is up for grabs, but not with the direction.
- Some businesses (sports, authentic experiences, human-connection products) will become more valuable, since people stay wired to care about other people.
- He praises Toby for using the tools himself and sending detailed product feedback, and notes that being hands-on is the only way to get a real feel for what the models can do.
- He admits to using his computer the old way despite having Codex. His view is that the bigger limit now is the context AI has on him, not model intelligence. He wants an agent that reads Slack, customer stories, and papers at a scale no person can.
- He expects "the greatest boom in people starting smaller businesses that we have ever seen." He says the AI field has not talked enough about empowerment and autonomy, and that a pitch of giving up control for a cure for cancer is "a terrible sales pitch."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman explains how OpenAI's new proactive assistant "Dots" gave him back his deep-work mornings. He argues AI creates a renaissance of builders rather than one all-consuming lab, and that demand for new things is limitless. He also covers speed as the next frontier after cheaper intelligence, and what he looks for as an investor.

chunks.heading: Sam's morning problem: overnight fires pollute deep-work time, and "Dots" fixes it
chunks.text:
- Sam says early morning is his favorite working time and his peak creative window. He used it for the day's deep, complex projects.
- Running a company this big, things often break overnight. If he doesn't check his phone right away, a problem can get worse within an hour.
- The catch: once he checks his phone, he "pollutes" his mind with everything else and loses the deep-work window.
- Now he trusts his Dot (the assistant OpenAI launched at DevDay) to judge what he needs to see. He looks at something only if it is truly urgent. Otherwise the Dot handles it.
- Sam says this gave him back that creative space, or time with his kids. He calls it "simple" but "a massive improvement" in his life.
- Example from DevDay: 5 minutes before a keynote demo, another exec's Dot messaged him that it saw a production issue likely to break the demo, and offered to fix it.
- Example from his own day: just before the interview, his Dot flagged one specific thing to watch in a short gap between meetings. He says he would have missed it and it would have caused a mess.
- His Dot's name is "Dotty". He tried "Alfred" before and is still looking for a better name.
- Sam says the system needed a model smart enough, which he credits mostly to "Astra", along with many other things that had to be built.

chunks.heading: Using a Dot as a continuous idea-to-prototype loop
chunks.text:
- Sam had a new feature that was hard to explain in enough detail for others to build, and he wasn't sure which of many approaches to pick.
- He kept dropping raw notes to his assistant whenever an idea hit, such as on a walk. The assistant built five or six versions and he gave feedback and refined them.
- Feedback ran whenever he had a spare moment or a new thought.
- He also leaves a long voice message while falling asleep. In the morning the work is built, and the assistant has also done the next seven steps.
- He says this works for any category where the idea is fuzzy, or building it takes a lot of effort from him or someone else.
- He calls the ability to dump raw ideas and get continuous feedback "amazing", and "a really great way to express things".

chunks.heading: Dots as a background agent that finishes tasks Sam gave up on
chunks.text:
- Sam often uses Codex to search Slack, since he says Slack search is clearly bad.
- He spent 10 to 20 minutes searching for something he was sure he'd seen. He tried different approaches, failed, and assumed he'd dreamed it. Codex doesn't usually fail, so he gave up.
- The next day his Dot told him it had noticed he couldn't find it, kept thinking about it overnight, and found it.
- It turned out to be a screenshot, not text. Sam had forgotten that. The Dot went through the images and analyzed each screenshot until it found it.
- Sam's takeaway: the Dot stayed patiently looking for something useful to do, and he "would have given up" on that task.
- He also says a Dot can pull context from his whole life (the example given was that it read his Slack, not just his calendar). The context-gathering is among the most useful things about it.
- He frames this as an agent that helps against the flood of information and attention-hijacking. After a few weeks on Dots, he realized social media, phones and notifications hijack attention much more than he had understood.

chunks.heading: "Living documents" and the personal dashboard
chunks.text:
- Sam describes a new idea he says has no good name yet: "living" documents. They update automatically as people interact or the world changes, and many people's assistants can work on them together.
- The point is not only sharing information. Assistants for seven people can work together to create something new that was latent in everyone's heads but emergent.
- He says this has been fun while thinking about new features to explore.
- On writing: for a genuinely new idea he still prefers to write it the traditional way, because writing helps him think. He may then have his assistant (or others) follow up.
- His own use case is the company dashboard. Before, he shared one with many people. Now he has a personal, constantly changing business summary based on the evolving things he does or doesn't care about.
- It reads all his Slack messages, builds something new for him, and keeps updating it.
- What he cares about shifts. Six months earlier he cared more about revenue, growth and traditional business metrics. Lately his focus has been the safety and security alignment challenge.
- He'd be curious to see what his Dot thinks he cares about most each day, tracked over years. He says he hasn't been able to get his Dot to find a good way to visualize it.

chunks.heading: Spaces and why software needs rethinking for human-AI collaboration
chunks.text:
- Sam's team launched three office-suite-style tools in one release, which he calls a big bet. It wasn't the original plan.
- His reasoning: software as a whole wasn't designed for collaborating with AI. You can use it yourself or have the AI use it for you.
- For close collaboration, especially with multiple people and multiple AI systems working together, many of today's abstractions "fall apart".
- He calls human-AI collaboration an important area to explore.

chunks.heading: Platform strategy: a renaissance of builders, not one giant company
chunks.text:
- Sam says AI model companies have two schools of thought: one believes or hopes there will be only one company in the world, and the other (his, and OpenAI's) expects a renaissance in the number of companies.
- He expects a big drop in the bar for individuals, one-person companies and small teams to create new products and services, and wants to go all out on the platform to enable that.
- He says OpenAI hasn't found the equivalent of the app store yet, but has figured out how to help millions of people build valuable products and companies.
- He lists what they opened up at DevDay:
  - Apps inside ChatGPT.
  - Letting users take their subscription anywhere.
  - An app store.
  - The same tools OpenAI uses internally.
- Reasons: there are now many ideas to build, and what's missing is the creative spirit to invent them. Sam believes there are far more good ideas outside OpenAI's building than inside.
- He wants to put that creative energy in people's hands and connect developers with the people who will find the technology useful.
- He is confident there will be apps or plugins he'd love that nobody at OpenAI can imagine today.
- On bringing a ChatGPT subscription everywhere: he says OpenAI wants this itself. He hates subscribing to 100 services, and when he tries a new app he wants it to have full AI power.
- On "OpenAI will crush a startup" tweets: he says they perform because people like pessimism, but it "never actually happens". He says OpenAI is committed to pushing the boundaries of model access.
- He says OpenAI did several things at DevDay no other AI lab would, and that it likes developers partly because of his startup background.
