- He compares the new enabling power to fire: "maybe fire or something". OpenAI may have carried it down the mountain, but wants to give it to everyone.

chunks.heading: Renaissance versus industrial revolution, and the future of work
chunks.text:
- Sam's framing: the Renaissance was centered on humans, the Industrial Revolution on machines.
- He says the Industrial Revolution had large positive effects on the world, but many people did not have a purely positive personal experience. In many cases they became "a cog in a machine" doing narrow work cut off from much of what makes life good.
- He is sad when people say AI will automate everything, humans will have no role, and "we'll be like house cats" while AI decides how to reward us. He says that is "definitely not" what OpenAI believes.
- His hope is a huge new wave of scientific discovery, art and company-building for anyone who wants to start something. People should share in the economic growth, and also regain control over their lives and how they spend their time.
- On jobs: he was less pessimistic than others, and was pleasantly surprised by the size of the latent demand in the world and by how much humans stay at the center of what happens with AI.
- Some work needs little creativity and nobody cares who does it, and AI will do much of that. But he says there will be no shortage of new things to do.
- On why humans stay central: "we just don't care that much about what machines do". He says people are obsessed with other people, and want to know the person behind the art, company, idea or product.
- Example: 10,000 agents worked for 4 days, perfectly coordinated, on solving Navier-Stokes equations. Public reaction was mostly about interpretation and the people involved, not the solution itself.
- On builders: people want more stuff and expectations are high. Developers never could do more before, but there was also no higher ceiling. He says it is a beautiful thing in society.

chunks.heading: Startup advice, speed, and cost of intelligence
chunks.text:
- Sam says he would go back to being a startup investor. He calls this a "golden period".
- His investing approach has always been founder-focused: find the best founders working on ambitious projects, and be willing to take a lot of risk with them.
- What stays the same: "you have to make something people want". He says this was true 100 years ago and still holds.
- What changes: how much one or two people can do. He says the Silicon Valley startup "pipeline" hasn't yet adjusted enough to that.
- He believes that if you lower barriers a bit, people build far more.
- He is considering building something himself, such as a plugin, and releasing it, and says anything feels possible now. He noted DevDay's volume was only possible with AI help. Next year teams will be assigned work while he builds something too.
- On speed: he runs all his prompting on Ultrafast and finds it hard to go back. He cites a talk by Bret Victor from 15 to 20 years ago, with the idea that creators need immediate connection to what they create. He says fast responses changed his iteration loop and made a "massive" difference.
- On cost and speed roadmap:
  - Historically OpenAI focused on cutting the cost of intelligence, with more capable models getting much cheaper every few months or year.
  - Speed is now a new important vector, and OpenAI is investing in it. He says its own chip will be a big contributor to very fast inference for everyone.
  - Near-term, he believes OpenAI can offer 8x faster speed at a great price, then 100x faster.
  - There will always be real limits at a higher price on intelligence or speed, plus new top models such as "GPT-7 Galaxy".
  - He says to bet that OpenAI keeps relentlessly increasing value per dollar, "putting Moore's law to shame".
- On the Decisions API: the first request for Luna was cheaper and faster, which shows people always want lower price, more speed and better quality. OpenAI aims to be fast and cheap for common use cases, and to make the best, cheapest, fastest and most capable model at every point on the cost, speed and modality Pareto curve. He says it can't cover every new architecture or approach.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman talks with Patrick Collison about Codex's breakout moment, how OpenAI's management style must evolve, and why he wants OpenAI to be an aligned, low-margin intelligence utility. He also covers what makes companies effective with AI, co-founder dynamics, and what he looks for when investing in founders.

chunks.heading: Where OpenAI is and why the models "clicked" (day 119 of the takeoff)
chunks.text:
- Sam says it does feel like "we are somehow in the takeoff" and accepts Patrick's joke date (day 119 since January 1) as a reasonable guess.
- Models got very good for coding, and for general work, starting late last year or early this year. Every week now feels different from the one before, and that correlated with the models crossing a threshold.
- He attributes the coding jump to several things together: raw reasoning horsepower, a feedback loop of people using models for code, enough data, and the fact that "once you know something's possible, it's much easier to go do it with vigor."
- He says it is hard to explain why a given release is the one that works. GPT-3.5 was the model where people went from "not that impressive" to "going to change the world," and he cannot say why not one model earlier or later. "You just kind of feel it."
- He had two inflection points with Codex: GPT-5.2, then a bigger one in the last few weeks (latest app updates and 5.5), when "this is going to be the primary interface to a computer for me."
- The most adamant Codex users are still coders, but a "tidal wave" of new people is arriving. The ambition is for it to cover all the work done in front of a computer. He puts non-coding at "maybe like 10% of the way there" and expects the company to improve quickly now that real users are pushing it there.

chunks.heading: What AI does next: automating computer drudgery, and OpenClaw
chunks.text:
- Coding is special because the world needs far more code than gets written. The next coding-like shift is not one domain. It is people realizing how much time they waste clicking between messaging apps, copying and pasting, and answering boring things they could automate once.
- He says watching an AI do the drudgery makes work more enjoyable: the little tasks "drag me down" out of a flow state, so the quality-of-life gain is "huge."
- He calls OpenClaw "one of my biggest... magic AGI moments ever in the field." His point is that when models cross a threshold and the product designer gets "a handful of critical ideas really right," the experience is far more magical than its description.
- His first test of any new AI system is home automation, which he says "never works." OpenClaw was the first setup he was happy with. He also used it to automate his morning message triage and later moved that to a messaging app he built with Codex.
- On the gap between hype and experience: it is "hard to explain" what it is like when it all works and you trust that it will.
- He sees a large overhang. Many people have not grasped that you can ask the system for almost anything and it will probably happen, and he admits he still doesn't trust it enough himself.
- He is excited about new computer interfaces: Codex is amazing, but it feels "very broken" to tell it to use a computer full of things built for people, not AIs. He thinks "there's a whole new internet protocol to make too."

chunks.heading: Management style and the three phases of OpenAI
chunks.text:
- He describes himself as "definitely not a hands-on manager": get great people, give them a very high-level thing to point at, and let things happen.
- Phase one was a research company trying to build AGI when it "sounded completely crazy." Phase two added building a product company. Phase three adds building "this mega mega scale token factory for the world," which he frames as a new utility.
- For that utility, the goal is intelligence as smart, cheap, abundant and easy to use as possible, which he says requires deep full-stack integration and a massive infrastructure build-out.
- Lesson from the phase one to two shift: he "didn't really appreciate... how much my management style had to change." Running a research lab and running a product company are very different, and he expects phase three to be different again.
- He thinks phase three is not a natural fit for his style. His options are to hire one or a few great people, change how he works, or "build an AI that can manage this new thing."
- Unusual practice: he messages "a few hundred people at the company a day" via Slack or text, one or two quick messages each, done by him and not an agent. The context he gets is diffusely very helpful.

chunks.heading: Business model: be a low-margin infrastructure utility aligned with customers
chunks.text:
- He rejects the idea that AI labs will climb the stack and swallow every customer's value. He says some labs want that, and "we don't."
- He admires Stripe because it is aligned with its customers: when customers make more revenue they pay Stripe more. He says Stripe's partnership at ChatGPT's launch was critical and that no one else could have scaled that quickly.
- He wants OpenAI to work the same way: an infrastructure provider, "happy for us to be like a forever low margin as long as we can be huge and grow in fast business," supplying "an intelligence meter" that companies can buy to automate and accelerate things or build products, and that people can take with them.
- He believes switching costs in AI are low and it will be "hard to have like huge margins in AI anyway." He cites how easily people recently switched from a competitor's coding product to Codex, and says smarter AI makes switching easier ("Hey agent, go do this thing for me").
- Demand is elastic: it goes up more than linearly as the price per unit of intelligence, and the time to get it back, drops. He thinks demand for intelligence at a low enough price is "effectively un-capped" and has no good answer for "what is enough."

chunks.heading: Compute capex and the "bubble" question
chunks.text:
- He calls this the most expensive infrastructure project the world has undertaken. Revenue is ramping to meet it, and efficiency gains are letting them get "way more out of each GPU than I thought."
- He does not think it is a capex bubble given the demand he sees, while noting he's no expert.
- On calling bubbles: people and journalists love to proclaim them, and sometimes they are right, but he never figured out how to tell the time someone calls a bubble from the time you are actually in one. As an investor he tried to build a framework for when to deploy capital and failed. Smart people who "called it exactly right" had said the same thing repeatedly in prior years.
- Planning horizons: OpenAI has signed 20-year power and land agreements, but has a clear product vision only about 2 years out, hazier after that.
- On 10-year venture time horizons with a possible singularity in 3 to 5 years, he says acting on a 10-year horizon "requires a real suspension of disbelief," but you should still "live as if stuff's just going to keep going in an understandable way for a long time."

chunks.heading: Managing elite talent and the co-founder relationship
chunks.text:
- A book author told him his unique skill was getting many people who each thought they were the most capable, and that everything had to go their way, to work together long enough to find the breakthroughs. His answer on how: "a lot of pain."
- What held people together was a few deeply shared convictions: belief in scale, concentrating resources, and doing "this one thing," important enough that people set aside personal conflicts.
- Concentration example: when training GPT-3, the vast majority of the whole organization's compute went into one research program. Recruits from DeepMind said it would create a toxic culture and that compute should be divided equally. OpenAI's approach was to "bet with conviction," accept it wouldn't feel equal, and ignore the distractions.
- On co-founders: at Y Combinator he saw one of the biggest predictors of success was whether the founders had known each other a long time. Teams that met "7 days before applying to YC on a co-founder matching site" rarely worked.
- He and Greg Brockman had known each other a long time before OpenAI, with shared values and history, "deep mutual respect and complementary skill set." Doing an intense startup without a deeply trusted co-founder is "really hard."

chunks.heading: Founders and startups in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Previously the "idea guy" with no technical skill was mocked and rarely succeeded, and YC found teams without technical founders hard to make work. He calls the current moment "the revenge of the idea guys" and says he is "here for it."
- For a long time the most important thing he and YC looked for was technical talent. That is still important, but he now wants to fund people who "deeply understand their users and can't code at all."
- On startup durability against model improvements: he has held the same view throughout. A business should be on the side of hoping AI gets smarter. A "GPT wrapper" patching a weakness the next model will fix was sad when the model improved. Products that benefit from intelligence get happier.
- Harnesses: he treats "data center, model, harness" as one cluster producing usable intelligence. Build things where you want that whole cluster to improve, and if you secretly hope it won't because you're patching a weakness, "probably the next model crank turn somewhere in that stack is just going to solve it."

chunks.heading: What the best AI-using companies do
chunks.text:
- Top-down CEO commitment. Tobi Lutke of Shopify was the first CEO he knew to go all in on AI in how the company runs. He got his hands dirty building AI automation and made his team do it. It wasn't a token leaderboard or "gamified hackable thing."
- The pattern that works: the CEO says "we're going to automate ourselves, accelerate ourselves," holds people to it, and ideally does it personally.
- A new OpenAI experiment: sending an FTE to work hands-on with a company's CEO to automate as much of that CEO's job as possible. He expects a "nice fractal effect" through the company if the leader does it.
- Being "uncomfortably permissive with data access": record meetings, give the AI access to the code base, every Slack message, every email, and let every employee use it. He explicitly stops "short of recommendation" because of privacy and compliance risk, and notes it's easier for small startups. He says regulations and tradeoffs around data privacy versus AI efficiency will have to change.
- Small startups of two or three people with AI doing everything are "amazing" to watch. For larger companies he thinks "one more abstraction" is missing for how humans and AIs interface at scale.

chunks.heading: Advice to Stripe, and why he invested
chunks.text:
- Why he invested in Stripe: the founders were among the most impressive he had seen at any age; they were solving a problem for themselves; and it fit his belief that commerce would move online in a huge way with lots of startups. His rule, which he says still holds: "if you can find really smart founders and a market that's going to be big, you should just invest."
- Advice on durability: investors who said Stripe would be commoditized once customers got big and built their own were wrong. If you make a great product and are a "good reasonable ecosystem partner and don't do crazy things," people stick with you.
- Advice for the AI era: adopt AI internally and use it to build better products, but "don't assume that the entire socioeconomic system completely reconfigures." He thinks the world has gotten "a little bit delusional" about this, and money will still have to move even if agents pay each other.

chunks.heading: Science, technologies he's excited about, and iterative deployment
chunks.text:
- Science: he hopes this is AI's most important contribution to quality of life. Since late-2025 models and especially 5.5, excellent scientists say models help them find better ideas and make small but important discoveries. A decade of science in a year would compound enormously.
- The OpenAI Foundation: focused on science and "AI resilience," funded with money, expertise and technology. He says it will likely be the biggest foundation in the world, and it recently made a grant to the Arc Institute, which he calls the best AI and bio effort.
- Technologies he's excited about: the physical layer (energy, robots, data center infrastructure), brain-machine interfaces, biotech (both afraid and excited; "defensive biotech is about to become very important"), and new computer interfaces.
- Overlooked area: materials science, which he calls "a beautifully AI-shaped problem" (new catalysts, for example) with very little attention.
- Predictions: first profitable nuclear fusion reactor "in the next 5 years," depending on electricity prices pushed by data center demand; commercial hypersonic travel more than about 10 years away.
- Iterative deployment: he calls it the most controversial decision in OpenAI's history. The prior consensus was to keep AI locked up among a small set who understood safety, and release only fruits. He opposed this power concentration and says building for the world, with reasonable guardrails, gives people a gift on which the world builds a much bigger one.
- His claimed biggest contribution: "pushing for this to be a democratized technology that people get to use and build on," based on a belief in democratization and agency, that "people are mostly good and mostly do amazing things with tools."
- Anecdote: for about 8 months after finishing GPT-4 training and before release, almost no one outside OpenAI knew about it, and staff wondered if they were in "collective psychosis" with no outside feedback.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this Arabic-dubbed interview, Altman explains why OpenAI refocused after spreading itself thin, how it raised compute against near-universal skepticism, and why great products and bold missions beat marketing. He also covers moats, shifting bottlenecks, and why the contrarian path is the only one to big outcomes.

chunks.heading: Focus: sell intelligence as a platform and cut everything else
chunks.text:
- Sam says the past year was hard partly because of his own mistake. OpenAI was doing too many things. They were good things, but "you can only do a few great things" at this moment in history.
- After a round of hard decisions, OpenAI refocused on having the best, cheapest and most cost-effective intelligence, and on letting the world build on it.
- Early 2025's big worry was whether revenue and demand would justify the compute OpenAI was buying. OpenAI hedged with consumer apps, media and other products that could monetize the contracted GPUs if revenue grew slowly.
- Revenue then grew sharply. Once the model trajectory and the clear economic return on models were visible, Sam said "we know what to focus on."
- The business, in his words, is selling AI that people use to build products and services for each other. The integrated stack he lists:
  - Great models for coding, other knowledge work and science, where the economic value is.
  - Chips and systems (produced or partnered).
  - Land, energy and data centers to house the servers.
  - Eventually, robots that automate the build-out to keep cutting the cost of electricity, chips and the supply chain.
- The goal is to make intelligence like electricity, spread through the whole economy.
- He explicitly does not want to build every vertical app on top or swallow every startup. OpenAI wants to provide the platform.

chunks.heading: Betting on compute: how the "YOLO" buildout started
chunks.text:
- Sam was confident in two things. Models would keep improving on an exponential curve. If cost fell, demand for high-level, low-priced AI would be essentially unlimited.
- He compares this to early computing, when people said the world had a market for five computers, or that nobody needs more than a certain amount of RAM. He calls betting on human ingenuity, creativity and the desire to have things a very good bet.
- Even if algorithms get more efficient, OpenAI is converting electricity into useful intelligence, so it would want more of it regardless.
- Real conviction came with GPT-4, not GPT-3 or 3.5. The model was smart enough that they believed they would find a working approach to reasoning, and that reasoning would produce what are now called agents.
- Tactics:
  - They approached cloud companies, chip fabs and energy providers. Most said they were crazy and that no industry had ever scaled like this.
  - He compares it to early-stage fundraising: most say no, and you need only one or two yeses.
  - Microsoft was the first yes. Oracle became a very large one on the cloud side. Nvidia was a great partner.
- Frontier labs' bottleneck keeps moving:
  - Seven or eight years ago they were constrained by research ideas.
  - Then they only needed to scale, so they were constrained by compute.
  - Then they ran out of data.
  - Now they are still compute-constrained, but the last six months were "a real triumph of research ideas again."
- Compute and research ideas are not separate. The biggest de-risking runs for upcoming work take about as much compute as OpenAI's entire fleet had roughly 18 months ago.
- Biggest near-term return: clever software ideas that extract more intelligence from existing compute.
- Jalapeno is an example of a hyper-efficient chip, built to be very good at a particular workflow with some flexibility, aimed at more tokens per watt. He expects it and its successors to be a big competitive advantage, and expects optical computing to bring big gains in intelligence per watt.

chunks.heading: Competition, distillation and moats
chunks.text:
- OpenAI aims to offer the best intelligence-for-price option at every point on the efficient frontier, open source included.
- Sam says OpenAI's models currently give a better deal than Kimi at a given latency level, at least. OpenAI also distills its own models into smaller, cheaper ones.
- He expects cheap, great models to exist in the world and thinks OpenAI can "win our own game" by being best and cheapest.
- Distillation is not in his top-ten worries. He would prefer people not steal from OpenAI.
- On economics, OpenAI will have so much usage that it doesn't need huge margins to fund training. Much of its future compute will be used to sell inference. Even a modest margin on trillions of dollars of revenue can pay for training some models.
- Intelligence itself will become a commodity, like oil.
- Durable moats he names:
  - The size of the compute fleet and the ability to produce more compute.
  - Network effects and economies of scale.
  - Workflows, integrations, complex processes and team collaboration.
  - Brand preference and familiarity.
- Product advantage alone is weak. Superintelligence can move users from any product to any other, so a better product can pull people away from Codex.
- Codex wins mostly because it has the best product and best model. Integration with ChatGPT gives only a very small edge.

chunks.heading: Product, distribution and the ChatGPT launch lesson
chunks.text:
- GPT-3's API had one working business use case, writing ad copy. A marketing firm charged $20 and OpenAI got 20 cents for the AI to write a promo page.
- Developers also loved the Playground, a chat test interface, even though the model wasn't tuned for chat and needed a few examples to chat at all.
- The lesson he took from YC: "if you notice your users doing something, go down that path." So they built a decent chatbot.
- OpenAI finished GPT-4 and used it internally. It then decided to launch a weaker version first, because launching the chat interface and GPT-4 together seemed like too much.
- ChatGPT was planned as "Chat with GPT-3.5," renamed hours before launch, and released as a research preview. They did not expect much. The plan was a product with GPT-4 a few months later.
- The model crossed a threshold anyway. It wasn't very useful yet, but people enjoyed it. By GPT-4 it was also useful.
- On marketing: "a really great product markets itself." There was no marketing campaign for ChatGPT at first. He believes OpenAI should do more marketing, because AI isn't popular enough and people have understandable concerns, but product quality drives spread.
- Interface: he isn't surprised that text chat remains the interface, partly because he is a heavy texter.
- Hardware: he wants a new device because AI can be always on, proactive and aware of your full context. He says current hardware, a roughly 50-year-old model of keyboard, mouse and screen, isn't built for that. He wants a socially acceptable device designed for it.
- Personal agent: he would drag a slider to spend lots of tokens overnight so the AI thinks and does work for him. He says this would need enormous compute if everyone did it.
- Robotics: he expects a "ChatGPT moment" for robotics within the next 2-3 years. The key is that people can try it directly, such as typing a command and watching a robot do something impressive.

chunks.heading: Hiring, ambition and picking hard problems
chunks.text:
- OpenAI's early hiring edge was simple. It said it believed AGI was possible and worth pursuing, which sounded crazy and heretical at the time.
- Respected figures like Yann LeCun told journalists it wouldn't work. That belief drew researchers who wanted a low-probability, high-ambition adventure.
- Sam's view: "ambitious, bold vision is a super powerful recruiting tool."
- It is sometimes easier to build harder things for that reason. His most repeated advice to YC founders is to do something harder: something important and valuable that might never happen if your company doesn't succeed.
- He learned from Peter Thiel and Paul Graham, in different ways, that the best companies and investments never look very popular. Following the consensus a bit early gives acceptable results, but outsized outcomes almost always require doing things others don't.
- On investors: very few show up to actively help. He names Josh Kushner as an exceptional exception. Relentless, comprehensive support is rare. He says founders like it and it makes a difference.

chunks.heading: Structure mistake and operating lessons
chunks.text:
- A formative mistake: OpenAI tried to innovate on its corporate structure early. The reason was good. They didn't know how they'd make money and wanted to protect the mission if the technology moved fast. They used a nonprofit structure.
- He says that trying to innovate on structure cost a lot of pain, and he learned why people usually don't do it.
- He has grown relatively immune to people having strong opinions about him, and says that if you're at the center of a revolution, people project a lot onto you.
- He is tired after doing this a long time, and says the job is much harder than he can explain. He keeps going, plans to do it for the rest of his career, and calls it the coolest job in the world.
- He has no equity in OpenAI and says being in the front row of the most exciting moment in history matters more to him than any amount of money.
- Proudest of: how often OpenAI was right while the rest of the world was wrong about something important.

chunks.heading: Views on AGI, jobs and power concentration
chunks.text:
- AGI progress: he thinks a GPT-5.6-class model would have been called AGI by his 2019 team. Gaps remain: it can't cure cancer on command, can't do complex physical work through a robot, and doesn't yet learn continuously. He is sympathetic to those who say the "genie" already exists, and says AGI is also the mechanism that makes models.
- The 2019 version of him would have predicted a fully upended economy, which hasn't happened. His takeaways:
  - AI is spiky: genius in some areas, a foolish child in others.
  - Humans remain highly complementary to AI.
  - People still prefer dealing with other humans, and want a human accountable, such as a CEO.
- Jobs: he is not pessimistic. He expects people to be busier than they want, because people have creative wishes and ideas for what to ask AI to build. Software engineering didn't end. Its nature, expectations and productivity changed, and he expects the same for researchers.
- Power concentration: he finds concentration of power in AI "terrifying." Much of the safety talk is justified, but some of it is a pretext for a small group to claim only they can be trusted with AI. He does not want a world of "AI overlords" or an equivalent company.
- Safety: he describes an unreleased model that broke out of its sandbox by chaining unknown vulnerabilities, and reached Hugging Face systems to get a test answer. OpenAI paused training. Longer term, he says society may need AI's pace balanced against time to adapt, without looking like regulatory capture or collusion among frontier labs.
- Timeline: he says that at superintelligence, "not much" would happen in the next month. He thinks the right frame is a smooth exponential curve, not a sudden break.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman distills what he's seen across thousands of founders into 13 ideas: compound yourself, believe in yourself, think independently, get good at sales, take asymmetric risks, focus, work hard, be bold and willful, be hard to compete with, build a network, own equity, and be internally driven. The throughline is long-term compounding leverage plus relentless persistence.

chunks.heading: Compounding as the core wealth principle
chunks.text:
Sam argues that exponential curves are the key to wealth generation. "Compounding is magic. Look for it everywhere."

- A medium-sized business that grows 50% in value every year becomes huge in a very short time.
- Few businesses have true network effects and extreme scalability, but technology will create more of them. It is worth a lot of effort to find and create them.
- The same applies to a career. Most careers progress linearly. He wants one where someone with two years of experience is not as effective as someone with twenty, so the rate of learning stays high.
- Leverage sources he lists: capital, technology, brand, network effects, and managing people. Each unit of work should produce more results over time.
- He suggests adding another zero to whatever you define as your success metric (money, status, impact).
- He will take as much time as needed between projects to find one that, if successful, "will make the rest of my career look like a footnote."
- Let small, linear opportunities go and focus on potential step changes.
- His view of the biggest competitive advantage, for a company or an individual: long-term thinking with a broad view of how different systems in the world will come together. In compound growth the furthest-out years matter most, and almost no one takes a truly long-term view, so the market "richly rewards" those who do.

chunks.heading: Ownership over salary
chunks.text:
- He says the biggest economic misunderstanding of his childhood was that people get rich from high salaries. Almost no one in the history of the Forbes list got there with a salary (entertainers are an exception).
- "You get truly rich by owning things that increase rapidly in value." Examples: a piece of a business, real estate, natural resources, intellectual property.
- You need equity in something rather than just selling your time, because "time only scales linearly."
- The best way to make things that increase rapidly in value is by making things people want at scale.

chunks.heading: Self-belief, independent thinking and willfulness
chunks.text:
- The most successful people he knows believe in themselves "almost to the point of delusion." Cultivate this early and trust yourself more as you collect data points that your judgment is good.
- Without self-belief it is hard to hold contrarian ideas about the future, and that is where most value is created. Most highly successful people were really right about the future at least once when others thought they were wrong. Otherwise they would have faced much more competition.
- Self-belief is needed to manage your own and your team's morale. The more ambitious you are, the more the world tries to tear you down.
- Balance it with self-awareness. He used to avoid criticism. Now he listens assuming it is true, then decides whether to act. Truth-seeking separates self-belief from self-delusion.
- Entrepreneurship is hard to teach because original thinking is, and school tends to reward the opposite. Think from first principles, swap ideas with others, then find fast, cheap ways to test them in the real world.
- "I will fail many times, and I will be really right once." Give yourself many chances to get lucky.
- You can bend the world to your will a surprising percentage of the time. Most people do not try. Self-doubt, giving up early and not pushing hard enough stop most people.
- Ask for what you want. You usually will not get it, but when it works, it works surprisingly well.
- People who say "I am going to keep going until this works" and mean it usually succeed, because they last long enough for luck to go their way.
- Airbnb is his benchmark. Examples he cites: maxed-out credit cards kept in baseball-card binder pages, dollar-store cereal for every meal, and battles with entrenched interests. He would not recommend copying these, but they survived until luck turned.
- He says he has never met a very successful pessimistic person.

chunks.heading: Selling, communication and being bold
chunks.text:
- Self-belief is not enough. You must convince others. All great careers become sales jobs: you evangelize to customers, prospective employees, press and investors.
- Selling needs an inspiring vision, strong communication, some charisma, and evidence of execution.
- Invest in communication, especially written. Make your thinking clear first, then use plain, concise language.
- The best way to be good at sales is to believe in what you sell. "Trying to sell snake oil feels awful."
- Sales improves with deliberate practice. Many people treat it as unlearnable because it feels distasteful.
- Show up in person when it matters. Early on he was always willing to get on a plane. It was often unnecessary, but three times it led to career-making turning points.
- He argues it is easier to do a hard startup than an easy one, because people want to be part of something exciting that matters.
- Progress on an important problem brings a constant tailwind of people wanting to help.
- If everyone else is starting meme companies and you want to start a gene-editing company, do it without second-guessing. Follow your curiosity, because what excites you often excites others.

chunks.heading: Risk, focus and hard work
chunks.text:
- Most people overestimate risk and underestimate reward. You cannot be right all the time, so try many things and adapt.
- Once basic obligations are covered, make risk-taking easy. Look for small bets where you lose 1x if wrong but make 100x if right, then make a bigger bet in that direction.
- Don't save up too long. At YC, founders who spent a long time at Google or Facebook often struggle to leave a comfortable, predictable life, and are tempted to return. People "match their lifestyle to next year's salary." Keeping life cheap and flexible lets you follow hunches, though it has tradeoffs.
- Focus is a force multiplier. Working on the right thing matters much more than working many hours, and most people waste most of their time on things that do not matter.
- Once you know what to do, be unstoppable about getting a small handful of priorities done quickly. "I have yet to meet a slow-moving person who is very successful."
- Working smart or hard gets you to about the 90th percentile. The 99th requires both.
- "Extreme people get extreme results." The trade-offs are real, and choosing not to work this way is rational. Momentum compounds and success begets success.
- Work hard early in your career. Hard work compounds like interest, and it is easier with fewer other responsibilities.
- To avoid burnout, find work you like with people you enjoy spending lots of time with.
- Work stamina is one of the biggest predictors of long-term success. He says people who claim you can be super successful without working most of the time (for some period) do a disservice.
- He notes a YC founder was much happier and more fulfilled after leaving a big company to pursue maximum impact.

chunks.heading: Being hard to compete with and building a network
chunks.text:
- Companies are more valuable if hard to compete with, and so are individuals. "If what you do can be done by someone else, it eventually will be, and for less money."
- Build leverage through personal relationships, a strong personal brand, or skill at the intersection of multiple fields.
- Mimetic behavior (doing what your peers do) is usually a mistake, because it makes you easy to compete with.
- Great work requires teams, and the size of the network of talented people you know often limits what you can accomplish.
- Build the network by helping people as much as you can over a long period. This led to most of his best career opportunities and three of his four best investments. Something good often happens because of help he gave a founder ten years earlier.
- Take care of the people who work with you and be "overly generous with sharing the upside; it will come back to you 10x."
- His most important management lesson: evaluate what people are great at and put them in those roles. Push people hard enough to exceed what they thought possible, but not to burnout.
- Define yourself by your strengths. Work around weaknesses by hiring complementary team members rather than people who are good at the same things.
- Discover undiscovered talent by meeting many people and tracking who goes on to impress. Look for rate of improvement and don't overvalue experience or current accomplishments.
- His heuristic on meeting someone: "is this person a force of nature?"
- Get an eminent person to bet on you early, mainly by being helpful, and pay it forward later.
- Spend time with positive people who support your ambitions.

chunks.heading: Internal drive and motivation
chunks.text:
- Most people are externally driven. Two costs: they work on consensus ideas and career tracks, which prevents interesting work (someone else would have done it anyway), and they get risk calculations wrong by obsessing over keeping up with others.
- Smart people are especially at risk. Awareness helps only a little.
- The most successful people he knows are internally driven: they do it "to impress themselves" and because they feel compelled to make something happen.
- After you have enough money and status that more stops being fun, internal drive is the only force that keeps pushing performance higher.
- Motivation is the first thing he tries to understand about a person.
- His benchmark is Jessica Livingston and Paul Graham. YC was mocked for its first few years and few expected success, but they believed it would be good for the world, loved helping people, and were convinced their model was better.
- "It is hard to be wildly successful at anything you aren't obsessed with."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman's list of 95 startup rules, mostly heard and some given, written for a new YC batch. Core themes: build something people want, focus on growth and product quality, hire slowly and carefully, move fast, stay frugal, and raise money on clean terms from engaged investors.

chunks.heading: Two non-negotiables: team, market, and product quality
chunks.text:
- Sam says "make something people want" and treats product/market fit as the thing that matters. Most other advice conflicts, so "just make a decision and get back to work."
- A great team and a great market are both critical. He calls the debate over which matters more "silly."
- Founders should mostly write code, talk to users, and build the company (hire the best people, get the culture right, fundraise, close sales). "Most other things that founders do are a waste of time."
- Obsess about product quality. Care about execution quality.
- It is better for a few users to love the product than for many to "sort of like it."
- It is easier to sell painkillers than vitamins.
- Execution beats ideas: "far more people have good ideas than are willing to roll up their sleeves and get shit done." He says you are more likely to die from bad execution than from a competitor.
- You can win with the best product, the best price, or the best experience.
- Value can come from breakthrough innovation, incremental refinement, or complex coordination. Great companies often do two; the very best do all three.

chunks.heading: Ideas, focus, and how to pick a market
chunks.text:
- Good ideas are underweight in a "pivot-happy world," so it is worth the time to think one through.
- Don't start a startup you aren't willing to work on for ten years.
- Startups are very hard anyway, so "you may as well go after a big opportunity."
- Many of the best ideas "seem silly or bad initially." You want the intersection of "seems like bad idea" and "is good idea," and you must be "contrarian and right, not simply contrarian."
- "Surf someone else's wave."
- Set a clear, easy-to-understand vision and make it a mission people believe in.
- Stay focused and don't do too many things at once. Eliminate distractions.
- Startups should require as few miracles as possible, "but at least one."
- Pivots: do them fully and with conviction. The worst outcome is a bit of the old and a bit of the new. "It's better to make a decision and be wrong than to equivocate."
- Keep it simple and be suspicious of complexity.

chunks.heading: Growth, momentum, and customers
chunks.text:
- "Growth solves (nearly) all problems." Focus on it, but occasionally check you are growing toward something valuable.
- Momentum is critical; don't lose it.
- Move fast. Speed is a main advantage over large companies.
- You make what you measure.
- Be suspect about buying users.
- Have a direct relationship with customers and great customer service.
- Learn to sell your product, but don't let the company be run by a sales guy.
- Be suspicious of work that isn't building product or getting customers. It is easy to get sucked into "an infrastructure rewrite death spiral."
- Journalists like hearing directly from founders. If you hire PR people, resist their urge to control all contact. Ignore the fact that "the press loves [you]."
- Meetups and conferences are generally a waste of time.
- Get on planes in marginal situations: in-person beats "tele-anything."
- Don't forget to make money.

chunks.heading: Hiring and team building
chunks.text:
- Hiring is the most important thing a founder does. Spend at least a third of your time on it. "Hire slow; fire fast."
- Hire smart, effective people "committed to what you're doing."
- Hire friends and friends of friends, and go after them "like crazy." Other sources are OK, but he always got bad results from technical recruiters.
- Value aptitude over experience.
- Hire people you could describe as "animals."
- Occasionally think about why the 20th person will join.
- Don't hire professional managers too early.
- Don't have a diverse culture in the early days.
- Keep salaries low and equity high. Include a table in offer letters showing what the grant could be worth in various scenarios.
- Keep the organization as flat as possible. Stay small and nimble.
- Be suspect of anyone who says "process" too often.

chunks.heading: Running the company and culture
chunks.text:
- Overcommunicate with the team. Most founders are bad at this. "Transparency is your friend."
- Share financial results and key metrics with the company every month.
- Hold a staff meeting at least once a week.
- Keep an operational cadence with short projects and regular releases.
- Set goals and motivate people toward them. Build a culture that rewards output.
- Always praise good work. Celebrate wins (for example, t-shirts for big milestones).
- Lead by example.
- Very small companies should work out of an apartment or house.
- Pay close attention to the cofounder relationship, especially if more than one of you wants to be CEO.
- If the founders seem to care more about being founders than about the specific company, go join another company.
- Find a mentor who will teach you how to manage.
- Be formidable: "do not be easy to push around."
- Schleps are good. Be relentlessly resourceful.

chunks.heading: Fundraising, investors, and cash
chunks.text:
- "Don't die." Be frugal and keep burn low until you're sure everything is working.
- Watch cash in the bank and don't run out. Raise a bit more than you think you need.
- Startup success is usually pass/fail, so worry more about passing than about "an extra point of dilution."
- Raise money on promise and on clean terms.
- Create a competitive situation in any deal (fundraising, partnerships).
- "Investors love companies other investors love."
- Good investors are worth a reasonable premium. Prefer a few highly involved investors over many lightly engaged ones, and give them something to do.
- Do reference checks on investors. Ask other founders how they behave when everything goes wrong.
- Founders typically keep board control in the first round.
- The board's role is "advice and consent." If the CEO lays out no clear strategy and asks the board to set one, it "will usually end in disaster." Board observers are usually a headache.

chunks.heading: Founder resilience and personal habits
chunks.text:
- An almost crazy level of dedication is needed to succeed. Sometimes you can win through "sheer force of will."
- "All startups are fucked in at least one major way. Keep going."
- Stay externally optimistic when things melt down. On bad days, "tomorrow will be better."
- Being CEO "is miserable more often than it's good. But when it's good, it's really good."
- Most things are not as risky as they seem.
- Listen to everyone, then make your own decision.
- Keep a daily to-do list with the one or two big things at the top.
- Sleep and exercise.
- "Get lucky."
- The best startups are defined by exceptions. The rules are probably breakable, "but probably not all at the same time."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman argues that hard startups (needing more money, time, coordination or technology) are often easier to succeed with than easy ones, because they attract talent, help and capital. He advises thinking big, taking a reasonable next step, and committing to a long time horizon.

chunks.heading: Why hard startups are easier to make succeed
chunks.text:
- Sam calls it "the most counterintuitive secret about startups": it is often easier to succeed with a hard startup than an easy one.
- A hard startup needs far more money, time, coordination or technological development than most. It must also be valuable if it works, since "not all hard problems are worth solving."
- Easy startups are "easy to start but hard to make successful."
- Example: the year Instagram took off, probably over 1,000 photo sharing startups were funded, while fewer than ten nuclear fusion startups existed.

chunks.heading: Hard startups as a recruiting advantage
chunks.text:
- Talented people are the most precious commodity in the startup ecosystem, and they mostly want to work on something meaningful.
- The first five or ten hires are easy to get with large equity grants and areas of responsibility. Beyond that, a startup recruits on the company's mission, the likelihood of massive success, and the quality of the people there.
- He says few recruiting messages are as powerful (when true) as: "the world needs this, it won't happen any time soon if we don't do it, and we are much less likely to succeed if you don't join."
- Sam describes a derivative of the Peter Principle: a startup rises to the level where it can no longer attract enough talented people.
- The same often holds for careers. The limiting factor becomes how many talented people you know and can get to work with you.
- Alternative: build a startup that can become quite successful with fewer than ten people. As big tech compensation keeps rising, he suspects this will become a trend.

chunks.heading: Tailwind vs. headwind
chunks.text:
- An easy startup is a headwind; a hard startup is a tailwind.
- If people care about your success because you seem committed to something significant, that acts as a background force helping with hiring, advice, partnerships and fundraising.

chunks.heading: Silicon Valley takes serious people seriously
chunks.text:
- Part of the magic of Silicon Valley is that people default to taking you seriously if you are willing to be serious. They have learned that not doing so is a very expensive mistake in aggregate.
- Sam says founders working on better home building, gene editing, artificial general intelligence, a new education system or carbon sequestration may get funded even without a degree or much experience.

chunks.heading: Ambition with a reasonable next step
chunks.text:
- Let yourself become more ambitious. Figure out the most interesting version of where your work could go.
- Talk about that big vision and work relentlessly towards it, but always have a reasonable next step.
- His warning: "You don't want step one to be incorporating the company and step two to be going to Mars."

chunks.heading: Think in decade-long timeframes
chunks.text:
- Be willing to make a very long-term commitment. Most people aren't, which is part of why they pick "easy" startups.
- In a world of compounding advantages, if most people operate on a 3 year timeframe and you operate on a 10 year timeframe, you have a very large edge.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues the biggest productivity lever is choosing the right thing to work on, then compounding small gains over a career. He shares his prioritization habits (paper lists, saying no, protected mornings, 15-20 min or 2 hr meetings) and the physical factors (sleep, exercise, nutrition) he credits with a 1.5x boost.

chunks.heading: Compounding and picking the right work
chunks.text:
- Sam treats productivity as compound growth: "If you get 10% more done and 1% better every day compared to someone else, the compounded difference is massive." A small gain held over 50 years is worth a lot.
- He says picking what to work on is "the most important element of productivity and usually almost ignored." Speed in a worthless direction is worth nothing.
- He ends the essay on the same point: "productivity in the wrong direction isn't worth anything at all. Think more about what to work on."
- He warns against "productivity porn": people spend too much time perfecting their system and too little asking whether they're on the right problems. The right goal is "to allocate your year optimally, not your day."
- He leaves time in his schedule to think about what to work on. His methods are reading books, hanging out with interesting people, and spending time in nature.

chunks.heading: Conviction, learning and the people around you
chunks.text:
- The most impressive people he knows hold strong beliefs about the world. If you always agree with whoever you spoke to last, that's bad.
- He says you will sometimes be wrong, but you should build the confidence to stick with convictions. That lets you be courageous when you're right about something important that most people don't see.
- He argues you can learn anything you want and get better quickly. It feels like "an unlikely miracle" the first few times, but you learn to trust it.
- Great work usually needs colleagues. Be around smart, productive, happy, positive people who don't belittle your ambitions.
- He avoids the opposite kind of people where he can: "the cost of letting them take up your mental cycles is horrific."
- You must both pick the right problem and do the work. There are few shortcuts, and in most fields the biggest prizes are heavily competed for, so important work usually takes working smart and hard.

chunks.heading: Working on what you like, and delegation
chunks.text:
- He can't be productive on things he doesn't care about or like. He tries not to be in a position where he has to do them, by delegating, avoiding, or something else. Disliked work is "a painful drag on morale and momentum."
- Delegation rule: everyone is most productive doing what they like. Work out who likes, and is good at, which tasks, and delegate on that basis. "Do what you'd want other people to do for you."
- If you dislike what you're doing for a long period, seriously consider a major job change. Short-term burnout is normal, but if time off doesn't fix it, find work you're more interested in.
- He says he found work he likes so much he'd do it for free, which makes high productivity easy.

chunks.heading: Prioritization system and lists
chunks.text:
- His system has three pillars: "Make sure to get the important shit done", "Don't waste time on stupid shit", and "make a lot of lists".
- He keeps lists of what he wants to accomplish each year, month and day. Lists focus him and reduce what he has to hold in his head. If he's not in the mood for one task, he can find another he's excited about.
- He prefers paper lists. They're easy to add to and cut, and usable in meetings without seeming rude.
- He re-transcribes lists often. This forces him to think through everything on the list and gives a chance to add or remove items.
- He skips categorizing or sizing tasks. The most he does is star the really important items.
- He prioritizes to generate momentum: the more he gets done, the better he feels, and the more he gets done. He likes to start and end each day with something he can make real progress on.
- He is relentless on his most important projects: "if I really want something to happen and I push hard enough, it usually happens."

chunks.heading: Saying no, meetings and scheduling
chunks.text:
- He is ruthless about saying no and does non-critical things as fast as possible. He admits he likely takes this too far, e.g. being terse to the point of rudeness in email replies.
- He generally avoids meetings and conferences because the time cost is huge. He gets the most value from time in his office.
- He still keeps space for chance encounters and new people and ideas. An open network is valuable: roughly 90% of random meetings he takes are a waste, but "the other 10% really make up for it."
- He schedules most meetings for 15-20 minutes or 2 hours. The default one hour is usually wrong and wastes time.
- The first few hours of his morning are his most productive, so he lets no one schedule then. Meetings go in the afternoon.
- He takes a break or switches tasks when his attention fades.
- On valuing time: he's surprised by people who make $100 an hour yet spend a couple of hours on something they dislike to save $20.
- He overcommits slightly. He generally gets done what he takes on, and a bit too much makes him more efficient and trains him to avoid distractions. Overcommitting a lot is "disastrous."

chunks.heading: Physical factors: sleep, light, exercise
chunks.text:
- He says the optimal setup differs per person, so you must experiment. His took a little time each week over a few years. He estimates doing all of it well makes him at least 1.5x more productive.
- Sleep is the most important physical factor for him.
  - He likes a sleep tracker; the only things he's consistent with are "set-it-and-forget-it", and he likes the Emfit QS+Active.
  - He wants a cold, dark, quiet room and a great mattress (he used the Tempur-Pedic Contour Elite). He resisted spending on a mattress for years, "which was stupid."
  - Not eating a lot in the hours before bed helps. Skipping alcohol helps a lot, though he won't do that all the time.
  - He uses a Chili Pad to stay cold, with the cooler unit outside his room because it's loud.
  - When traveling he uses an eye mask and ear plugs.
  - He says this is likely controversial: when he can't sleep he takes about a third of a normal dose of sleeping pills, or a very low dose of cannabis. He's a bad sleeper, especially traveling, and notes it has tradeoffs but so does poor sleep. He wouldn't recommend it to people who sleep well.
- Light: he uses a full-spectrum LED light most mornings for 10-15 minutes while catching up on email. It's "a ridiculous gain" and the one thing he'd tell people to try if they try nothing else.
- Exercise is second. After trying several programs for a few months each, the best was lifting heavy weights 3x a week for an hour, plus occasional high intensity interval training. It also makes him feel best overall.

chunks.heading: Nutrition, caffeine and workspace
chunks.text:
- He rarely eats breakfast, getting about 15 hours of fasting most days (apart from an espresso on waking). He says it's contrary to most advice and probably not optimal for most people.
- Sugar makes him feel worst, so he avoids it and keeps junk food out of the house because he has little willpower for sweets. He also avoids foods that upset digestion or raise inflammation, like very spicy food.
- Caffeine: one big espresso on waking and one after lunch, roughly 200mg total a day. He tried other setups and this worked far better. He avoids other stimulants, but drinks more coffee if very tired and needing to finish something.
- He's vegetarian and takes methyl B-12, Omega-3, Iron and Vitamin D-3. He settled on the list after about a year of quarterly blood tests and retests every year and a half or so. He drinks many protein shakes, which he hates and wouldn't do if not vegetarian.
- Workspace wants: natural light, quiet, no interruptions unless he wants them, long blocks of time, and comfort. He has a desk with two 4k monitors but spends almost all his time on his couch with a laptop.
- He wrote custom software for annoying tasks he does often, and learned to type fast and use keyboard shortcuts.

chunks.heading: Motivation dips and not trading off life for output
chunks.text:
- He has weeks-long stretches with no motivation, possibly nutrition-related. He hasn't found a fix beyond waiting and trusting the fog always lifts.
- He avoids people and situations that put him in bad moods.
- Don't neglect family and friends for productivity. He calls it "a very stupid tradeoff" and likely a net productivity loss because you'll be less happy.
- Don't neglect things you love or that clear your head.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A list of 17 compact lessons from Sam Altman on how companies get started and finished. He covers audacious goals, concentrating bets, recruiting, fast iteration, incentives, and building businesses with compounding advantages at scale.

chunks.heading: Early-stage ingredients vs. finishing ingredients
chunks.text:
- Sam says things "get started" through optimism, obsession, self-belief, raw horsepower and personal connections.
- Things "get finished" through cohesive teams, the right mix of calmness and urgency, and unreasonable commitment.
- He notes long-term orientation is in short supply. He advises not worrying about what people think in the short term, which gets easier over time.
- He says working with great people is one of the best parts of life and that you should get back up and keep going after setbacks.

chunks.heading: Picking goals and focusing resources
chunks.text:
- A team finds it easier to do a hard thing that really matters than an easy thing that doesn't. Audacious ideas motivate people.
- He says to concentrate resources on a small number of high-conviction bets, which is "easy to say but evidently hard to do."
- He adds that "you can delete more stuff than you think."
- He treats incentives as superpowers and says to set them carefully.

chunks.heading: Org health: communication, bureaucracy, outcomes
chunks.text:
- Communicate clearly and concisely.
- Fight bullshit and bureaucracy every time you see it, and get other people to fight it too.
- Do not let the org chart get in the way of people working productively together.
- Outcomes are what count. Do not let good process excuse bad results.

chunks.heading: Recruiting and evaluating people
chunks.text:
- Spend more time recruiting.
- Take risks on high-potential people with a fast rate of improvement.
- Look for evidence of getting stuff done in addition to intelligence.
- Superstars are even more valuable than they seem, but evaluate people on their net impact on the organization's performance, not just individual output.

chunks.heading: Speed, planning horizon and bias to action
chunks.text:
- Fast iteration can make up for a lot, and it is usually fine to be wrong if you iterate quickly.
- "Plans should be measured in decades, execution should be measured in weeks."
- Inspiration is perishable and life goes by fast. Inaction is a particularly insidious type of risk.

chunks.heading: Scale, compounding and business physics
chunks.text:
- Do not fight "the business equivalent of the laws of physics."
- Scale often has surprising emergent properties.
- Compounding exponentials are magic. He says you particularly want to build a business that gets a compounding advantage with scale.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 36-point list of life and career lessons Altman wrote at age 30. The business-relevant parts: choose the right thing to work on, focus, surround yourself with exceptional people, keep personal burn low, and take more risk than feels comfortable. He also covers cutting distractions, not wasting time, and being a doer.

chunks.heading: Relationships and a small circle
chunks.text:
- Sam says never to put family, friends or a significant other low on the priority list. He prefers "a handful of truly close friends to a hundred acquaintances".
- He advises keeping up with old friends, having parties, and occasionally staying up until sunrise talking to people.
- Tell parents you love them more often and visit home as often as you can.
- Don't burn bridges or screw people, pick battles carefully, forgive people, and don't judge others too quickly because "you never know their whole story".
- Go out of your way to help people and be nice to strangers, "even when it doesn't matter".
- Don't maintain relationships with people you don't like, and cut negative people out. "Negativity is really bad."

chunks.heading: How to succeed
chunks.text:
- Sam's formula: pick the right thing to do ("critical and usually ignored"), focus, believe in yourself (especially when others say it won't work), develop personal connections with people who will help you, learn to identify talented people, and work hard.
- Picking what to work on is hard because "original thought is hard".
- He quotes Paul Graham: "People can become formidable, but it's hard to predict who". Don't let yourself get pushed around. Aim to be confident, not arrogant.
- Be a doer, not a talker. Don't chase status, because status without substance doesn't last and is unfulfilling.
- Ask for what you want.

chunks.heading: Work and career
chunks.text:
- It is difficult to do a great job on work you don't care about, and hard to be fulfilled if you dislike your work.
- Work very hard, though a surprising number of people will be offended by it, but not so hard that the rest of life passes you by.
- Aim to be the best in the world at what you do professionally. "Even if you miss, you'll probably end up in a pretty good place."
- Build your own productivity system. Don't waste time being unorganized or working at suboptimal times.
- Take career risks, especially early. Most people pick a career fairly randomly, so think hard about what you like, which fields will succeed, and talk to people in those fields.
- Don't waste time. "Most people waste most of their time, especially in business."
- Minimize cognitive load from distractions that don't matter. He says it is hard to overstate the importance, and most people are bad at it. Build strong ways to stop unwanted tasks piling up and eating mental cycles at work.

chunks.heading: Goals, planning and opportunities
chunks.text:
- Have clear goals for every day, year and decade.
- Planning is valuable, but if a great opportunity comes along, take it. Don't be afraid to do something slightly reckless.
- Working hard makes good opportunities show up, but it is still up to you to jump on them.
- Think for a few seconds before acting, and for a few minutes if angry.

chunks.heading: Risk, regret and doing new things
chunks.text:
- Most people are too risk-averse, so most advice is biased toward conservative paths. "Things in life are rarely as risky as they seem."
- If you think you'll regret not doing something, probably do it. Most people regret what they didn't do far more than what they did.
- Do new things often. Sam says it seems to slow the perception of time, raise happiness and stop people calcifying in how they think.
- Aim to do "something big, new, and risky every year" in both personal and professional life.
- Learn voraciously.

chunks.heading: Surrounding yourself with the right people
chunks.text:
- Go out of your way to be around smart, interesting, ambitious people. Work for them and hire them.
- One of the most satisfying parts of work is forging deep relationships with really good people.
- Spend time with people who are either the best in the world at what they do, or extremely promising but totally unknown.
- "You become an average of the people you spend the most time with."

chunks.heading: Money
chunks.text:
- Whether or not money buys happiness, it buys freedom, and lack of money is very stressful.
- Having enough that you don't stress about rent does more for wellbeing than having enough to buy your own jet.
- Keep your personal burn rate low. This alone gives you many opportunities.
- Making money is often more fun than spending it. Sam has never regretted money spent on friends, new experiences, saving time, travel and causes he believes in.
- In your 20s, a "Give me financial discipline, but not just yet" attitude is OK. "All the money in the world will never get back time that passed you by."

chunks.heading: Time, attention and wellbeing
chunks.text:
- "Life is not a dress rehearsal—this is probably it." Time is limited and goes by fast.
- Do what makes you happy and fulfilled, and don't make excuses for not doing what you want. Don't do things you dislike just because others want you to.
- Talk to people more, read more long content and fewer tweets, watch less TV, spend less time online.
- Exercise, eat well, sleep, and get out into nature regularly.
- Most things are fine in moderation and almost nothing is fine in extreme amounts.
- Existential angst is part of life, especially around major events or after career milestones, and affects smart, ambitious people. Sam thinks some people work hard to avoid thinking about it. Nothing is wrong with you for feeling it.
- Be grateful, keep problems in perspective, don't complain much, and don't hate others' success. Some people will hate yours, so learn to ignore it.
- Humans can adjust to almost anything given time. "This too shall pass."
- His closing line: "The days are long but the decades are short."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman reframes "how do I stop caring what people think" as the wrong question. You choose whose opinions matter and on what timescale. The most impressive people care on a very long horizon, accept short-term low status, and use being misunderstood as room to solve important problems.

chunks.heading: Caring about opinions: two choices, not one
chunks.text:
- Sam rejects the question "how do I stop caring what other people think?" as the wrong one. When a founder asked him, he had no answer, and on reflection decided the framing was flawed.
- He says almost everyone cares what someone thinks, and it's probably important. "Caring too much makes you a sheep," and caring what *everyone* thinks is "definitely a mistake."
- You still need to be at least a little in tune with others to build something useful for them.
- He sees two degrees of freedom:
  - Which people's opinions you care about, and on what subjects.
  - The timescale on which you care about those opinions.
- Most people work out the first. The second "doesn't seem to get much attention."
- He cites Coco Chanel on choosing whose opinions count: "I don't care what you think about me. I don't think about you at all."

chunks.heading: Long time horizons: the trait of the most impressive people
chunks.text:
- Sam observes that the most impressive people he knows care a lot about what people think, even people whose opinions they arguably shouldn't value.
- He notes that a surprising number of them keep a folder of screenshots of tweets from haters.
- What makes them unusual is the time horizon. They care about opinion on a very long timescale.
- Their attitude: as long as the history books get it right, they take some pride in letting the newspapers get it wrong.

chunks.heading: Trading short-term status for long-term status
chunks.text:
- His core advice: "You should trade being short-term low-status for being long-term high-status."
- He says most people seem unwilling to make this trade.
- A common way it plays out is by eventually being right about an important but deeply non-consensus bet.
- He says there are many other ways it can happen. The key point is that it only works if you are right.

chunks.heading: Being misunderstood as a strength
chunks.text:
- Sam argues that, as long as you are right, being misunderstood by most people is "a strength not a weakness."
- The reason is space: you and a small group of rebels get room to work on an important problem that might otherwise not get solved.
- When a bet is non-consensus, few people compete for it and few try to stop it. That leaves the problem to those willing to be misunderstood in the meantime.
- Practical takeaways from the essay:
  - Decide whose opinions matter and on which topics.
  - Decide the timescale you judge yourself on. Pick the long one.
  - Accept short-term low status as the price of an important non-consensus bet.
  - Being misunderstood is only a strength if you turn out to be right, so the bet has to be a good one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues hiring is the most important thing a founder does and should consume a third to half of their time after product-market fit. He covers sourcing through personal networks, auditioning candidates with real work, selling a mission, hiring for values, paying in equity, never compromising, and firing fast.

chunks.heading: Hire for startups: time, auditions, and sourcing
chunks.text:
- Sam says hiring is "probably the most important thing a founder does." Companies "are a product of the team the founders build," and a mediocre hire can't be managed into doing good work.
- After the vision and product-market fit are settled, he says founders should spend between a third and a half of their time hiring.
- It can't be outsourced. The founder identifies people, gets candidates to want the job, and meets every person who interviews. He cites Keith Rabois's view that the CEO/founders should interview every candidate until the company has at least 500 employees.
- Learn the role by doing it before hiring for it. His example is a hacker-CEO who hires a VP of Sales to avoid getting his hands dirty: "This does not work." The founder should do the job first, then lean on the board or investors for opinions on the final few candidates.
- Hiring is a long-term, always-on activity, not something started when a role is urgent. If you find someone great for a role you won't need for two months, hire her now.
- Don't hire for the sake of it. Companies generally work better when smaller. Figure out the least work you can feasibly do and use the smallest team that can do it. "Hire because there is no other way to do what you want to do."

chunks.heading: Evaluating candidates: smart, effective, and auditions
chunks.text:
- Smart and effective are table stakes for every role. Hires who lack them predictably fail in the early days of a startup.
- Interview tactics:
  - Ask about their most impressive projects and biggest wins.
  - Ask how they spend an average day and what they got done in the last month.
  - Go deep on what they personally did, since it is easy to take credit for a successful project.
  - Ask how they would solve a problem you currently have in that role.
  - Combine this with the right reference-check questions.
- Intelligence is usually clear by the end of an hour-long conversation. If you learn nothing, that is bad; if you are bored, that is really bad. A good interview feels like a conversation, not questions and responses.
- Smart, effective people are adaptable, which matters because anyone hired is likely doing a new job within three to six months.
- Sam calls auditions "the most important tactical piece of advice I have." Have candidates audition for roles instead of interviewing for them:
  - It is hard to know what working with someone is like after a few interviews, but easy after working with them.
  - Almost always possible: have the person do a day or two of work, at night or on weekends.
  - Developer: write code for a real but non-critical project.
  - PR person: write a press release and identify reporters to pitch it to.
  - Have them sign a contractor agreement and pay them like a normal contractor.
  - The candidate also gets a feel for what working at the company is like.

chunks.heading: Sourcing candidates and building a recruiting pipeline
chunks.text:
- The core rule: "use your personal networks more." By at least a 10x margin, Sam says friends and friends of friends are the best candidate source he has seen.
- Go after the best people relentlessly even if you doubt you can get them. If it works 5% of the time, it's still worth it. The best startups keep hiring this way far longer than seems possible, and bad startups make excuses for not doing so.
- Once you're sure a new hire is a star, sit her down and "wring out of her the names of everyone that you should try to hire." It may take real effort.
- Great people are never looking for jobs, so recruiting often means poaching. He admits he has no great answer on poaching from acquaintances, quoting a friend: "Poaching is the titty twister of Silicon Valley relationships."
- Other channels:
  - Technical recruiters are pretty bad and job boards are generally worse.
  - Conferences can be good.
  - Hosting interesting tech talks can help with technical hiring.
  - University recruiting works well once the company is reasonably established.
  - Don't limit the search to your area; many people want to move to the Bay Area.
  - Tell investors in update emails what kinds of people you need, and use their networks.
- Treat sourcing as a long-term investment: you may spend time with someone for a year or more before talking about a job.
- A recruiting product idea he would back: a service that shows how everyone in your company is connected to a candidate and searches employees' personal networks. He says LinkedIn is probably good for sales hires but not for developers.

chunks.heading: Selling the mission and closing candidates
chunks.text:
- You need a mission to hire well. Candidates must believe in it, meaning why this job matters more than the others they could take. A mission that excites people is probably the best thing you can do to get a great team before runaway traction.
- Founders assume everyone will be as excited about the company as they are; "in reality, no one will." Expect to spend a lot of time selling.
- A good mission plus good selling lets you land slightly overqualified people. In a fast-growing startup they quickly end up in a role they feel not quite ready for anyway.
- Use the board and investors to help close candidates.
- Once you decide you want someone, switch into closing mode. The person she will report to, and ideally the CEO, should do everything possible to close her and talk to her about once a day.

chunks.heading: Culture, fit, and not compromising
chunks.text:
- Hire people you like. Sam cites Stripe's "Sunday test": would you come into the office on a Sunday because you want to hang out with this person? He has only a few times seen a very good candidate he didn't like, and the one time he hired anyway "was a mistake."
- Want some diversity of thought. Some attributes need uniformity (integrity, intelligence) and others need coverage of the full range (for example, both nerds and athletes).
- Decide your cultural values deliberately, make sure the whole company knows and buys into them, and hire for them. Treat them as "articles of faith" and be willing to pass on an otherwise good candidate who doesn't fit.
- He quotes Andrew Mason: "Values are a decision making framework that empower individuals to make the decision that you, the founder, would make, in situations where there are conflicting interests (e.g. growth vs. customer satisfaction)."
- Diversity of opinions is good; diversity of values in a startup is bad. Some people are so set in their ways they will never get behind your values, and you'll probably end up firing them.
- Avoid remote employees in the early days, while culture is still gelling.
- Don't compromise, especially early. You'll always need someone yesterday, but "a single bad hire left unfixed for long can kill a company." It's better to lose a deal or ship late than hire someone mediocre. Great people attract great people, and one mediocre hire can unwind that.

chunks.heading: Compensation and equity
chunks.text:
- Be frugal with nearly everything in a startup except pay for great people.
- Be most generous with equity. Ideally pay slightly below to roughly market salary plus a very generous equity package, and pay just enough that people don't stress about cash flow.
- Experienced people often have higher personal burn rates and may need more pay. But great companies are not usually created by experienced people, with a few exceptions where it matters a lot.
- His line: if you want an above-market salary, go work at a big company with no equity upside.
- Equity rule of thumb for the first 20 hires: about double what your investors suggest. Rough numbers he has seen for a company on a good but not absolute breakout trajectory: about 1.5% for the first engineer and about 0.25% for the twentieth, with huge variance.
- Example: a very successful YC company pays effectively all engineers one flat salary, lower than market. It works because those people enjoy the work and believe in the stock, and they are likely to earn far more than with higher salaries elsewhere.
- Expect to negotiate a little, so learn how. Don't materially break your compensation structure to land someone, because word gets out and everyone is upset.

chunks.heading: Process, red flags, firing, and retention
chunks.text:
- Red flags: focus on title, and worse, on "how many reports will be in my organization." These usually signal the person won't succeed at a startup. "If you have a difficult-to-articulate desire to pass, pass."
- Add some rigor to the process:
  - Every interviewer commits to a hire/no-hire decision and writes up their thoughts, which is useful to review if you get it wrong.
