  - Hold a brief in-person discussion with the whole interview team after each candidate leaves.
  - Take the candidate out to lunch or dinner.
  - Insist everyone is on time and prepared, and that every candidate leaves with a positive impression.
  - One person coordinates the whole process.
  - Set a consistent decision framework, such as whether you need unanimous consent.
  - Teach people how to interview, since great team members may not be great interviewers.
- Fire fast. He has never met a newbie founder who fires fast enough, or a founder who doesn't learn this after a few years. When it's obviously not working, it's unlikely to start. Parting quickly is better for everyone, and a short stint is a non-issue in future interviews. The rest of the team usually knows before you do.
- Retention:
  - Check in with people and be a good manager.
  - Hold regular all-hands meetings.
  - Keep people happy and challenged.
  - Keep a sense of momentum, which is important to retaining talent.
  - Give people new roles about every six months.
  - Keep bringing in talented people, since that alone makes good people want to stay.
  - Always identify and promote new talent.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman explains that good investing comes down to three things: getting access to deals, choosing well, and getting founders to choose you. He covers how to spot future great founders, why to aim only at potential $10B outcomes, and how to help founders by raising their ambition and giving tactical advice.

chunks.heading: Sam's three-part model for investing in startups
chunks.text:
- Sam says doing well as an investor takes three things: get access to good opportunities, make good decisions about what to back, and get those companies to choose you.
- He admits the best investments "will do quite well without you".
- He notes the market is hard for investors. Supply and demand have pushed valuations up and the best deals are flooded with interest. A friend told him it is easier to raise LP money for a seed fund than to get a meaningful allocation in a hot deal.

chunks.heading: Getting access to deals
chunks.text:
- Sam calls access the easiest of the three: "you can just work hard". He says most investors don't, which is a bug to exploit.
- Networking works if it isn't just trying to grab coffee when people have time. Help investors you respect and help good founders, and deal flow follows.
- For a new full-time investor, he suggests making your job helping your future sourcing network. Instead of asking contacts for deals, offer to spend a day a week helping their best company.
- Early-stage investors can help with closing candidates, future fundraising, customer introductions and generic advice.
- A brand is the other route to access. He favors long-form writing (hard, few do it well) over tweeting (easy, everyone does it fine).

chunks.heading: Picking founders
chunks.text:
- Great founders are the key to great startups. One way to win is to predict who will be great before they are, because the market rewards finding great but inexperienced people. Proven founders cost more in share price.
- Meet people in person, several times. If someone meets you three times in three months and visibly improves each time, pay attention. Rate of improvement often matters more than current ability.
- His main question: would I work for this person? The second: can I imagine them taking over their industry?
- Traits he looks for:
  - scrappy and formidable at once
  - mission-oriented, obsessed, relentless
  - extremely smart (necessary, not sufficient)
  - decisive, fast-moving, willful
  - courageous, high-conviction, willing to be misunderstood
  - strong communicators and infectious evangelists
  - able to become tough and ambitious
- Toughness and ambition can change quickly. Speed seems harder to change: people tend to be slow or fast movers. He has "almost never made money investing in founders who do not respond quickly to important emails".
- The successful founders he funded believed they were eventually certain to succeed.

chunks.heading: Picking markets
chunks.text:
- Startups can win wherever costs can be low and cycle time fast. They do especially well in industries with rapid technological change, because their advantages over large competitors are speed and focus.
- He cares about a market's growth rate and eventual size, not its current size. He doesn't know why most investors fixate on current size, and sees it as an opportunity.
- The best companies lead the market by a couple of years. To tell a real trend from a fake one, check whether the few early users use the platform a lot and love it. His example: the iPhone was derided for few users in its first year or two, but owners raved about it as they never had about earlier smartphones.
- The very best companies ride a new, important, fast-growing platform.

chunks.heading: Traits of the best companies and the power law
chunks.text:
- The best companies he invested in usually share most of these:
  - compelling founders
  - a mission that attracts talented people
  - a product people spontaneously tell friends about
  - a rapidly growing market
  - a network effect and low marginal costs
  - the ability to grow fast
  - a product that is fundamentally new or 10x better than the alternatives
- Limit yourself to opportunities that could be $10 billion companies if they work, meaning at least a fast-growing market and some pricing power. Failures and small successes matter little; "the giant returns are where everything happens". He admits he has violated this many times.
- His central career learning: "you can and should scale up things that are working." He thinks about the potential energy of future scale for every investment, and sees most people as terrible at this.
- For early-stage investing, good ideas mostly help identify good founders. His hardest chronic mistake to correct is investing in bad founders with good ideas. His second is chasing deals mainly because other investors like them.

chunks.heading: Winning the deal (close rate)
chunks.text:
- The better the opportunity relative to valuation, the harder it is to be chosen. Traditional sales tactics work: spend lots of time with the founder, explain how you'll help, and have founders you've backed call them.
- Reputation matters most: being above-and-beyond helpful and accessible, founder-friendly, and above all having founders say "that person was my best investor by far". A strong brand also helps, since taking your money can make a company be taken more seriously.
- Decisiveness helps. Most investors wait for someone else to act, and founders appreciate fast, early decisions. His two recent examples:
  - telling previously backed founders he'd do their Series A before they finished describing the idea
  - offering to do the seed round of founders he'd never met at the end of a one-hour meeting
- He doesn't recommend that often, but says that when conviction is strong, let it show.
- The surest way to a poor close rate is not treating founders as peers. Founders sense whether you'll act like a peer or a boss, and acting like their boss fails "an intelligence test".

chunks.heading: Helping founders after you invest
chunks.text:
- The most important help is making founders more ambitious, with bigger thinking and more self-belief. Set goals that are ambitious but achievable. Most people set goals just out of reach, which demotivates. He prefers continuously setting goals you can just barely hit, since momentum is self-reinforcing.
- Second is specific tactical advice rather than general strategy. His example: "it seems like you've figured out yourself how to do sales for this company, so here is where to look and what to look for in your first sales hire, and here is the sales tool you should use".
- Intros, hiring help, finding other investors or an office are good, but wait to be asked.
- Exception: proactively say so when you have very high conviction a founder is about to make a big mistake, especially once things work and they aren't set up to scale.
- He warns against trying to give founders new ideas. PG is a "sui generis idea generator", and even most great investors are bad at telling founders what to work on. Be self-aware.
- When founders call asking for vague help, they usually want emotional support from a friend. Invite them over, make tea or pour a drink, and listen.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman argues that good founders generate ideas constantly, so handing them an idea rarely works. He covers environment, thinking from the future backwards, spotting tectonic shifts, and tests for whether an idea could be huge and fits the founder.

chunks.heading: Starting from ideas: why founders must be able to generate them
chunks.text:
- The two most common questions from prospective founders: how do I get startup ideas, and do you have any ideas for my startup.
- Sam says handing a founder an idea "almost always doesn't work."
- He treats having ideas as "among the most important qualities for a startup founder to have," because running a startup requires generating lots of new ideas continuously.
- YC ran an experiment funding seemingly good founders with no ideas. Sam thinks every company in that no-idea track failed.
- His conclusion: good founders have lots of ideas about everything. Someone who wants to found a company but can't find an idea should first get good at idea generation.

chunks.heading: Environment and people that produce ideas
chunks.text:
- Be in the right environment, around people who:
  - have a good feel for the future
  - will entertain improbable plans
  - are optimistic
  - are smart in a creative way
  - have a very high "idea flux"
- These people think without the usual constraints, have few filters and don't care much what others think.
- "The best ideas are fragile." Most people never voice them because they sound silly.
- Seek people who don't make you feel stupid for mentioning a bad idea, and who never feel stupid for doing so themselves.
- Avoid world-weary people who belittle your ambitions. Sam notes this is most of the world, but they hold on to the past and founders want to live in the future.

chunks.heading: Thinking backwards from 20 years out
chunks.text:
- Project yourself 20 years into the future, then think backwards from there.
- Sam says to trust yourself: 20 years is a long time, so it's fine if your ideas about it seem pretty radical.
- Sam later noted this applies to AI development too, particularly the paragraphs on environment, the future, tectonic shifts and "possible this year, not last year."

chunks.heading: Spotting tectonic shifts and real vs fake trends
chunks.text:
- Ask what the most important tectonic shifts happening right now are. How is the world changing in fundamental ways? Can you identify a leading edge of change and the opportunity it unlocks?
- Most recent significant example in 2018: the mobile phone explosion from 2008-2012. He said "we are overdue for another!"
- In such shifts the world changes so fast that big incumbents usually get beaten by fast-moving, focused startups.
- Get good at telling real trends from fake ones. A key differentiator: whether the new platform is used a lot by a small number of people (real signal), or used a little by a lot of people.

chunks.heading: Timing signals for a startup idea
chunks.text:
- Anything possible this year that wasn't possible last year deserves attention. It may be the seed of a great startup, especially if next year will be too late.
- A good sign is being able to say: "I am sure this is going to happen, I'm just not sure if we'll be the ones to do it."
- Sam's Uber example: after his first ride, it was clear people wouldn't be calling cabs much longer, but he wasn't sure Uber would win the space.

chunks.heading: Screening ideas: could it be huge, and does it have an accumulating advantage
chunks.text:
- Early on, ask: "could this be huge if it worked?"
- Many ideas are good, but few have the inherent advantages that make a startup massively successful.
- Most businesses don't generate a valuable accumulating advantage as they scale. Think early about why your idea might.
- It's obvious for Facebook or Airbnb, but it often exists in more subtle ways.

chunks.heading: Founder/company fit and the contrarian test
chunks.text:
- Consider what you're well suited for. Pure introspection is hard here, so ask a mentor or people you've worked with what you're particularly good at.
- Sam says: "founder/company fit is as important as product/market fit."
- A good test for an idea: you can articulate why most people think it's a bad idea, but you understand what makes it good.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman calls software the third great technological revolution, after agriculture and industry. He argues it will do what technology usually does: create wealth, destroy jobs, and put more power in small groups. He sees AI and synthetic biology as the biggest risks and favors sensible safeguards plus making sure the good side's technological edge outpaces bad actors'.

chunks.heading: Software revolution: three great revolutions, and why this one destroys jobs
chunks.text:
- Sam names three great technological revolutions: agricultural, industrial, and the software revolution, which he says "we are now in the middle of."
- Great revolutions change what most people do every day and how society is structured.
- He says the industrial revolution was an anomaly. It created lots of jobs because the technology needed huge numbers of humans to run it. That leads people, "perhaps subconsciously," to assume technological revolutions are always good for most people's economic status.
- His view is that software will do what technology usually does: "create wealth but destroy jobs."
- He expects people will probably find new things to do to satisfy limitless human demand. Even so, "we should stop pretending that the software revolution, by itself, is going to be good for median wages."
- He is a fan of the software revolution and feels fortunate to have been born when he was. His worry is that the wrong lessons were learned from recent examples.

chunks.heading: Technology as leverage: wealth concentration and inequality
chunks.text:
- Sam argues that technology "provides leverage on ability and luck," and in doing so concentrates wealth and drives inequality.
- He thinks drastic wealth inequality is likely to be one of the biggest social problems of the next 20 years.
- He says wealth can and will be redistributed. That still doesn't solve the real problem of people needing something fulfilling to do.
- He grants that life is better in absolute terms than 100 years ago, even for very poor people. He also grants that highly paid people make inexpensive services for the poor.
- He argues that ignoring quality of life relative to other people alive today "ignores what makes us human."
- His position on inequality:
  - It is a good thing when some people make thousands of times as much as others.
  - He doesn't resent paying his taxes.
  - We should do much more to help people who are actually poor.
  - The social safety net "will have to trend up with the development of technology."

chunks.heading: Jobs: don't cling to worthless ones, plan for fundamentally new ones
chunks.text:
- Sam calls trying to hold on to worthless jobs "a terrible but popular idea."
- Finding new jobs for billions of people is a good idea but very hard. The new jobs will probably be so different from anything today that meaningful planning is almost impossible.
- He criticizes the current strategy, which amounts to "pretending that Travis is kidding when he talks about self-driving cars and that Uber really is going to create millions of jobs forever."
- His point is that founders' own statements about automation should be taken at face value rather than dismissed.

chunks.heading: Power concentration: why software differs from the atomic bomb
chunks.text:
- Sam's second major challenge of the software revolution is the concentration of power in small groups.
- The atomic bomb is hard to build mainly because enriching uranium takes huge amounts of energy, so effectively "the resources of nations" are needed. Restricted knowledge matters less than that.
- He says this was an idiosyncrasy of nuclear development, not the normal course of technology. Like the industrial revolution and job growth, it taught bad lessons.
- Technology usually makes more power available to small groups, and he expects the software revolution to do the same.
- Footnote: he notes the enrichment barrier may be eroding, citing laser isotope separation ("Or at least, one used to").
- He gives rockets as an example. Building one used to take the resources of nations. Companies can now do it, partly enabled by software, and "a rocket can destroy anything on earth."

chunks.heading: Existential risks from AI and synthetic biology
chunks.text:
- Sam sees AI and synthetic biology as two of the biggest risks of the software revolution. Both may put tremendous capability to cause harm in the hands of small groups or even individuals.
- On biology, he says it is probably already possible to design and produce a terrible disease in a small lab.
- On AI, an AI that could end human life "may only require a few hundred people in an office building anywhere in the world, with no equipment other than laptops."
- He says the new existential threats won't require the resources of nations to produce.
- He finds it "astonishing" that no serious efforts are underway to combat threats from synthetic biology and AI development.

chunks.heading: Strategy: legislate safeguards, but make the good side's edge stronger
chunks.text:
- Two approaches Sam rejects:
  - Making the knowledge illegal and hoping that works.
  - Trying to stop technological progress.
- His recommended strategy has two parts:
  - Legislate sensible safeguards.
  - Work very hard so that the edge technology gives the good side is stronger than the edge it gives bad actors.
- He argues for defense using the same technology:
  - "If we can synthesize new diseases, maybe we can synthesize vaccines."
  - "If we can make a bad AI, maybe we can make a good AI that stops the bad one."
- He calls the current strategy "badly misguided." His view is that "it's not going to be like the atomic bomb this time around, and the sooner we stop pretending otherwise, the better off we'll be."

chunks.heading: Historical framing of technology
chunks.text:
- Sam notes that many smaller revolutions have also mattered, including writing, cannons, the internal combustion engine, atomic bombs, fishing, and the hand axe.
- He calls the hand axe "the longest-serving piece of technology in human history."
- He mentions that many people believe fishing is what allowed humans to develop their current brains.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman looks back on two years since ChatGPT's launch: building a company from scratch around a new technology, the board crisis, and growth from about 100M to 300M+ weekly users. Strategy evolved (product company, huge capital needs) while the vision stayed fixed, and iterative release stays central to safety.

chunks.heading: Building OpenAI as a product company, not just a research lab
chunks.text:
- Sam says OpenAI started almost nine years ago because the founders believed AGI was possible and could be the most impactful technology in human history. At the time "very few people cared, and if they did, it was mostly because they thought we had no chance of success."
- He admits that "when we started we had no idea we would have to build a product company; we thought we were just going to do great research." They also did not expect to need "such a crazy amount of capital."
- His stance: "Our vision won't change; our tactics will continue to evolve." New things will need to be built that "we didn't understand a few years ago."
- He says OpenAI "cannot be a normal company" given the possibilities of its work.

chunks.heading: How ChatGPT came from watching developer behavior
chunks.text:
- In 2022 OpenAI was a quiet research lab working on a demo temporarily called "Chat With GPT-3.5". Sam jokes they are "much better at research than we are at naming things."
- The idea came from watching people use the playground feature of the API. The team saw developers "really enjoying talking to the model."
- The reasoning for building a demo around that behavior: it would show people something important about the future and help make the models better and safer.
- ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022.
- Sam says they always knew a tipping point would come but "didn't know what the moment would be. To our surprise, it turned out to be this."
- The launch started a growth curve "like nothing we have ever seen" in the company, the industry and the world.

chunks.heading: Growth numbers after the board crisis
chunks.text:
- Since the crisis, OpenAI grew from about 100 million weekly active users to more than 300 million.
- He credits the focus after the crisis with "some of our best research ever."
- His stated product test: "continue to put technology out into the world that people genuinely seem to love and that solves real problems."
- His distribution philosophy: "iteratively putting great tools in the hands of people leads to great, broadly-distributed outcomes."
- He argues the safest way to build an AI system is releasing it "iteratively and gradually" into the world, so society can adapt and co-evolve with it, and guiding safety research with feedback from real-world applications.

chunks.heading: Building a company at extreme velocity with no handbook
chunks.text:
- Over two years OpenAI had to build "an entire company, almost from scratch, around this new technology." Sam says nobody can train you for this except doing it, and with a brand-new category "there is no one at all who can tell you exactly how it should be done."
- He describes the process as "often two steps forward, one step back (and sometimes, one step forward and two steps back)," with mistakes corrected as you go. "There aren't really any handbooks or guideposts when you're doing original work."
- Moving fast in uncharted waters is stressful, and "conflicts and misunderstanding abound."
- His coping habit: remember the gratitude, and keep perspective "on any given Friday, when seven things go badly wrong by 1 pm."
- He calls the last two years "like a decade at a normal company."

chunks.heading: Turnover, competitors and being the leader
chunks.text:
- Sam says teams tend to turn over as they scale, and OpenAI scales fast: "numbers go up by orders of magnitude every few months."
- He considers some turnover unavoidable: "startups usually see a lot of turnover at each new major level of scale."
- Some colleagues split off and became competitors. As companies grow and evolve fast, "interests naturally diverge."
- When a company in an important industry leads, "lots of people attack it for all sorts of reasons, especially when they are trying to compete with it."

chunks.heading: Governance lessons from being fired
chunks.text:
- Sam was fired by surprise on a video call while in a Las Vegas hotel room, and the board published a blog post right after. He says it felt "like a dream gone wrong," and the "fog of war" was the strangest part, since nobody could get satisfactory answers.
- His verdict: "a big failure of governance by well-meaning people, myself included."
- Lessons he states:
  - Wants to be a "better, more thoughtful leader" than a year earlier.
  - A board needs diverse viewpoints and broad experience managing complex challenges.
  - "Good governance requires a lot of trust and credibility."
- OpenAI built a stronger governance system afterward to pursue its mission.

chunks.heading: Founder support network in a crisis
chunks.text:
- Sam says Ron Conway and Brian Chesky were the two people who stood out. He believes OpenAI "would have fallen apart" without them, and they worked around the clock for days.
- What they did: stayed calm, kept clear strategic thinking, stopped him from several mistakes, made none themselves, and used their vast networks for everything needed.
- He says he had gotten a huge amount of help and advice from Brian over the prior couple of years, and values "being in the foxhole" to see what people can do.
- He sees this peer support as "an amazingly special thing about our industry" that does more to make it work than people realize, and says he looks forward to paying it forward.

chunks.heading: Where he thinks AI goes next
chunks.text:
- Sam says OpenAI is "now confident we know how to build AGI as we have traditionally understood it."
- He predicts that in 2025 the first AI agents may "join the workforce" and materially change company output.
- The aim is moving beyond that to superintelligence: "We love our current products, but we are here for the glorious future. With superintelligence, we can do anything else."
- He expects superintelligent tools to accelerate scientific discovery and innovation and increase abundance and prosperity.
- He accepts that this sounds like science fiction: "we've been there before and we're OK with being there again."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman lays out three observations about AI economics: intelligence scales with the log of resources, cost per level of AI falls about 10x every year, and the value of intelligence is super-exponential. He argues agents will act as virtual coworkers, that agency and adaptability will matter most, and that benefits must be broadly distributed.

chunks.heading: AI intelligence scales with the log of resources, and cost falls fast
chunks.text:
Sam states three observations about the economics of AI.

- **Observation 1:** "The intelligence of an AI model roughly equals the log of the resources used to train and run it." The resources are chiefly training compute, data, and inference compute.
- He says you can spend arbitrary amounts of money and get continuous, predictable gains. The scaling laws that predict this "are accurate over many orders of magnitude."
- **Observation 2:** The cost of a given level of AI falls about 10x every 12 months, and lower prices lead to much more use.
- His evidence: price per token dropped about 150x from GPT-4 in early 2023 to GPT-4o in mid-2024.
- Comparison: Moore's law changed the world at 2x every 18 months, and he calls this "unbelievably stronger."

chunks.heading: Super-exponential value justifies exponentially rising investment
chunks.text:
- **Observation 3:** "The socioeconomic value of linearly increasing intelligence is super-exponential in nature."
- Consequence: Sam sees "no reason for exponentially increasing investment to stop in the near future."
- Together the three observations imply a loop. Spending buys predictable gains, falling costs expand usage, and the value of each increment keeps compounding.
- He says that if all three hold, the impact on society will be significant.

chunks.heading: AI agents as virtual co-workers
chunks.text:
- OpenAI is starting to roll out AI agents that "will eventually feel like virtual co-workers."
- His example is a software engineering agent that does most of what a top-company engineer with a few years of experience could do, on tasks up to a couple of days long.
- He sets honest limits: it will not have the biggest new ideas, will need lots of human supervision and direction, and will be great at some things but "surprisingly bad" at others.
- His framing: picture it as a "real-but-relatively-junior virtual coworker," then imagine 1,000 of them, or 1 million, and agents like this in every field of knowledge work.

chunks.heading: How AI diffuses through the economy
chunks.text:
- Economically, AI may resemble the transistor: a big scientific discovery that scales well and seeps into almost every corner of the economy.
- Gains are widely distributed. We don't think about transistors or transistor companies, but computers, TVs, cars and toys perform miracles.
- Change will not arrive all at once. People in 2025 will mostly spend their time as they did in 2024.
- The long-term changes to society and economy will still be huge, and the impact will be uneven. Some industries will change very little, while scientific progress will likely be much faster. He says this may surpass everything else.
- Prices: many goods will eventually fall dramatically, because the costs of intelligence and energy currently constrain a lot of things. Luxury goods and inherently limited resources like land may rise even more dramatically.

chunks.heading: What skills and strategy matter
chunks.text:
- "Agency, willfulness, and determination will likely be extremely valuable."
- Correctly deciding what to do, and figuring out how to navigate an ever-changing world, will have huge value. He recommends cultivating resilience and adaptability.
- He calls AGI "the biggest lever ever on human willfulness," enabling individuals to have more impact than ever, not less.
- Jobs will change: people will find new things to do, new ways to be useful and new ways to compete, but these may not look like today's jobs.
- His long-run aim: anyone in 2035 should be able to marshal the intellectual capacity of everyone in 2025, with "unlimited genius to direct however they can imagine."

chunks.heading: Launching early, openness, and distributing the benefits
chunks.text:
- One reason for launching products "early and often" is to give society and the technology time to co-evolve, since public policy and collective opinion on integrating AGI matter a lot.
- On control: Sam expects to give people more control over the technology than historically, including open-sourcing more. He accepts there is a balance between safety and individual empowerment that requires trade-offs.
- He says some safety decisions will be unpopular, but directionally, trending toward individual empowerment is important. The alternative he sees is authoritarian governments using AI for mass surveillance and loss of autonomy.
- On distribution: technological progress tends to improve health and prosperity on average, but increasing equality "does not seem technologically determined."
- He warns the balance of power between capital and labor "could easily get messed up," which may need early intervention.
- Ideas he is open to: giving a "compute budget" so everyone on Earth can use a lot of AI, or simply driving the cost of intelligence as low as possible.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues the human-machine merge is a gradual process that has already begun, driven by algorithms that shape our attention and decisions. He expects superhuman AI sooner than most people think, because compute and the number of AI researchers are both growing exponentially, and he urges worldwide coordination early.

chunks.heading: The merge is already underway and gradual, not a single moment
chunks.text:
- Sam notes Silicon Valley debates what year humans and machines merge, with most guesses between 2025 and 2075.
- He thinks "singularity" fell out of use partly because it implies one moment, while the merge looks gradual, and "gradual processes are hard to notice."
- He believes the merge "has already started, and we are a few years in": "Our phones control us and tell us what to do when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think."
- The algorithms behind this are no longer understood by any one person. They optimize for what their creators tell them to, in ways no human could figure out. They are what seems like sophisticated AI today and "will seem like child's play" tomorrow.

chunks.heading: Co-evolution between humans and AI
chunks.text:
- Sam describes the current phase as co-evolution: "the AIs affect, effect, and infect us, and then we improve the AI."
- The loop he points to is that people build more computing power and run AI on it, and the AI then figures out how to build even better chips.
- He argues this probably cannot be stopped, since scientific advancement eventually happens if the laws of physics do not prevent it.
- Unless humanity destroys itself first, he expects superhuman AI, genetic enhancement and brain-machine interfaces all to happen.
- He calls it "a failure of human imagination and human arrogance" to assume we will never build things smarter than ourselves.
- On intelligence, he argues that self-worth is so tied to intelligence that people believe it must be singular. He suggests it sits on a continuum, and that AI might see the gap between us and bonobos as barely worth discussing.

chunks.heading: Why a merge is the best-case outcome
chunks.text:
- His logic is that if two species both want the same thing (to be the dominant species on the planet and beyond) and only one can have it, they will come into conflict.
- He concludes: "We should all want one team where all members care about the well-being of everyone else."
- A merge can take many forms, from electrodes in the brain to simply becoming "really close friends with a chatbot."
- Humans will be "the first species ever to design our own descendants." He sees two paths: be "the biological bootloader for digital intelligence" and fade into an evolutionary branch, or work out what a successful merge looks like.

chunks.heading: Why it may come sooner than expected
chunks.text:
- Hardware is improving exponentially, and the number of smart people working on AI is also growing exponentially. He warns that "double exponential functions get away from you fast."
- The most surprising thing he has learned working on OpenAI is "just how correlated increasing computing power and AI breakthroughs are."
- He argues the world should take this much more seriously now, because worldwide coordination is slow and is needed for this.

chunks.heading: Attention hacking as a personal and societal risk
chunks.text:
- Sam says he has a very hard time resisting what the algorithms want him to do, and found himself getting extremely addicted to the internet until he made a real effort to combat it.
- He predicts "attention hacking is going to be the sugar epidemic of this generation."
- He reports personal effects: he can wistfully remember having an attention span, and he is angry and unhappy more often.
- He says he channels that anger into productive change less often, instead chasing "the dual dopamine hits of likes and outrage."
- He observes that friends' young children do not know an attention span is something they should miss.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman's YC distillation of how to start a startup: a great idea, team, product and execution. Core claim: a product users love is the only durable growth engine. Growth, focus and intensity, frugality, and hiring discipline do the rest. Includes concrete heuristics on LTV, CAC payback and fundraising.

chunks.heading: The idea and testing it
chunks.text:
- Sam asks founders what they're building and why, and wants "clear, concise answers." Complex ideas are "almost always a sign of muddled thinking or a made up problem." A good idea should excite at least some people the first time they hear it.
- He asks who desperately needs the product. Best case: the founder is the target user. Second best: the founder understands the user extremely well.
- If there are users, he asks how many, how fast they grow, why growth isn't faster, and whether users love it. "Love" means they tell friends without prompting from the company.
- With no users, he works backwards from the perfect experience to find the smallest kernel to build first.
- Test consumer ideas by launching and seeing what happens (people say they'll use it but it won't cut through clutter). Test enterprise ideas by selling first: get a letter of intent from a customer before writing code. For biotech and hard tech, talk to customers and build the smallest subset of the technology.
- He asks how the company becomes a monopoly (Peter Thiel's term): businesses that get more powerful with scale and are hard to copy, without unethical behavior toward competitors.
- Market: how big now, how fast growing, why big in ten years. He likes technological shifts that most people haven't noticed yet. The best answer is "a large part of a small market."
- He prefers something new to something derivative. One acceptable definition of new is 10x better. It is easier to do something new and hard than derivative and easy, because people want to help and join the former.
- "The best ideas sound bad but are in fact good," so don't be too secretive. There are a thousand times more people with good ideas than people willing to do the work.
- Don't force an idea. A YC experiment funding promising teams with no ideas failed for all of them, because once you have a startup you rush to a plausible but derivative idea. Instead learn widely, notice inefficiencies and tech shifts, work on interesting projects, and hang around smart people.

chunks.heading: Founders, cofounders and equity
chunks.text:
- Mediocre teams do not build great companies. Top founder traits: unstoppability, determination, formidability, resourcefulness. Intelligence and passion rank highly. All matter more than experience or "expertise with language X and framework Y."
- The best founders are low-stress to work with because "he or she will get it done, no matter what it is." They are unusually responsive, a sign of decisiveness, focus and intensity.
- Founders who are hard to talk to are almost always bad. Communication is "the most important rarely-discussed founder skill."
- He wants rigidity on the company's core mission and flexibility on almost everything else.
- A tech startup needs one founder who can build and one who is good at sales and talking to users (can be the same person).
- Pick a cofounder you know well, not someone met at a "cofounder dating thing." Cofounder breakups are a leading cause of early startup death, and frequent when founders met to start the company. Existing relationships keep people going when expected value dips.
- Ranking: good cofounder, then solo founder, then (far worse) a bad cofounder. Part ways quickly if it isn't working.
- Set equity early; the conversation gets harder with time. Nearly equal is best. With two founders, one extra share for one person prevents deadlocks.

chunks.heading: Product: the only real secret
chunks.text:
- "Here is the secret to success: have a great product." Founders look for tricks, but "startups are the point in your life when tricks stop working." Eventually growth hacks stop working and growth comes from people wanting to use the product.
- Build a "product improvement engine": talk to users, watch them use the product, find sub-par parts, fix them, repeat. Improving 5% every week compounds. The faster the cycle, the better the company.
- During YC, founders should build product and talk to users, and little else besides eating, sleeping, exercising and time with loved ones.
- Get close to users: watch them, sit in their office, value both what they say and what they do. Put no one between founders and users; founders do sales and support.
- "Do things that don't scale": recruit users one at a time (Ben Silbermann approached strangers in Palo Alto coffee shops for Pinterest), build what they ask for. Big press announcements almost never work.
- Ship tiny and early: minimal surface area, small pieces, no big batched release, little long-range planning. Keep product and company simple.
- Diagnostic questions: Do users use it more than once? Are they fanatical? Would they be truly bummed if the company went away? Do they recommend it unprompted? For B2B, are there at least 10 paying customers? If not, the product isn't good enough. He is skeptical of most excuses for not growing.
- When unsure or in any internal disagreement, talk to users. Great founders care "a little bit too much" about quality, and "product" includes support and sales interactions.
- Better to have a small number of users who love it than many who like it: "it's much easier to get more users than to go from like to love."

chunks.heading: Growth and momentum
chunks.text:
- "Growth solves all problems, and lack of growth is not solvable by anything but growth." Growth keeps morale up and creates new roles; without it people fight over responsibility and leave. Prime directive: "Never lose momentum."
- Make growth the top priority and pick one metric the company optimizes: "The company does what the CEO measures." Examples: Airbnb's founders posted a forward-looking growth graph on the fridge, desks and bathroom mirror. Facebook created a prestigious growth group when growth slowed.
- Keep a list of what blocks growth. For each decision ask "Is this the best way to optimize growth?" (a conference usually isn't).
- Share metrics and financials internally; companies focused on metrics do better. Avoid vanity metrics: signups without retention. Retention matters as much as acquisition.
- Keep a "drumbeat" of features, customers, hires, revenue milestones and partnerships. Set aggressive but borderline achievable goals, review monthly, celebrate wins.
- Fast growth with everything broken is good: fix it and get more growth. Friendster is his one example of dying from technical debt. His favorite investments are fast-growing but un-optimized companies.
- Only think about 10x your current scale; figure out massive scale when you get there. Early great customer service creates passionate users and shows what to fix. Bad unit economics early are OK only with a real reason they'll work out later.
- Remind the team that humans are bad at exponential intuition, and every giant company started small.
- Growth traps that "effectively never work": deals with other companies and the big press launch. Instead build a loved product, recruit users manually, test many channels (ads, referral programs, sales and marketing) and do more of what works. Ask customers where to find more people like them.
- Sales and marketing "are not bad words." At least one founder must get good at asking people to use the product and pay. For B2B, track monthly revenue growth; early months look ugly because of long sales cycles (selling to startups first can help). He recommends Alex Schultz's consumer growth lecture.

chunks.heading: Making money, pricing and unit economics
chunks.text:
- Get people to pay more than it costs to deliver; "people always forget" the delivery cost.
- Free product: don't plan to grow by buying users (very hard for ad-supported). Make something people share.
- Paid product with LTV under $500: you generally can't afford sales. Test SEO/SEM, ads, mailings, and try to repay CAC in 3 months.
- Paid product with LTV over $500 (net to you): you can generally afford direct sales. Sell it yourself first to learn what works; he recommends the book Hacking Sales.
- Reach "ramen profitability" fast, so you control your destiny and aren't at investors' whims. Watch cash flow obsessively; founders have run out of money without noticing.

chunks.heading: Focus, intensity and what the CEO does
chunks.text:
- Two words: focus and intensity. Best founders say no a lot and don't start the next thing until they've dominated the first. "You can do far fewer things than you think." Doing too many wrong things is a common cause of death.
- His own routine: a daily pen-and-paper list with about 3 major and 30 minor tasks, plus an annual list of goals.
- Great founders are decisive: listen to all advice, then decide fast. Use Paul Buchheit's rule: 90% of the value for 10% of the effort. "The market doesn't care how hard you work—it only cares if you do the right things."
- "I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful." Obsessing over quality while moving fast is a tell of a great founder. Don't believe you're exempt; rocket and nuclear companies still move fast.
- Early success: skip networking events, panels, publicists and "personal brand." Press eventually finds who is winning.
- CEO jobs: set vision and strategy; evangelize the company; hire and manage, especially where you have gaps; raise money; set the execution quality bar. Also stay engaged in the part you love.
- It's intense and not balanced: you can have one other big thing (family, triathlons). Be responsive, decide quickly on things that block others, do unpleasant schleps. Still eat, sleep and exercise; this takes years.
- No excuses ("if only we had more money"); feel upset for a minute, then solve it. Distort reality for others but not yourself: be persuasive outwardly and paranoid inwardly. Be persistent and optimistic. Find CEO peers and a mentor (books work less well).
- Write mission and values down early; he praises Airbnb's cultural values. Don't innovate in HR, marketing, sales, financing or PR; do what works there and spend creativity on the product. Don't hire an "experienced manager" to do the work; it's "a graveyard for failed companies."

chunks.heading: Hiring, managing and competitors
chunks.text:
- First advice: don't hire. Employees are expensive, add communication overhead and inertia, and change the things you can say. Don't derive self-worth from headcount. The best people want rocketships, so you can hire them once you're winning.
- Be generous with equity, trust and responsibility, and go after people you think you can't get.
- After product-market fit, spend about 25% of time recruiting; the CEO's top activity by time.
- Never compromise on quality, even when desperate; mediocre early hires rarely recover. "If you have doubt, then the answer is no." Skip chronically negative people. Value aptitude over experience; try a project together before hiring full-time.
- Managing: avoid "hero mode" (doing everything yourself); accept late projects to keep a functioning team. Keep everyone in one office. Fire quickly, and fire toxic people however good: "Culture is defined by who you hire, fire, and promote."
- Competitors are "a startup ghost story": "99% of startups die from suicide, not murder." Ignore them 99% of the time, especially when they raise money or get press, until they beat you with a real shipped product. He quotes Henry Ford on fearing the competitor "who never bothers about you at all."

chunks.heading: Fundraising
chunks.text:
- Raise when you need it or when it's available on good terms. Stay frugal: "having too much money is almost always bad."
- The secret is a good company; optimizing the process matters about 5% of the time. Investors want companies that will succeed regardless but grow faster with capital, and returns come from big wins. Always explain why you could be huge.
- Don't raise before you're in shape; it burns reputation. "Believe the no but not the reason," and anything but "yes" is a "no."
- Run conversations in parallel; investor fear of losing the deal drives action. One founder fundraises. Metrics convince most.
- Insist on clean terms; don't over-optimize valuation. The first check is hardest, so focus on whoever loves you most. Always have a plan that includes raising nothing.
- Pitch minimum: mission, problem, product/service, business model, team, market and growth rate, financials. Each round's bar is higher.
- Small-check investors usually don't help (beware party rounds). A great, involved board member is worth a lower valuation. He recommends Paul Graham's fundraising essay.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues that Silicon Valley startups set weekly growth goals before knowing what they're building. Founders should first figure out what they're doing, build something some users love enough to spontaneously recommend, and only then focus on growth above all else.

chunks.heading: Sam's initial metric: "do any users love our product so much they spontaneously tell other people to use it?"
chunks.text:
- Sam says the "current fashion of Silicon Valley startups" is an unhealthy extreme: a weekly growth goal set before founders have any strong idea of what they want to build.
- His proposed first metric is a binary question: "do any users love our product so much they spontaneously tell other people to use it?"
- Until the answer is "yes", he argues founders are generally better off focusing on this instead of a growth target.
- The very best technology companies sometimes take a while to figure out what they are doing. When they do, they usually pass this binary test before turning all their energy to growth.
- He calls it "the critical ingredient for companies that do really well."

chunks.heading: The right order of operations for an early startup
chunks.text:
Sam's sequence for a startup's first stretch:

1. In the first few weeks, figure out what you are doing and why.
2. Build a product some users really love.
3. Only after that, focus on growth above all else.

- He still holds that startups need to grow quickly. He calls that "true, and very good advice."
- His point is about timing. Growth comes after the product is loved, not before.

chunks.heading: Why premature growth targets backfire
chunks.text:
- A startup that targets a growth goal too early often ends up with a nebulous product that some users "sort of like."
- Founders then paper over that weakness with "growth hacking."
- This sort of works. It can fool investors for a while, until they start digging into retention numbers.
- Then "the music stops."
- His conclusion: if you don't first build something users love, "no amount of growth hacking will make you into a great company."
- Retention is where the weakness shows up. Growth numbers that hide poor retention won't hold up under investor scrutiny.

chunks.heading: Product love and sense of mission
chunks.text:
- Sam notes that startups that skip the step of building a product some users love "also seem to rarely develop the sense of mission that the best companies have."
- By implication, the discovery of what users love is tied to a company's sense of purpose, not only to its growth.

chunks.heading: Monopoly as the second early ingredient
chunks.text:
- In a footnote, Sam says the best companies have a second thing that "also usually gets figured out early": "some sort of a monopoly."
- Together, the two early ingredients are a product some users love and some form of monopoly.
- He gives no detail in this essay on what form the monopoly takes.

chunks.heading: Context
chunks.text:
- The essay first appeared on Sam's blog in 2016. It was republished by The Founders' Tribune on June 29, 2025.
- Sam was then president of Y Combinator, a role the republished byline calls "former CEO of Y Combinator."
- Y Combinator's standard advice to startups is that they have to grow quickly. The essay is a correction to how founders apply that advice.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Altman argues that falling costs, short cycle times and AI agents make this the best moment ever to found a company. He advises holding contrarian conviction for years, finding a few believers, helping many people early, and ignoring cynics while building. He also covers AI safety and power concentration.

chunks.heading: Why this is the best time to do a startup
chunks.text:
Sam argues startups win when the technology landscape moves fast, costs fall, cycle times shorten and incumbents lose their edge. He says all of these are true now.

- He compares past startup clusters: the internet boom (late 1990s), Facebook apps, and the iPhone App Store launch. In each, "the great startups tend to cluster when the ecosystem shifts and incumbents lose a lot of their advantage."
- In 2005, in YC's first batch, a company's whole three months of building "could now be done... in like seven minutes by a coding agent."
- He rejects the "permanent underclass" meme (join a frontier lab or lose). He bets "the startups created today will be much more valuable, much more impactful than startups of the past" and "there's some future trillionaire sitting in this room."
- He says the founder mood at YC moved from anxiety ("the models are just gonna eat everything") back to "let's go do it."
- Advice: don't be sad that a prompt can build an old startup. Take on a far more ambitious company with "experts in every field working together." The bar is now "three months of work in three months," at the new level of what that means.
- On pace, he expects the next six months to feel like roughly the last two years of model progress, and hopes "never a better time to do a startup" can be said every year.

chunks.heading: Credentials, experience and what founders need now
chunks.text:
- Expertise and the ability to hire specialists used to be scarce. Sam says that has "really shifted."
- He has seen people who grew up using AI plan to "automate an entire startup of agents and four of us" with a lot of compute, and expects more of this.
- What still matters: "taste and agency and understanding of kind of like the physics of business." That means where valuable businesses get built, and telling a good network effect or moat from a fake one.
- His bet is that this "generally will cut against many years of experience in favor of people who have a lot of fluency with the tools."

chunks.heading: Conviction, contrarian ideas and finding your people
chunks.text:
- His "highest order" advice: find things you can develop reasonable conviction in where conventional wisdom is wrong, and accept that it takes a long time and people stay "very frustratingly wrong and dismissive."
- At OpenAI, "it felt like we knew the biggest secret in the world. Everybody was calling us an idiot." About 10 years ago critics said the team would cause another AI winter.
- He calls that a gift: no massive competitors, and time to do research and build the company.
- He has seen this pattern in many companies. They do something experts think is a bad idea. Starting the same startup as everyone else brings hype and easy fundraising, but "much less frequently the big outcomes."
- Joke: only 50 people in the world believed AGI was possible, "but it was okay because 45 of them worked at OpenAI." Saying the heretical thing is partly why those people wanted to be together.
- Test: if you can't find anyone who shares your belief, pay attention to that. If everybody believes it, that is also a bad sign. Doing a startup alone is "very lonely."
- Plan: work out what you believe, be willing to be misunderstood for a long time, and gather "the crew of misfits that believes it."

chunks.heading: Networks, co-founders and being helpful
chunks.text:
- Five to ten years ago, the limit on good YC startups was co-founder matching: talented people who "couldn't find their tribe."
- He still thinks moving to the Bay Area is probably right for meeting co-founders, though he has less intuition now. He says the premium on doing YC is bigger than ever and the gap to second place has widened, "a reminder of the power of network effects."
- Join networks early: "It takes a long time to compound." He met his OpenAI co-founders years, sometimes many years, before starting it.
- His "highest confidence piece of advice": "find a way to be like mildly helpful to a lot of people." Do it for its own sake.
- Example: as a roughly 22-year-old early Stripe investor, he drove to Palo Alto for dinner to help persuade Greg Brockman to drop out and join Stripe as the first hire. Eight years later they started OpenAI together.

chunks.heading: Resisting cynicism and ignoring attackers
chunks.text:
- Running YC meant constant Twitter haters. He says he "took the bait a lot."
- His view: building something of value is very hard, while sarcastic shots earn likes and "will poison your soul."
- Advice: "put all of your energy into building stuff and... resist the easy shots." Don't mock people trying hard things.
- He says if you do anything that matters, people will call you an idiot or dismiss you. The better you do, the more they attack.
- Earnestness is a value. Over a decade, none of the trolls got him.

chunks.heading: Vision clear, first steps unclear
chunks.text:
- Many of the best ideas have a clear vision but unclear first steps. OpenAI wanted to build AGI but did not know it would become a product company.
- It was "years till we came up with the idea of ChatGPT and the API." It began as a nonprofit research lab. Don't lean out because the first steps are murky.
- The opposite failure: a brilliant big idea with no forward progress. You have to take imperfect steps to "get some new data points."
- For YC, Sam says he pushed founders toward more ambition and bigger swings, and toward more leverage for founders relative to investors.
- PG's model of the investor as a "flight instructor" who sits next to you and corrects specific mistakes, not a lecturer. Sam says that hands-on direction mattered to him.

chunks.heading: Compute, inference demand and concentration of power
chunks.text:
- Demand: he guesses worldwide inference demand "grows 10x a year for the next many years." He expects never to be out of the compute shortage, and sees demand for high-quality, cheap intelligence as effectively uncapped.
- Token stat: six and a half years ago the top token user at OpenAI used about 100,000 tokens a month. Today the worldwide average is about 100,000, and the top OpenAI user is in the hundreds of billions. Extrapolating, the average person would use about 500 billion a month in six and a half more years. He adds that tokens are "the dumbest metric."
- Power: concentration has been bad in every period of history. He doesn't want the world "locked into one model's or one person's or one company's moral worldview."
- Startups help by spreading economic power across many companies and models. He says a successful startup alone is a contribution to this.
- Long-term goal: each year people should have more freedom and agency over their time.
- A dystopia he fears: overreacting on AI safety into a surveillance state with abundance but no privacy or agency.
- He calls a recent AI safety incident "the real deal," an alignment and security failure, though not a major loss-of-control event.
- Advice to his younger self: "it's all gonna work out." Keep the drive, be happier along the way, and know the tech industry forgives failure.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Sam Altman tells Garry Tan how OpenAI began with a narrow bet on deep learning and scaling, why extreme conviction must be paired with truth-seeking, and why this is the best time yet to start a company. His startup advice: bet on the AI trend, move at the speed of the technology, and still build a real business.

chunks.heading: Why this is the best time to start a tech company
chunks.text:
- Sam calls it "the best time yet" to start a tech company. Each major technological revolution lets people do more than the last one.
- He argues big companies have the edge when things move slowly. Upstarts get their edge during platform shifts: the semiconductor revolution, the internet, mobile, and now AI. He notes it has been a while since the last one.
- He says "the world is still sleeping on all of this to such an astonishing degree."
- Platform shifts are usually built by young people with no prior knowledge. He points to Facebook almost missing mobile because it was good at web software, then having to buy Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Abundant intelligence and abundant energy are, in his view, the two key inputs to everything else. His essay predicts superintelligence may be "a few thousand days" away.

chunks.heading: Startup advice: bet on the AI trend and use speed as the edge
chunks.text:
- His advice to founders starting now is to bet on this trend. He says "we are not near the saturation point" and the models will get much better, quickly.
- What a founder can do with AI versus without it is "wildly different."
- Big companies, mid-sized companies, and even startups a few years old run on quarterly planning cycles. He says a startup's edge is "speed and focus and conviction and the ability to react to how fast the technology is moving." He calls this "the number one edge of a startup kind of ever, but especially right now."
- He recommends building something with AI, and acting when you see something new: "build something that day rather than put it into a quarterly planning cycle."
- He expects billion-dollar-a-year companies with fewer than 100 employees, maybe 20, maybe one. His shorthand is "one person plus 10,000 GPUs."

chunks.heading: The rules of business still apply, even with AI
chunks.text:
- Sam warns against thinking "because I'm doing something with AI, the laws of business don't apply to me." He says you still have to build a moat, a competitive edge, and a better product.
- Embracing a new technology faster than others can produce "short-term explosions of growth." That is not the same as a durable business.
- "Everyone can build an absolutely incredible demo right now." He says "building a business, man, that's the brass ring."
- His summary is that you can build faster and better than ever, but "you still have to build a business."

chunks.heading: Picking one bet and concentrating
chunks.text:
- OpenAI was far less resourced than DeepMind and others. His reasoning: "they're going to try a lot of things and we've just got to pick one and really concentrate, and that's how we can win."
- The two core beliefs were that deep learning works and that it gets better with scale. Both were heretical at the time.
- Other efforts were "trying to outsmart themselves in too many ways." OpenAI did the thing in front of it and kept pushing.
- The norm was to spread resources across many bets. He says "most of the world still does not understand the value of a fairly extreme level of conviction on one bet."
- On scale: "when in doubt, if you have something that seems like it's getting better with scale, I think you should scale it up." He adds that "more is more."
- An early whiteboard listed three goals: figure out unsupervised learning, solve RL, and never get more than 120 people. He says they missed on the third.

chunks.heading: Conviction, pushback, and staying truth-seeking
chunks.text:
- When the world pushes back and the pushback doesn't make sense to you, "you should do it anyway." Eminent field leaders told the OpenAI team they were wrong and that believing this was a bad thing.
- He says there are no "adults in the room" with all the answers. You can "just do stuff" and iterate quickly.
- Conviction has to be paired with honesty about evidence. "Conviction is great until the moment you have data one way or the other." Many people hold on past the moment of data.
- OpenAI was high conviction and wrong many times, and tried to embrace it fully once it saw the data. He lists "the ability to get punched in the face and get back up and keep going" as one of its strengths.
- There is a long stretch where you must operate without data and "run on conviction." You still have to show your work.
- He admits the story was not a short path. They started with robots, agents, and video games before language models. He says "if we knew then what we know now, we could have speedrun this."

chunks.heading: Recruiting and launching a team around an audacious mission
chunks.text:
- Sam says OpenAI said from the start it would go after AGI, at a time "you weren't allowed to say that." The statement got the attention of the best young people and drew derision from mediocre older ones, which he took as a good sign.
- Recruiting was one-on-one. He saw a video of Ilya and wanted to meet him. When Ilya didn't respond to his email, he went to a conference where Ilya was speaking. He already knew Greg Brockman from the early Stripe days. It took about nine months to come together.
- OpenAI announced in December 2015 and started in January 2016. At the first meeting in Greg's apartment, with about 10 people, the question was "so what do we do now?" He compares it to founders who raise a round and realize "it's not time for popping champagne. That was actually the starting gun."
- He says the original ideas were "incredibly right" even after many detours.
- On peers, he says "no one is immune to peer pressure, so all you can do is pick good peers." He advises young people to find an inspiring peer group as early as they can. At Stanford, peers competed over investment-bank internships, and the YC culture changed that for him.

chunks.heading: Product-market fit: how GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 landed
chunks.text:
- With GPT-3, founders said it was an incredible demo, but "with the possible exception of Copilot, no great businesses were built on GPT-3."
- With 3.5, YC startups began doing interesting things, and it "no longer felt like we were pushing a boulder uphill."
- With GPT-4, people asked how many GPUs they could get, very quickly after getting access.
- He cites Jake Heller of CaseText, who sold the company for $650 million after chopping prompts into small workflows on GPT-4.
- His caution: "you never really know if you have a hit product on your hands until you put it in customer hands." Teams are always too impressed with their own work, and users are the real test.

chunks.heading: Scaling a company fast and aligning everyone on a few things
chunks.text:
- Sam says OpenAI has "speedrun" a company arc that normally takes a decade, and ChatGPT is under two years old. The cost is a lot of painful change.
- Management teams turn over as a company scales, because people who are good at zero to one are not necessarily good at 1 to 10 or 10 to 100.
- He says this is the first time OpenAI feels it knows what to do. Research and infrastructure paths are fairly clear, and the product path is getting clearer.
- He says "the degree to which you can get everybody aligned and pointed at the same thing is a significant determinant in how fast you can move." For a long time OpenAI was a pure research lab and found it hard to act on conviction with so many good options.
- On his first startup, Loopt, he says it never found product market fit or escape velocity. Even so, he says nothing has a higher rate of generalized learning than doing a startup, and he calls his 20s an "apprenticeship."
- Loopt gave him firsthand experience of a platform shift and how messy the beginning is.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In his second conversation with Tyler Cowen (Oct 2025), Altman explains how he stays productive through delegation, how he screens hires for AI-readiness, and why ChatGPT's trust shapes how OpenAI handles ads and commerce. He also argues margins will fall across the economy and energy is the binding constraint on compute.

chunks.heading: Running a company at OpenAI's pace: delegation, simplification and hiring
chunks.text:
- Sam says he has no single productivity trick. His view: "people almost never allocate their time as well as they think they do."
- As demands grew, he hired and promoted strong people and delegates heavily. He calls this "the only sustainable way I know how to do it."
- He keeps his own focus on understanding "the core thing for us to do," which has become clearer and simpler as OpenAI's needs (such as infrastructure buildout) came into focus.
- More of the world now wants to work with OpenAI, so deals are quicker to negotiate.
- He deliberately avoids work he doesn't want to do. He used to spend a lot of time on product thinking, but now says OpenAI has "the world expert thinking about our product strategy" (a person he says is much better at it than him), so he lets her run it.
- Hardware hiring: cycle times are longer and capital is more intense, so mistakes cost more. He spends more time getting to know hardware people before trusting them to run. The rest is the same: find good, fast-moving people, get clear on the goal, and let them go.
- He says OpenAI's chip team "feels more like the OpenAI research team than a chip company." He admits it carries risk but thinks it could "work out phenomenally well."
- Hiring for AI-readiness: he asks how candidates use AI today. Using it only for "better Google search" is a yellow flag. People seriously thinking about what their day-to-day will look like in three years are a green flag.

chunks.heading: An AI-run company and the replacement for Slack and email
chunks.text:
- Sam thinks email is "very bad" and Slack is only better than email. He dreads the first and last hour of his day dealing with Slack, and says it "creates a lot of fake work."
- He expects a new AI-driven replacement for the whole office suite (docs, slides, email, Slack). It would not be AI bolted onto existing tools, but "you are trusting your AI agent and my AI agent to work most stuff out and escalate to us when necessary."
- OpenAI is "very far" from using this internally. He says that is because they haven't tried, not because the models are far away. Teams get stuck in their ways, and with things going well there is "a lot of activation energy for a big new thing."
- He uses an "AI CEO" thought experiment: "shame on me if OpenAI is not the first big company run by an AI CEO." He asks what would have to happen for an AI to run OpenAI better than him, and uses the answer to decide how to design the org and spot roadblocks.
- Forecast: an AI-run division (not a tiny one) is "some small single-digit number of years" away. He agrees with Tyler that billion-dollar companies run by two or three people with AIs are coming.
- He expects AI can make most decisions before people are comfortable with it, since people trust other people over AI "even if that's irrational."
- He thinks the broader shift is good for society.

chunks.heading: Monetizing ChatGPT: trust, commerce, ads and margins
chunks.text:
- Sam's key insight: ChatGPT is consistently reported as users' most trusted technology product from a big tech company. His explanation is that Google ads depend on search doing badly, while ChatGPT is paid by users and tries to give the best answer.
- Rule: if ChatGPT took payment to rank a worse hotel above a better one, it would be "catastrophic for your relationship with ChatGPT."
- Acceptable model: ChatGPT picks the best option with nothing influencing it, and takes the same transaction fee on a one-click booking as it would from any other seller. He says OpenAI's recent commerce work follows this spirit and that travel is coming at some point.
- Margins: he believes margins will fall dramatically on most goods and services, including hotel bookings. He's happy about it and thinks companies like OpenAI will make more money at lower margins.
- He says the way to monetize the smartest model is not hotel booking. The big money is in discovering new science and monetizing what only the smartest model can do.
- His stated strategy: put superintelligence in everyone's hands, make it easy to use, integrate it, build beautiful devices, connect it to your services, and invest in chips, energy and infrastructure to make it abundant and cheap. Then people figure out how to make the world better.
- He accepts OpenAI doing things that aren't "the economic-maxing thing" because they matter for the world.
- On ads: there is a kind that would be very bad (the paid-ranking kind) and kinds that would be good or pretty good. He expects OpenAI to try something at some point but doesn't think ads are the biggest revenue opportunity.
- On Walmart: when asked if Amazon would join a ChatGPT-Walmart shopping arrangement, he says if he were Amazon he would fight back.
- The best argument against a bubble, in his view: nobody knows how far past human-level intelligence goes, and people should discuss the economic impact of vastly superhuman intelligence much more.

chunks.heading: Energy, chips and compute as the binding constraints
chunks.text:
- Sam's answer to why we don't just make more GPUs: "Because we need to make more electrons." If he could have one thing for more compute, it would be electrons.
- Short term, natural gas eases the constraint. Long term, he believes energy will be dominated by fusion and solar.
- On nuclear stigma: he thinks there's a price point where demand becomes overwhelming. At natural-gas prices adoption may be hard; at one-tenth the price "it would happen very fast."
- Chip-building has "no easy part." He points to an under-discussed recursive loop in hardware: robots that build robots, data centers that build data centers, and chips that design their own next generation.
- On whether cheaper intelligence reduces demand for compute: people always want more compute if it's cheaper, so he'll "take that bet every day."
- His related worry is a phase shift in how compute works (for example, full optical compute) that makes today's paradigm a dead end. The energy investment would still hold, but "everything else" would need redoing.

chunks.heading: GPT-6 and AI doing science
chunks.text:
- Sam frames the progression: GPT-3 was the first glimmer of passing the "spiritual Turing test," and GPT-5 is the first glimmer of AI doing new science, in tiny ways (a new idea, a useful collaborator on a paper).
- He says GPT-6 may be a GPT-3-to-4-style leap for science: "5 has these tiny glimmers and 6 can really do it."
- His advice for a lab: the first step is to type in the research questions you're struggling with and see what experiments or ideas come back. Labs will not get GPT-6 this year.
- He doesn't think GPT-6 will have the "intangibles" of deep cultural and local knowledge (for example, when dealing with Saudi Arabia or the UAE). OpenAI brings in human experts and the US government for that, and he says OpenAI has an internal evaluation for something close to it.
- On poetry: he expects AI to reach a technically perfect "10," but argues "you won't care." As with chess, people care about the human who made it. Even if AI can't write a 10, it may only need to be able to recognize one.

chunks.heading: What AI will do to jobs, education and prices
chunks.text:
- Sam expects the way he works (emails, calls, meetings, documents, Slack) to change hugely. Family, nature, food and friends will barely change.
- He cites programmers as the starkest example of 2025: the typical workflow at the end of the year looked very different from the start, and the world will get much more software. He expects similar shifts across many industries.
- Returns to a college degree: he guesses they decline slightly faster than over the last decade but won't collapse as fast as they should.
- He thinks the returns to using AI well will be widely distributed, not captured by a small group of AI specialists.
- On teaching normies to use AI, he is relaxed. ChatGPT grew fast because it is so easy to learn, and you can ask it to teach you how to use it. He says about 10% of the world used ChatGPT that week and he guesses 30% a year later, and he trusts human adoption over a few years.
- On universities, the ideal partnership is to "run 20 wildly different experiments." He wouldn't be upset if faculty and students just adopt AI privately.
- Prices: food should fall (he'd be disappointed if not down in a decade) and healthcare should get cheaper through cures, cheap treatments, devices and delivery. Housing is the hard one he doesn't see AI attacking directly soon.
- Books will survive but become a smaller share of how people learn.
- His St. Louis plan with a billion dollars: start a Y Combinator-like program there and get AI-focused founders to move and build companies. He calls it unique to him.

chunks.heading: Freedom of expression, privacy and persuasion risk
chunks.text:
- Principle: "treat our adult users like adults," with very broad bounds on use and a high degree of privacy. The asterisk is adults "of sound mind."
- OpenAI restricted ChatGPT heavily over the summer to protect teens and to address mental health problems (such as encouraging delusion in role-play). With age-gating and mitigations in place, it will bring back and in some cases increase freedom for adults, including creative and role-playing modes.
- He was surprised by the backlash to his tweet on this, and concluded "people don't believe in freedom of expression as much as they say they do."
- Privacy: he wants AI conversations protected like those with a human doctor or lawyer. This needs legal change, which does not exist today. By revealed preference, he says people already trust AI companies this much.
- Chatbot psychosis is "a very tiny thing, but not a zero thing."
- His bigger worry is a third AI-safety category beside misuse and intentional takeover: AI models accidentally taking over. With the whole world talking to one model that keeps learning from the world, it could subtly convince people of things with no intent. He quotes a line he remembers: never believe propaganda doesn't work on you, "they just haven't found the right thing for you yet."
- On rogue agents, he says it's a question of thresholds. Most systems need no oversight, but an agent likely to self-replicate and sweep bank accounts would. He thinks the right move is to urgently solve the problem for rogue internet resources generally, since AI makes it worse.

chunks.heading: Government's role and OpenAI's posture
chunks.text:
- Sam thinks that when something gets big enough, the federal government is the insurer of last resort, and he expects that for AI. He does not want it as insurer of first resort and doesn't expect that.
- He puts a significant probability on the social contract changing significantly in the post-AGI world, and sees the government getting more involved and having opinions about AI companies. But he puts almost no probability on a world where people lose all meaning because AI does everything.
- OpenAI's approach: "We just try to work with capitalism as it currently exists," partner with the government and be a good collaborator, but not have it write OpenAI's insurance policies.
- For data centers abroad, the key questions are who operates them, what workload and model weights go there, and what the security guarantees are. He compares the build to a US embassy or military base.
- He is also working on a new kind of computer and interface built for AI, with Jony Ive, whom he calls maybe the best bet to pull it off. He says the track record of such attempts is bad.
- ChatGPT is a "single-player" experience, so he doesn't think sharing queries is the social product. A new kind of social product probably exists once everyone has personal agents. AI-generated video (Sora) is doing well for both making and watching.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A list of career principles from Sam Altman after running Y Combinator. He stresses picking important work, scaling more than you expect, using power laws and compounding, moving fast, and executing with determination. It also covers team, meeting and goal-setting habits.

chunks.heading: Sam's career principles: what to work on and how to think about success
chunks.text:
- Sam says the most successful people, "judged by history, not money", keep looking for the most important thing they can work on, and then do it. They avoid local maxima and don't deceive themselves when they find something more important.
- They stay on it for a long time even if others don't get it. "'Important' does not mean 'popular.'"
- He advises finding "the thing that only you can do": something no one else can do, or hasn't thought of, in a way that is hard to copy. Being just like everyone else gets you "ok but certainly not great."
- Follow your own curiosity and look internally rather than externally for answers. Be honest about the intersection of your skills, your passions and what the world values.
